detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 67.54 MB PSI-117Version 2 Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis Investigation Submitted Date: 18-Sep-2024 Initial Release Date: 10-Jun-2026 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/gz0q-b577 Research Area: Combustion Science SubResearch Area: Droplet Related Investigation: PSI-69, PSI-142 License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Ground Investigation Proposal Title Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis Investigation Start Date 02-15-2017 Investigation End Date 02-14-2022 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), PSI grant NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives The objective of this ground investigation was to use flight data obtained from PSI through NASA’s Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) to quantify how externally imposed thermal and convective perturbations regulated the dynamics and ultimate fate of already established droplet cool flames, and to explain run-to-run variability by isolating the roles of deliberate heating and unintentional drift-induced convection. Focusing on both small and large droplets, the work mapped stability windows for ignition, sustained oscillation, transitions to hot ignition and warm-flame behavior, and extinction under microgravity. By leveraging and extending the FLEX data in the PSI, this study produced reusable models and sensitivity analyses that coupled low-temperature chemistry with transport and radiative effects. Approach OpenFOAM was used to develop a 3-D CFD model of n-alkane droplet cool flames in microgravity, coupling variable-density Navier–Stokes flow with low-temperature combustion chemistry, coupled heat and mass transfer, and radiation. Model fidelity was established against ISS FLEX measurements, after which controlled simulations examined three forcing modes (i) convection alone to mimic droplet drift, (ii) imposed heat flux, and (iii) combined convection plus heating applied to both large (1–4 mm) and sub-millimeter (~0.5 mm) droplets. To accelerate progress, the study began with simplified chemistry and transitioned to reduced mechanisms for parameter sweeps over forcing amplitude and frequency, ambient composition (including ozone-assisted cases), and pressure. From each case, predictive observables were extracted (ignition delay, oscillation frequency and amplitude, stand-off and extinction diameters), and were used to construct stability maps that delineated conditions for cool-flame onset, persistence, and quenching. These maps were reconciled with FLEX observations and were used to guide next-generation test matrices for both large- and small-droplet experiments. Hypothesis External thermo-convective perturbations (imposed temperature gradients, non-uniform heating, oscillatory/shear inflow) were expected to govern cool-flame ignition, oscillation, transition to hot ignition, and extinction by shifting residence time and scalar dissipation. In microgravity, where buoyancy was suppressed, this forcing was anticipated to dominate transport. A multidimensional, multi-physics CFD model was used to map perturbation-dependent stability boundaries and predict observables for comparison with FLEX data. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits Space Benefits: Potential to improve spacecraft fire-safety modeling by resolving cool-flame/extinction behavior in microgravity; leverages FLEX to define safer operating envelopes/materials. Earth Benefits: Advances low-temperature combustion understanding relevant to engine knock, efficiency, and emissions; delivers validated CFD tools transferrable to practical combustors. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 3.77 GB PSI-137Version 1 Phase Transitions in Colloid-Polymer Mixtures in Microgravity Investigation Submitted Date: 03-Nov-2023 Initial Release Date: 12-May-2026 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/gkmk-v597 Research Area: Complex Fluids - Soft Matter SubResearch Area: Colloids Related Investigation: PSI-27, PSI-28, PSI-29, PSI-30 License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Ground Investigation Proposal Title Phase Transitions in Colloid-Polymer Mixtures in Microgravity Investigation Start Date 12-05-2019 Investigation End Date 11-03-2023 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), PSI grant NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives The objective of this PSI grant was to advance the understanding of phase transitions in colloid–polymer mixtures under microgravity conditions by integrating experimental observations with predictive modeling. Specifically, the research sought to determine how depletion interactions, arising from non-adsorbing polymers, influence the kinetics and morphology of phase separation and crystallization in complex fluids. By analyzing image data from NASA’s Binary Colloidal Alloy Test (BCAT-3 through BCAT-6) experiments conducted on the International Space Station, the project aimed to isolate the effects of gravity on phase behavior, quantify domain growth over multiple orders of magnitude in time and length scale, and develop a theoretical framework that connects these dynamics to hydrodynamic and thermodynamic parameters. Ultimately, this work sought to establish colloidal systems as model analogues for atomic and molecular phase transitions, providing insight relevant to both fundamental soft-matter physics and applied materials design. Approach The approach combined data-driven analysis of PSI-archived BCAT imagery with a phase-field modeling framework that coupled the Cahn–Hilliard and Stokes equations to simulate phase separation in colloid–polymer mixtures. Experimental image sequences were processed for BCAT-3, -4 and -5, using algorithms in ImageJ and MATLAB to remove background noise, enhance contrast, and compute spatial autocorrelation functions for extracting characteristic domain length scales. Theoretical modeling of BCAT-5 incorporated concentration-dependent mobility and viscosity, along with Korteweg stresses to represent interfacial tension effects, allowing for the inclusion of hydrodynamic interactions that influenced domain coarsening. The governing equations were solved using a pseudospectral semi-implicit numerical scheme, and simulation results were quantitatively compared to flight data from the BCAT experiments. Model parameters were tuned using physical data from PSI to validate predictions and refine understanding of hydrodynamic coupling, phase-domain morphology, and kinetic arrest in colloid–polymer systems. This integrated experimental–theoretical approach yielded a comprehensive, microgravity-validated description of soft-matter phase transformation mechanisms. Hypothesis Introducing non-adsorbing polymers into colloidal suspensions generates depletion-induced attractions that alter phase-transition kinetics; in microgravity, free from sedimentation and convection, these interactions can be directly modeled to reveal the intrinsic role of hydrodynamics in phase separation. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits This research provided benchmark insight into soft-matter phase transitions without gravitational interference, improving predictive capability for self-assembly, crystallization, and gelation relevant to materials manufacturing and fluids research aboard the ISS. It has also improved understanding of phase-transition kinetics and rheology in colloid–polymer mixtures, informing materials science, pharmaceutical, and chemical engineering applications, and advancing the design of next-generation coatings, gels, and nanostructured materials. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 8.19 GB PSI-174Version 1 Micromechanics Based Modeling of Cement Solidified in the Microgravity Investigation Submitted Date: 31-Jan-2025 Initial Release Date: 11-May-2026 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/h3jk-9m26 Research Area: Materials Science SubResearch Area: Cement hydration License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Ground Investigation Proposal Title Micromechanics-based Modeling of Cement Solidified in the Microgravity Investigation Start Date 11-01-2021 Investigation End Date 06-30-2024 Sponsoring Agency NASA, PSI grant NASA Center Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) Objectives Micromechanics‑Based Modeling of Cement Solidified in the Microgravity aimed to advance knowledge of the mechanical properties of cement binders formed in reduced gravity by leveraging microgravity materials data, such as SEM/BSE micrographs, available in the PSI database. This project sought to connect microstructure (e.g., porosity, phase morphology such as portlandite) observed in ISS‑cured tricalcium silicate (C3S) pastes to bulk mechanical/transport behavior through modeling, thereby informing design and engineering of cementitious materials for extraterrestrial construction and providing validated simulation data that scale sparse flight samples to application‑relevant sizes. Approach In this work, the micromechanics analysis code with generalized method of cells (MAC/GMC) was used to predict the structure-property relationship of these unique cement samples. First, the sparse data of cement hydrated in microgravity environment was converted to high-fidelity 3D microstructure with the aid of a deep learning-based microstructure methodology. The reconstructed sub-volumes were compared against micro-CT data using statistical descriptors. Second, the sub-volumes (partitioned based on individual constituents) of such reconstructed 3D structures were fed into the NASA Multiscale Analysis Tool (NASMAT) to obtain homogenized properties of the cement. A semi-automated Python script was developed to complete the workflow. Owing to the high computational demand, the analyses were carried out in NASA Advanced Supercomputing (NAS) servers. Phase‑discerned ISS and ground BSE/SEM images were segmented and reconstructed into 3D volumes using a deep learning microstructure framework; these Representative Volume Elements (RVEs) were then analyzed with NASA’s Multiscale Analysis Tool (NASMAT) to homogenize and predict effective properties. Reconstruction quality was validated against statistical descriptors and micro‑CT data, and the modeling spans length‑scale partitioning to capture porous, multiphase behavior. The experimental basis originated from the MICS investigation (PSI‑84 in the database), which conducted controlled ISS/ground hydration in sealed Burst Pouches, keeping temperature/pressure/humidity constant so gravity is the sole variable, followed by porosimetry, TGA, XRD, EDS/EMPA, and image analysis to quantify phase fractions and pore structures that feed the modeling pipeline. Hypothesis Consistent with the microgravity MICS investigation, the central hypothesis was that minimizing gravity‑driven transport (buoyancy, sedimentation, convection) yields a diffusion‑controlled hydration process in microgravity, producing more uniform phase distributions and distinct microstructures (e.g., higher porosity, altered portlandite morphology) relative to 1g; these differences are expected to translate into measurably different mechanical properties for µg‑hardened cement paste versus terrestrial cement. The grant tested this by quantifying microstructural features from flight/ground samples and propagating them through micromechanics to predict property deltas attributable to gravity effects. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits This research provides the first reference simulation data and a practical route to predict how cement (including regolith‑based mixes) behaves when fabricated in space, which can inform Artemis‑aligned or other space-based habitat concepts and construction logistics where transporting bulk materials is prohibitive. On Earth, the deep-learning-assisted reconstruction and micromechanics workflow developed can be applied to other multiphase materials, enabling materials-by-design even when only a limited samples are available. By clarifying how processing conditions in microgravity affect cement structure and performance, such as the ~70% porosity and plate-like portlandite observed in ISS samples, this work improves predictive models for optimizing mix designs and curing conditions in constrained environments. These advances also benefit low-resource or extreme-environment construction on Earth and contribute more broadly to the ICME community. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 433.26 MB PSI-153Version 1 Fabrication of Amorphous Metals in Space(FAMIS) Investigation Submitted Date: 21-Aug-2025 Initial Release Date: 01-May-2026 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/rjm7-5p94 Research Area: Materials Science SubResearch Area: bulk metallic glass License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 10-01-2010 Investigation End Date 09-30-2025 Sponsoring Agency NASA NASA Center Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) Objectives The primary objective of this investigation was to understand the effect of microgravity processing on composition and microstructure evolution in metallic glass forming alloys or bulk metallic glass (BMG). Specific questions to be answered were: (a) How does processing in microgravity change the composition of the matrix of the glass-forming alloys compared to processing in gravity? (b) How does the volume fraction of the W spheres affect the composition and properties of the matrix? (c) How does the composition and viscosity of the glass-forming alloy affect the diffusion of W in microgravity? (d) How do the different diameter of W spheres affect the diffusion of W into the matrix? (e) Does the dissolved W provide a mechanism to improve the wear resistance and toughness of the matrix by providing reinforcement for brittle phases? Approach The objective of the flight experiment is to process 12 samples of two glass-forming alloys (Vitreloy 106 and Zr48Cu47.5Al4Co0.5) in microgravity with three different volume fractions of W spheres (5%, 15% and 30%) with two different diameters of W spheres (25-36 μm diameter and 140-150 μm diameter). The cast composite samples were 15 mm in diameter and 12 mm long cylinders. The W particles were distributed as homogeneously as possible without sedimentation. On orbit, the samples were loaded into the Low Gradient Furnace (LGF) on the Materials Science Research Rack. They were held for 120 minutes at 1,200 °C (1,473 K) in microgravity with the intent to dissolve the W particles into the matrix and to create a fine distribution of W dendrites homogenously distributed throughout. The samples were then cooled back to room temperature slowly, solidifying the morphology and composition. The Vitreloy 106 samples were compared with Zr48Cu47.5Al4Co0.5 in terms of composition of the matrix, morphology of the W dendrites, and mechanical properties, with comparisons drawn between samples produced on-orbit and on the ground to distinguish the effects of microgravity. Hypothesis The hypothesis for the experiment is that microgravity promotes composite formation by stabilizing the interface between the W nano-particle nuclei and the bulk liquid. In contrast, on Earth, the heavy W particles would fall out of the system as they form. Therefore, the composition of the solid formed on Earth will differ from that formed in microgravity. On Earth, the samples should solidify in a manner consistent with the Scheil solidification approximation meaning: (a) liquid diffusion is instant over experimental timescales (b) solid-state diffusion does not occur (solid falls out of the system as it forms) (c) the solid composition profile will follow the solidus as the system cools, until all the liquid is consumed. In contrast, in microgravity, the solid/liquid interface lifetime is much longer, so there is more opportunity for solid back-diffusion. For this case, the composition profile will approach (but not reach) that of the equilibrium solidification case. After processing in both gravity and microgravity, experimental compositional data at the matrix-sphere interface will be obtained. It is expected that composites formed on Earth will solidify consistent with Scheil solidification and composites formed in microgravity will deviate from Scheil, approaching equilibrium solidification. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits The development of innovative new materials is a fundamental part of future terrestrial and space technologies. These materials have a tremendous benefit towards improving life on Earth, from improving the accessibility and cost of solar power, to making cars safer and stronger, to reducing the mass of aircraft, for example. Innovative technologies typically require new materials tailored for those applications. This drives materials development. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 54.76 MB PSI-138Version 2 Pool Boiling Heat Transfer Mechanisms in Low Gravity: Numerical Experiments of MABE and NPBX Data Investigation Submitted Date: 30-Nov-2024 Initial Release Date: 12-Mar-2026 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/2bvb-0r98 Research Area: Fluid Physics SubResearch Area: Boiling and Condensation Related Investigation: PSI-85, PSI-81 License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Ground Investigation Proposal Title Pool Boiling Heat Transfer Mechanisms in Low Gravity: Numerical Experiments of MABE and NPBX Data Investigation Start Date 12-01-2020 Investigation End Date 11-30-2025 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), PSI grant NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives The primary objectives for this PSI grant include establishing a deeper mechanistic understanding of nucleate boiling under low-gravity conditions by conducting high-fidelity numerical simulations that replicate the flight conditions of prior ISS-based boiling experiments, specifically MABE and NPBX. The investigation seeks to characterize key mechanisms governing bubble growth, waiting time, vapor spreading, coalescence, and detachment under variable gravity levels, degrees of wall superheat, and levels of liquid subcooling. Central to the objectives is quantifying how heat flux divides between nucleate boiling and natural convection modes, evaluating how the contact angle modulates wall adhesion forces, and determining the precise contribution of microlayer evaporation to heat transfer during low-gravity operation. By leveraging validated direct-numerical-simulation approaches tied to empirical MABE and NPBX measurements, this objective generates fundamental physics-based insights that enable predictive modeling of boiling processes relevant to spacecraft systems and advanced thermal architectures. Approach The project approach was to use validated high-fidelity Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) ground-based computational simulations to numerically reproduce MABE- and NPBX-like boiling environments over a controlled range of heater temperatures, wall superheat conditions, and fluid subcooling levels. The research draws directly from ISS-acquired datasets that include detailed bubble growth dynamics, heat-flux profiles, and heater-surface imaging, which serve as reference benchmarks that guide simulation fidelity. Multiphase DNS simulations incorporate fluid phase-change physics, contact-line motion, interphase mass transport, and three-dimensional flow-field resolution to connect bubble behavior to instantaneous and time-averaged heat transfer. Iterative simulation campaigns then probe how variable gravitational acceleration, wettability contrast, bubble confinement, and microlayer evaporation influence overall heat-flux partitioning. The resulting database enables first-principles analysis of changes in boiling performance between terrestrial and microgravity settings while supporting quantitative model development applicable to spaceflight hardware, thermal architectures, and advanced electronic cooling systems. Hypothesis The research was based on the hypothesis that, in microgravity, shifts in the relative influence of buoyancy, capillary forces, and microlayer evaporation fundamentally alter bubble-growth behavior and reduce heat-flux performance. It further hypothesized that these low-gravity effects can be accurately captured using high-fidelity Direct Numerical Simulations (DNS) validated against historic ISS boiling data from the MABE and NPBX experiments. By exploring variations in gravity, surface wettability, and thermal conditions, the study aimed to test the mechanisms governing bubble dynamics and heat transfer for application to spacecraft thermal management. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits Space Benefits: This investigation provides high-resolution insight into how boiling heat-transfer efficiency degrades under reduced gravity, enabling the development of more reliable spacecraft thermal-management systems that do not depend solely on buoyancy-driven vapor removal. Improved understanding of microlayer-based transport, contact-line wetting, spatial heat-flux distribution, and boiling-mode transition directly supports the design of future ISS and deep-space thermal architectures, power-electronics packaging, life-support thermal management, and compact, energy-efficient cooling platforms for extended-duration missions. Earth Benefits: The computational foundations and physics-based insights gained through this study directly advance terrestrial thermal-management strategies for high-power electronic systems, including server-class processors, power-dense computing architectures, and high-performance energy-conversion systems. The work improves predictive control of boiling-induced heat removal, enabling higher operating throughput, greater component longevity, and reduced power consumption in heat-intensive commercial and defense electronics. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 892.04 GB PSI-187Version 2 Plant Water Management(PWM) Investigation Submitted Date: 31-Jul-2025 Initial Release Date: 18-Feb-2026 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/bvbr-k768 Research Area: Fluid Physics SubResearch Area: Fluid Dynamics License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Proposal Title Plant Water Management 5 and 6 Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 02-16-2023 Investigation End Date 11-27-2025 Sponsoring Agency NASA NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives The primary objectives of the Plant Water Management (PWM) experiments were to: a) Experimentally characterize and validate the use of passive capillary and geometric control for plant watering in microgravity. The research quantified the stability limits of capillary-driven flow under varying conditions, evaluated aeration and bubble management performance within root-zone analogs, and assessed start-up, shutdown, and drainage behaviors of the fluidic system on orbit and also correlated observed flow regimes and saturation levels with computational capillary flow models to improve predictive design tools for reduced-gravity systems. b) Advance the PWM technology toward higher Technology Readiness Levels (TRL), demonstrating reliable, scalable configurations for integration into future space-based plant growth habitats. The resulting data and models informed the design of next-generation, low-mass, low-power life-support and food-production systems for long-duration missions on the Moon, Mars, and beyond. Approach PWM employed passive capillary-based fluidic systems to deliver water and nutrients to plant root zones under microgravity aboard the ISS. Growth modules were designed with controlled channel geometries and surface-wetting properties to direct liquid flow, manage gas-liquid separation, and maintain root-zone aeration. Both hydroponic and soil-based configurations were tested to evaluate performance across different growth media. Measurements included monitoring liquid distribution, root-zone moisture levels, aeration efficiency, and bubble formation, alongside comparing observations to predictive capillary flow models. By systematically varying system geometry, wetting conditions, and operational parameters, the experiments defined design guidelines for robust, low-maintenance plant growth systems for space and analogous terrestrial applications. Hypothesis This research was based on the hypothesis that, in microgravity where gravity-driven fluid behavior is absent, capillary forces, surface tension, and geometric design could provide reliable water and nutrient delivery to plant root zones. Passive physical mechanisms replaced gravity in distributing and reclaiming fluids within the growth systems. Surface-wetting characteristics and channel geometry were designed to maintain root-zone hydration, facilitate aeration, and manage liquid–gas separation without pumps or active components. These mechanisms sustained water availability and oxygen exchange, preventing oversaturation or desiccation. The approach demonstrated that passive capillary systems could support consistent, low-maintenance plant watering and aeration in reduced-gravity environments. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits Demonstrating passive fluid management in plant growth systems is enabling reliable water and nutrient delivery in microgravity, supporting long-duration space missions. Advancing capillary-based irrigation is reducing system mass, complexity, and power requirements. In relation to agriculture on Earth, results from this research are improving precision irrigation, conserving water, and enhancing root-zone aeration in hydroponic and soil systems. Generating validated models of capillary-driven flow is guiding efficient, resilient plant growth technologies. Supporting scalable, low-maintenance systems is fostering innovations in both space life-support and sustainable food production on Earth. Contact(s) Mark M. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 1.27 MB PSI-189Version 1 Validation of a CFD Model for Gas-Liquid Flows in Packed Bed Reactors to Enable Thermo-Fluid Analysis in Microgravity Investigation Submitted Date: 06-Aug-2025 Initial Release Date: 10-Feb-2026 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/2e14-qv79 Research Area: Fluid Physics SubResearch Area: Packed Bed Reactor License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Ground Investigation Investigation Start Date 11-19-2021 Investigation End Date 12-30-2024 Sponsoring Agency NASA, PSI grant NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives 1. Develop and validate computational models for gas-liquid two-phase flow in porous media under microgravity using the PBRE (Packed Bed Reactor Experiment) flight data available in Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI). 2. Understand capillary-dominated fluid dynamics in low-gravity environments where traditional gravity-driven models fail. 3. Advance CFD tools to support the design and scale-up of life support and thermal control systems for spacecraft, space stations, and lunar/Martian habitats. Approach In this grant, our approach combined high-fidelity simulations with reduced-order modeling to better understand and predict two-phase gas-liquid flows through packed bed reactors in microgravity. We began by developing interface-resolved CFD simulations using the Volume of Fluid (VOF) method to capture detailed bubble dynamics in a representative volume of the reactor. These simulations were validated using PBRE imagery and pressure data available in PSI. To address scale-up and improve computational efficiency, we also developed a two-fluid model (TFM), which treats the gas and liquid phases as interpenetrating continua rather than tracking individual interfaces. We calibrated the drag closure in this model using PBRE data, allowing us to predict pressure drop behavior across different flow regimes. By combining detailed CFD with a validated TFM, we created a versatile modeling framework that supports the design of life support and thermal systems for future space missions. Purdue University Research Repository. doi:10.4231/VHB3-EN13. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits In space, fluid behavior becomes unpredictable. This grant developed and validated advanced computational models using real data from microgravity experiments to improve our understanding of how gas and liquid mixtures flow through packed bed reactors in space systems. This research can enable the design of more reliable and scalable systems for future missions to the Moon and Mars. On Earth, the same fluid dynamics apply to industries like chemical processing, wastewater treatment, and energy systems. The resulting models and insights from this research can improve efficiency and reduce costs in these applications. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 11.48 GB PSI-182Version 2 Colloidal gels: Aging in microgravity, Structure of highly polydisperse gels Investigation Submitted Date: 24-Apr-2025 Initial Release Date: 26-Jan-2026 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/bpn5-6m38 Research Area: Complex Fluids - Soft Matter SubResearch Area: Colloids Related Investigation: PSI-13 License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Ground Investigation Proposal Title Thermal fluctuations of colloidal gels Investigation Start Date 12-01-2021 Investigation End Date 11-30-2024 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), PSI Grant NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives Data are from two projects: one related to aging, one related to polydispersity. The first project has data under folders with a name containing AGING. The second has data under folders with a name containing POLYDISPERSE. ------- Project 1: Objectives specific to aging of colloid gels •Quantify coarsening of colloidal gels under microgravity conditions. •Quantify changes in thermal fluctuations of colloidal gels under microgravity conditions. •Understand aging of colloidal gels over time scales range from seconds to tens of hours. Project 2: Objectives related to structure of polydisperse colloidal gels •Measure fractal dimension of polydisperse colloidal gels (on Earth) •Understand how particle size relates to contact number •Quantify tetrahedral structures, and how particle size influences tetrahedral structure in colloidal gels Approach Project 1: We studied colloidal gels using the data from the Advanced Colloids Experiment-Microscopy-1 (ACE-M1) experiments. Colloidal gels are formed from sticky micron-sized solid particles in a liquid, where over time the particles stick together and form random clumps that eventually bridge across the entire sample chamber in tangled networks. The ACE-M1 data set consists of a large number of optical microscopy movies of colloidal gels. In microgravity, these gels are long-lived, rather than collapsing under their own weight as happens in ground-based experiments. We have analyzed these microscopy movies using particle tracking, studying the visible thermal fluctuations and the gel structure as it evolves over time. Some gels have thick aggregated regions, while others have more tenuous gel strands and free particles. We show that the structure and dynamics change over the several-day period of each experiment. Project 2: In a second project, we did ground-based experiments to study the structure of colloidal gels composed of polydisperse particles. In particular, we used confocal microscopy to image colloidal gels formed from highly polydisperse particles. We suspended our polydisperse particles in a density matched solvent, and let the particles spontaneously aggregate through the van der Waals force. The largest particles were more than 15 times the size of the smallest particles. As expected, larger particles have more nearest neighbors than small ones. This leads to an over-representation of large particles in tetrahedral structures where four particles are mutually nearest neighbors, showing that large particles help provide rigidity to the gel structure. The tetrahedral structures also suggest that particles are able to rearrange somewhat during the gelation process, until their motion is stabilized by the multiple contacts with their neighbors. Hypothesis Project 1: Colloidal gels in microgravity conditions will coarsen over time, and their thermal fluctuations will diminish over time as the gel gets coarser; the coarsening will continue indefinitely because gravitational collapse will not be possible. Project 2: Large particles play significant roles in highly polydisperse colloidal gels, as they serve as highly connected nodes in the structure. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits This research helps us understand the technical challenge of keeping particles dispersed in a colloidal suspension. A gel is one way to prevent particles from settling, although the long-time behavior of a gel is challenging to study under Earth gravity. title: The origin of fragility in high-temperature oxide liquids - towards fabrication of novel non-equilibrium oxides(ELF-6 PRONTO)

detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 382.06 GB PSI-178Version 2 The origin of fragility in high-temperature oxide liquids - towards fabrication of novel non-equilibrium oxides(ELF-6 PRONTO) Investigation Submitted Date: 09-Apr-2025 Initial Release Date: 26-Jan-2026 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/dnga-vp70 Research Area: Materials Science SubResearch Area: Thermophysical properties License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 08-15-2019 Investigation End Date 09-30-2025 Sponsoring Agency NASA NASA Center Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) Objectives This project investigated the high-temperature thermophysical properties of molten metal oxides, with a particular focus on molten titanates. These property measurements were used to establish correlations with atomic structure and glass formation. The research exploits the unique capabilities in microgravity to measure the thermophysical properties – density, thermal expansion coefficient, viscosity and surface tension – over a wide temperature range. Samples, including glasses, were recovered after melt processing in microgravity for ground-based analysis and comparison with materials made on Earth. The work underpins development of a materials property-structure data set that can help in development of new materials and in meeting requirements of material utilization, processing in space, and exploration. Approach Density, thermal expansion, viscosity, and surface tension of molten oxides were measured using the Electrostatic Levitation Furnace (ELF) onboard the ISS. Measurements included silhouette imaging and drop oscillation over a wide range of temperatures, including deep supercooling. Recovered samples included glasses and polycrystalline materials, which were characterized post-flight using a combination of X-ray scattering, neutron scattering, X-ray tomography, Raman spectroscopy, calorimetry, and electron microscopy. Space-made glasses were compared with terrestrial analogues to investigate how changes in fluid transport may influence structure and properties. Hypothesis Glasses are inherently non-equilibrium materials. Their structure and properties depend directly on the processing route used to form them. Because gravity affects fluid convection, glass formation and resulting structure may differ between different gravity conditions. We hypothesize that the superior control of fluid and thermal transport possible in microgravity will enable improved glass forming ability via melt quenching in containerless conditions, particularly for highly fragile liquid oxides. We hypothesize that the differences in thermal history - between microgravity and Earth-based processing - will manifest as differences in structure and thermodynamic properties. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits This project advances the understanding of oxide melt properties, atomic structure, and glass formation. This builds a foundation for the development of new functional glasses and related technologies, with applications on Earth and in space for exploration and utilization of local resources. The project was successful on several fronts: 1. Microgravity experiments enabled melting, drop imaging, drop oscillation and measurements of properties of approximately 30 samples. 2. First experiments in ELF that used melt processing to make and recover glass in space. 3. First publications that compare the structure of glasses made in microgravity vs. terrestrially. 4. First demonstration of laser action in a titanate-network glass and of a glass made by containerless processing. 5. Results were analyzed in collaboration with a variety of researchers leading to 12 peer-reviewed publications and more than 20 presentations. 6. Two patents are pending based on results of the work. These have a high impact on glass materials processing in space and development of new glass products both on-Earth and in reduced gravity. 7. The project met all of the stated goals: perform basic research in microgravity, develop applied knowledge to make new materials, build collaborations to advance the field, and establish the basis for new glass materials products made in reduced gravity. 8. The results are relevant to the applied research mission of NASA's Biological and Physical Sciences (BPS) to enable space exploration and utilize materials based on natural resources that are available in space. 9. Developed and fostered a productive international collaboration. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 44.57 MB PSI-190Version 1 Particle Engulfment and Pushing By Solidifying Interfaces(PEP) Investigation Submitted Date: 11-Aug-2025 Initial Release Date: 02-Dec-2025 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/99w7-5n19 Research Area: Materials Science SubResearch Area: Solidification, Metal Matrix Composites License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform Space Shuttle Investigation Start Date 02-01-1993 Investigation End Date 09-01-2004 Sponsoring Agency NASA NASA Center Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) Objectives The major scientific objectives of this investigation were as follows: · to enhance the fundamental understanding of dynamics of insoluble particles at the solid-liquid interface; · to obtain experimental data for the critical velocity of particle engulfment in a convection-free environment; · to validate present theoretical models; · to improve the understanding of physics associated with solidification of liquid metals - ceramic particles mixtures; · to investigate aspects of melt processing of particulate metal matrix composites in the unique microgravity environment which will yield some vital information for terrestrial applications; · to further develop the elements of the numerical model into a comprehensive model that takes into account convection effects. Approach The experimental approach was to perform directional solidification experiments with a pure metal, aluminum, doped with low volume fraction of insoluble particles, ZrO2. These experiments were carried out during the Life and Microgravity Science (LMS) mission on board the space shuttle Columbia. In addition, transparent organic matrices such as succinonitrile and biphenyl doped with polystryrene particles or glass beads were used to observe the interaction between the particle and solidification interface in real time. The experiments with the organic matrices were performed during the United States Microgravity Payload 4 (USMP-4) mission also on board the space shuttle Columbia. Planar interfaces were produced through appropriate manipulation of the solidification variables, so that a clear pushing/engulfment transition (PET) of the particles could be determined. Both ground and microgravity experiments were conducted. Recognizing that the interaction between the particle and the solidification front is not completely a steady state process, a dynamic non-steady-state model was developed based on the fact that a particle, initially at rest, must have an accelerated motion in order to reach the steady-state velocity, which is the solidification velocity. To account for the solutal fields in alloys a 2D FDM fixed Cartesian grid numerical model was also developed. The models were validated using benchmark microgravity and terrestrial data. Hypothesis During solidification of metal-insoluble particles systems the particles interact with the solidification front. The solutal and thermal field, as well as fluid motion at the solid-liquid interface (SLI) will influence both interface morphology and the particle/interface interaction itself. This investigation hypothesizes that based on the nature of interaction and balance of forces acting on the particle there is a critical SLI velocity below which particles are pushed ahead of the advancing interface, and above which particle engulfment occurs. For planar SLI the critical velocity results from the forces acting on the particle. These forces include particle-SLI interaction force, drag force on the particle, gravitational force, Saffman force, and Magnus force. The last three are strongly affected by the level of gravitational acceleration. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits A fundamental understanding of the phenomena associated with particle/interface interaction during solidification will permit the development of novel techniques for processing of particulate metal matrix composites through melting and solidification. Similar concepts apply to inclusion management in casting alloys. As for most other metallurgical applications it is desired to avoid inclusion segregation at grain boundaries. Results of this research can be extrapolated straightforward to “clean steel” technology. Another interesting application of particle pushing is in the processing of single crystals ceramic where strong flux pinning particles are desired to be homogeneously incorporated in the superconducting crystal. Insights from this investigation can also be applied to the field of cryobiology where the study of the interaction of cells (yeast cells, red blood cells) with ice crystals when freezing aqueous solutions makes it possible to investigate the mechanism of the mechanical destruction of biological structures by ice crystals on freezing biological materials. In addition, this investigation can be extended to the field of frost heaving of soils that can be reduced to the behavior of soil particles (i.e. clay) in a water/ice matrix. Contact(s) Doru M. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 785.91 GB PSI-169Version 1 Advanced Colloids Experiment-Nanoparticle Haloing(ACE-T12) Investigation Submitted Date: 24-Nov-2025 Initial Release Date: 24-Nov-2025 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/xs1c-p767 Research Area: Complex Fluids - Soft Matter SubResearch Area: Colloids License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Proposal Title Influence of Gravity on Electrokinetic and Electrochemical Colloidal Self-Assembly for Future Materials Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 10-01-2014 Investigation End Date 09-30-2019 Sponsoring Agency Experimental Program to Stimulate Competitive Research (EPSCoR), NASA NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives Nanoparticle Haloing (NPH) is a colloidal stabilization technique that has been discovered relatively recently. In NPH, highly charged nanoparticles are used to stabilize much larger (by 2 orders of magnitude or more), non-charged particles. To accomplish this stabilization, the volume fraction of nanoparticles within the suspension need only be on the order of 1e-5 up to 1e-4 to stabilize at 1 to 2 vol% suspension of the larger particles. The objective of this work is to gain fundamental insight into the physics of NPH with the aim of addressing the following unresolved questions: • How will NPH suspensions behave in thermal or electrical field gradients as they do under gravity? • How does the halo form or re-form if disturbed? • Can NPH (and manipulation thereof) be used to assemble and reconfigure colloidal crystals? • How does the nanoparticle charge impact halo formation? Approach The ACE-T12 experiment utilizes the Fluids Integrated Rack (FIR) and the Light Microscopy Module (LMM). The FIR is built to accommodate a wide range of experiments. Accordingly, the ACE-T12 experiment included confocal microscopy, which used a 532-nm frequency-doubled Nd:YAG laser, a confocal scanner, and an 8- to 12-bit digital CCD camera on a Leica DM-RXA microscope. The scanner captured 30 frames per second of confocal images by the CCD camera. ACE-T12 utilizes capillary cells. Three capillary cells with different concentrations of nanoparticles were provided in a sample module. Here is a brief high-level descriptive outline of the investigation on-orbit procedures that gives general experiment steps for each capillary. 1- Short mix of sample. 2- Ramp temperature to find critical temperature and reduce temperature and initiate a very long mix of sample. 3- Determine Region of Interest (ROI). 4- Ramp temperature continuously while imaging. 5- Mix sample followed by Single temperature step visits. 6- Mix sample followed by stepwise temperature ramp with image stacks. Hypothesis When NPH suspensions were allowed to settle under gravity, those that were stabilized (while in suspension) formed highly ordered, 3-dimensional colloidal crystal structures. Current theory suggests that nanoparticles create a charge layer by forming a cage, or Halo, around the larger particles. Another hypothesis regarding the NPH stabilization mechanism focuses entirely on nanoparticle adsorption to the surface of the larger particle. Based on the measurement of the interaction forces between two larger colloidal surfaces in a nanoparticle suspension, it was found that the force curves obtained could be fitted using a model based on nanoparticle adsorption. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits Ultimately, the ability to design colloidal particles with a variety of well-controlled three-dimensional bonding symmetries opens a wide spectrum of new structures for colloidal self-assembly, beyond particle assemblies whose structures are defined primarily by repulsive interactions and shape. Such materials might include photonic crystals with programmed distributions of defects. Optical technology utilizing such materials may offer intriguing solutions to unavoidable heat generation and bandwidth limitations facing the computer industry. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 1.90 TB PSI-159Version 1 Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases(ACME CFI-G) Investigation Submitted Date: 20-Nov-2025 Initial Release Date: 20-Nov-2025 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/cyt1-kh64 Research Area: Combustion Science SubResearch Area: Flames of Gaseous Fuels License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Proposal Title ISS: Collaborative Research: Spherical Cool Diffusion Flames Burning Gaseous Fuels Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Sponsoring Agency National Science Foundation (NSF), Center for the Advancement of Science in Space (CASIS) NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives 1. Plan and support flight testing on the International Space Station (ISS). 2. Determine the conditions for which cool diffusion flames occur for propane, n-butane, and n-pentane; normal and inverse flames; and a broad range of Zst, Tad, and fluent flow rate. 3. Support the flight tests with advanced CFD simulations. 4. Identify or develop a chemical kinetics mechanism that yields good agreement between the CFD predictions and the ISS measurements. 5. Disseminate the results as widely as possible. Approach Perform spherical diffusion flame tests aboard the International Space Station. Consider multiple fuels, a range of reactant dilutions, flow rates, and pressures for normal and inverse convection directions. Observe the flames with a broad suite of cameras, radiometers, photomultiplier tubes, and thermocouples. Hypothesis The hypotheses of this research are that testing aboard the ISS can demonstrate the following for the first time, contributing to an improved understanding of cool flame kinetics. 1. Steady-state cool diffusion flames on spherical porous burners. 2. Cool diffusion flames burning propane, n-butane, and n-pentane. 3. Cool diffusion flames for a wide range of Zst, Tad, and pressures. 4. Inverse cool diffusion flames. 5. Cool diffusion flames for which a decrease in fluent flow rate will cause extinction, whereas an increase will cause a transition to a hot diffusion flame, with oscillation possible between hot and cool flames. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits Combustion provides 86% of the world’s energy and an even higher fraction of the energy used for transportation. The internal combustion engines used for transportation generally have thermal efficiencies of 38% or lower because of thermal losses. These efficiencies may increase to 60% if future engines can take advantage of ultra-lean combustion. However, this progress is being impeded by the limited understanding of the chemistry of cool flames. Research into cool diffusion flames (whose peak temperatures are 500 – 1000 K) has grown exponentially since they were discovered in 2012. The measurements performed for this project will help to test and advance cool flame kinetics mechanisms. This should facilitate the development of more efficient internal combustion engines. hypothesis:
The hypotheses of this research are that testing aboard the ISS can demonstrate the following for the first time, contributing to an improved understanding of cool flame kinetics.
  1. Steady-state cool diffusion flames on spherical porous burners.
  2. Cool diffusion flames burning propane, n-butane, and n-pentane.
  3. Cool diffusion flames for a wide range of Zst, Tad, and pressures.
  4. Inverse cool diffusion flames.
  5. Cool diffusion flames for which a decrease in fluent flow rate will cause extinction, whereas an increase will cause a transition to a hot diffusion flame, with oscillation possible between hot and cool flames.
impacts: Combustion provides 86% of the world’s energy and an even higher fraction of the energy used for transportation. The internal combustion engines used for transportation generally have thermal efficiencies of 38% or lower because of thermal losses. These efficiencies may increase to 60% if future engines can take advantage of ultra-lean combustion. However, this progress is being impeded by the limited understanding of the chemistry of cool flames. Research into cool diffusion flames (whose peak temperatures are 500 – 1000 K) has grown exponentially since they were discovered in 2012.  The measurements performed for this project will help to test and advance cool flame kinetics mechanisms. This should facilitate the development of more efficient internal combustion engines.

Obtain soot-inception limits of quasi-steady normal and inverse spherical diffusion flames as functions of flow rate, Zst, amount of inert (N2 or CO2), and pressure for C2H4 and CH4 flames. Identify the corresponding temperatures in hot regions. Obtain similar limits and temperatures for inverse and normal coflow flames. B. Obtain detailed measurements in quasi-steady normal and inverse spherical diffusion flames for C2H4 and CH4. Determine the effects of flow rate, Zst, amount of N2, and pressure on flame temperature, size, color, and soot volume fraction. Evaluate the possible existence of steady flames. C. Obtain extinction limits as functions of Zst, amount of N2, and pressure for normal and inverse spherical C2H4 and CH4 flames. Identify the corresponding temperatures in hot regions. Identify the presence of radiative or kinetic extinction. Evaluate whether pseudo-flammability limits can be obtained for these flames. Approach Perform spherical diffusion flame tests in drop towers and aboard the International Space Station. Consider a broad range of reactant dilutions, flow rates and pressures for normal and inverse convection directions. Observe the flames with a broad suite of cameras, radiometers, photomultiplier tubes, and thermocouples. Hypothesis 1. Soot formation requires a region where local C/O ratio and T exceed their critical values, and where strain rate is sufficiently low. 2. Microgravity spherical diffusion flames extinguish when the peak temperature first decreases below 1130 K. 3. Steady-state spherical diffusion flames are possible. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 9.47 KB PSI-62Version 1 Concurrent Flame Spread Modeling using Flamelet Generated Manifolds in Microgravity with Comparison to BASS Experiments using Two-Color Tomography Investigation Submitted Date: 30-Apr-2021 Initial Release Date: 14-Nov-2025 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/e9xp-ex83 Research Area: Combustion Science SubResearch Area: Spacecraft Fire Safety Related Investigation: PSI-25, PSI-26 License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Ground Investigation Proposal Title Concurrent Flame Spread Modeling using Flamelet Generated Manifolds in Microgravity with Comparison to BASS Experiments using Two-Color Tomography Investigation Start Date 05-01-2019 Investigation End Date 04-30-2021 Sponsoring Agency NASA, PSI grant NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives The objective of this research was to develop and validate new flamelet generated manifold (FGM) modeling techniques for concurrent flame spread in microgravity. Concurrent flame spread presented one of the greatest modeling challenges in combustion science due to the intricate coupling between heat transfer, mass transport, and chemical kinetics near the solid-vapor interface. Traditional modeling strategies often relied on hybridized turbulence and chemistry models that were not fully consistent and failed to capture important intermediate reaction pathways. To overcome these shortcomings, this PSI grant advanced the use of an unsteady flamelet generated manifold (UFGM) framework that reduced the complexity of reacting systems by mapping them into lower-dimensional manifolds. The research aimed to leverage this methodology to simulate solid fuel combustion processes with high fidelity, using the NASA Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS and BASS-II) experiments as benchmarks. Ultimately, the long-term goal was to enable accurate prediction of flammability limits for spacecraft materials and to provide a tool that could also serve as a subgrid-scale model in large-eddy simulations of fires, supporting spacecraft safety and hazard mitigation. Approach The approach combined high-resolution computational modeling with experimental validation to study concurrent flame spread in microgravity. A previously developed computational framework was employed to run fully coupled simulations of fluid–solid responses, focusing on materials subject to charring and ablation. Within this framework, the unsteady FGM method was implemented and tested on various BASS geometries, including flat sheets, spheres, and rod-shaped polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) samples, as well as wax cylinders. Experimental imagery found in PSI from the BASS and BASS-II investigations was post-processed using newly developed two-color tomography methods with DSLR cameras, enabling 3D reconstructions of soot and temperature fields for direct comparison to model predictions. The evaluation metrics included flame geometry, temperature distribution, soot volume fraction, and flame spread rate, with special emphasis on reproducing the “Goldilocks” flammability zone reported by Olson and Ferkul. Comparative analyses were also carried out with a parallel NSF-supported terrestrial flame spread project, ensuring that the predictive capabilities of the UFGM approach were assessed across both microgravity and normal-gravity conditions. Hypothesis The unsteady flamelet generated manifold (UFGM) approach was believed to be able to accurately reproduce concurrent flame spread in microgravity, including phenomena such as the “Goldilocks” flammability zone, by coupling near-wall thermal, mass transport, and chemical processes with far-field flow dynamics. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits This research provides predictive tools for screening new materials’ flammability limits, which can lead to the design of safer spacecrafts. The development of Large Eddy Simulation subgrid models is expected to improve hazard assessment capabilities critical for managing fire risks during long-duration space missions and within confined spacecraft habitats. On Earth, these advancements could improve combustion modeling by deepening our understanding of coupled thermal, chemical, and flow processes, which betters fire safety standards. The computational methods being refined have the potential to enable more effective fire prevention and mitigation strategies and foster innovations in diagnostics and simulations applicable across a variety of combustion scenarios. Overall, this research can contribute significantly to safer human exploration in space and improvements to fire safety protocols on Earth. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 916.84 GB PSI-188Version 1 Advanced Colloids Experiment-Temperature 4(ACE-T4) Investigation Submitted Date: 03-Oct-2025 Initial Release Date: 03-Oct-2025 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/a1k6-wt47 Research Area: Complex Fluids - Soft Matter SubResearch Area: Colloids License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Proposal Title Low Volume Fraction Entropically Driven Colloidal Assembly Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 06-01-2020 Investigation End Date 09-14-2020 Sponsoring Agency NASA NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives Original Objective: The ACE-T4 experiments were designed to explore the disorder-induced transformation between a crystal and a glass. The experiments introduced disorder by added colloidal dopants into the samples; these dopants introduce structural frustration into the crystals which, in turn, can transform the crystals into disordered solids (polycrystalline) and glasses with novel mechanical properties. The experiments varied the concentration and character of particle dopants in three-dimensional colloidal crystals and employed direct visualization of an evolving crystal microstructure and dynamics in microgravity to derive fundamental insight into the nature of the transition and the glasses formed. Revised Objective: Before the ACE-T4 experiment on the International Space Station (ISS) was conducted, the master hard disk controlling the Light Microscopy Module (LMM) failed and delayed starting this experiment by many months. This extended delay had a detrimental effect on the samples that resulted in the gelation of the samples before the experiment began. The originally planned experiments were no longer possible due to gelation, but the ACE-T4 experiment based on the changed samples (gels) provided qualitatively different insights into the behavior of 3D colloidal gels over a range of temperatures and temperature gradients. Some effects were visible with LMM and provide an opportunity to study the microstructure, dynamics, and stresses in gels that can lead to microcracks, an important problem that, for example, could affect 3D printer inks. Approach The ACE-T4 experiment used confocal microscopy to observe the gels over a range of particle packing-fractions (temperatures), using pure, monodisperse poly(N -isopropylacrylamide) (pNIPA) particles in one sample, and then mixtures of pNIPAM particles with different amounts of particle dopants in five other samples. All of the samples formed gels. There was no crystallization in any sample . The data obtained permits the study of 3D gels with and without dopants as a function of temperature; the temperature changes vary the particle size and thus properties of the gels. In addition to the revised ACE-T4 experiment, ground-based soft matter research was completed and published. Hypothesis The ACE-T4 experiments were intended to explore the transformation between a crystal and a glass by varying the density and character of particle dopants in three dimensional colloidal crystals. The original hypothesis stated that ''dopants introduce structural frustration into the crystals which, in turn, can transform the crystals into disordered (polycrystalline) solids and glasses with novel mechanical properties. Direct visualization of the evolving crystal microstructure and dynamics in microgravity will provide fundamental insight into the nature of glasses and into processes such as nucleation and melting.'' Research Impacts/Earth Benefits By frustrating their structural order, the transition from ordered (crystal) to disordered (glassy) materials can alter the macroscopic behavior of ordered materials. Moreover, these experiments could also provide fundamental insight into the nature of nucleation, aging, and melting in materials with varying degrees of order. This information could benefit observation and synthesis of new colloidal materials (e.g. g., meta and photonic materials) for many applications ranging from color control to random laser. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 7.56 KB PSI-60Version 1 Computational and Experimental Analysis of SPICE Data Sets Investigation Submitted Date: 29-Aug-2022 Initial Release Date: 30-Sep-2025 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/mzjm-yv57 Research Area: Combustion Science SubResearch Area: Gaseous Related Investigation: PSI-107 License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Ground Investigation Proposal Title Computational and Experimental Analysis of SPICE Data Sets Investigation Start Date 06-05-2019 Investigation End Date 08-29-2022 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), PSI grant NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives This ground investigation sought to increase understanding of the issues that control the large discrepancy between soot formation in 1g and in 0g flames. The objective of this investigation was to integrate computational and experimental methods to derive temperature distributions and soot volume fractions from the Smoke Point in Coflow Experiment (SPICE) data available in PSI. By analyzing over 1600 raw DSLR images and incorporating advanced soot models, the study sought to improve understanding of soot formation, oxidation, radiative re-absorption, and aggregate growth in heavily sooting flames. The work further aimed to reconcile microgravity and normal gravity flame behavior, identify key physical and chemical processes influencing smoke point development, and provide a framework for evaluating model parameter sensitivity. Approach The approach was to combine image processing, experimental diagnostics, and detailed soot modeling. Raw Nikon NEF images were decoded into three color channels and analyzed using color-ratio pyrometry to extract soot temperature fields. Absolute light calibration from SPICE was then used to calculate soot volume fractions. For computational modeling, a coupled flow–species–soot system was implemented, modified to include radiation re-absorption and discrete-sectional aggregate formation. Simulations were performed for both Yale and ACME burner configurations under normal and microgravity conditions. Comparisons between experimental data and computed results guided sensitivity analyses of soot evolution parameters, including the effects of radiation, scattering, boundary conditions, and heat transfer to the burner structure. Hypothesis Microgravity conditions would produce longer, more diffuse flames with lower temperatures and increased soot concentrations compared to normal gravity, and that careful integration of experimental temperature fields into the simulations would reduce discrepancies between measured and predicted soot distributions. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits This study sought to enhance understanding of soot formation, flame structure, and radiative transport under microgravity and normal gravity, improving predictive models for combustion in both spacecraft and terrestrial systems. For space applications, the results support safer fire detection, suppression, and cleaner combustion technologies critical for long-duration missions. On Earth, the insights help reduce pollutant emissions, optimize combustion efficiency, and inform the design of cleaner energy and industrial systems. Contact(s) Mitchell D. Smookeemail,Marshall B. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 32.35 MB PSI-191Version 1 Advanced Colloids Experiment-Temperature 5(ACE-T5) Investigation Submitted Date: 18-Nov-2025 Initial Release Date: 29-Sep-2025 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/2zsv-zs73 Research Area: Complex Fluids - Soft Matter SubResearch Area: Bijels, Colloids License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Proposal Title Bijel processing: decoupling the roles of Marangoni and gravitational forces Flight Platform International Space Station Investigation Start Date 10-01-2013 Investigation End Date 12-08-2023 Sponsoring Agency NASA NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives The overarching goal of the project was to gain a better fundamental understanding of the relationship between bijel morphology, rheology, mechanical stability, and processability through combined ground-based and microgravity experiments and theoretical calculations. Approach Mixtures of propylene glycol/nitroethane (PG/NE) at their critical composition were prepared. Partially hydrophobic silica particles were suspended in the PG/NE mixture and the suspensions were filled in different cuvettes. On orbit, these cuvettes were heated to 25C, mixed in-situ, and then quenched from 25C to 0C. Following the quench, an imaging protocol was used to collect a stack of 100 images in the Z direction at a spacing of 5 mm. Hypothesis This investigation hypothesizes that interparticle interactions have a profound impact on the rheology of bijel particulate suspensions and attempts to answer the fundamental scientific question as to how the various forces at the colloidal scale are affected by Marangoni convection in microgravity. The nature of interparticle interactions and its impact on rheology has profound implications for the processability of bijels and the ability to transform them into functional materials. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits The ability to design and fabricate the unique 3-dimensional bijel structures opens a wide spectrum of new structures for applications that can benefit from synthesis of hierarchically porous monoliths and composites with a spinodal-like microstructure in which every constituent phase is naturally continuous throughout the entire sample volume. This type of tailored porous microstructures can improve the physical properties and performance of materials used in a number of space and terrestrial applications. Space exploration applications include improved energy storage batteries and fuel cells, and catalytic microreactors for lower mass and volume designs in spacecraft life support and ISRU systems. There is a diverse array of potential terrestrial applications in electrochemical energy conversion and storage, tissue engineering, sensing, microstructured composites with optimized mechanical properties for MEMS, microfluidic heat exchangers and catalytic reformers, separations. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 193.70 GB PSI-167Version 1 Advanced Colloids Experiment - Imaging, Folding and Assembly of Colloidal Molecules(ACE-T9) Investigation Submitted Date: 06-Jan-2025 Initial Release Date: 17-Sep-2025 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/a3n8-6918 Research Area: Complex Fluids - Soft Matter SubResearch Area: Colloids License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 09-01-2013 Investigation End Date 08-31-2019 Sponsoring Agency NASA NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives In ACE-T9, the imaging capability, folding dynamics, and assembly behavior of linear colloidal chains, colloidal dimers, and lock-and-key particles were studied by the combination of a proper design of particle architecture and tunable colloidal interactions (e.g., double layer repulsion and hydrophobic attraction). In the case of colloidal chains, for example, the single chain dynamics should sensitively depend on the chain flexibility and monomer-solvent interactions. Under the microgravity environment, we hoped to observe qualitative three-dimensional, real-time dynamics of single colloidal chains (using pre-confocal - bright field and fluorescent microscopy. We also aimed to observe three-dimensional structures assembled from colloidal dimers and lock-and-key particles and to measure the binding equilibrium constants that are impossible to measure in earth experiments due to the effect of sedimentation. Approach The imaging goal is to observe (1) real-time and three-dimensional particle centroid positions of colloidal chains over both short (30 minutes) and long period (one week); (2) assembled structures, crystallites, and resolve particle centroid positions for colloidal dimers and Janus spheres. For short-time imaging, the video should be taken with 5 fps over 30 minutes. For both cases, the x-y positions of particles should be determined with less than 5% error (with respect to particle diameter). The z-positions should be determined within 1 micron. For fluorescence imaging, lamp should be shuttered between image sets to prevent sample bleaching. Hypothesis In the microgravity environment, we will study the folding dynamics of single colloidal chains where the chain architecture can be varied systematically, and the monomer-solvent interaction can be tuned by varying salt concentrations. Furthermore, by tuning the balance between electric double layer repulsion and hydrophobic attraction on both colloidal dimers and lock-and-key particles, we aim to study the assembly of those colloidal molecules into complex three-dimensional structures and measure the binding equilibrium constants. This set of experiments provide insight into the relation between particle shape, colloidal interaction and structure. With the wide variety of attributes that characterize anisotropic interactions, we will probe previously inaccessible regions of complex phase space. Our studies will move significantly beyond hard spheres and towards experimental models appropriate for studying fundamental questions associated with complex symmetries. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits In-situ manipulation of anisotropic interactions and dynamic pathways, based on rational colloidal particle design and proper use of external fields, could lead to crystalline and a periodic structures beyond those seen in nature. Results from this study will lead to improved control of non-covalent assembly of molecules, efficient tailoring of lattice symmetries, and the scalable processing of nano-structured materials. The development of new colloidal molecules and their associated assembled structures have considerable technological impact as well. Such structures will generally lead to arrays with reduced symmetry and enhanced directionality. They can interact with a broad range of electromagnetic radiation in unique ways and can exhibit collective photonic, plasmonic, mechanical, electronic, or magnetic properties that are not manifested at the level of single particles. As a result, they have significant potential as next-generation functional materials. Contact(s) David Marremail,Ning Wuemail,Michael Solomonemail,John B.
