title: Enhanced Particle Tracking in STDC Data and Its Industrial Application of Marangoni Convection
objectives: The primary objective this grant was to extract and understand the detailed thermo-fluid mechanics of the original NASA Surface Tension Driven Convection Experiment (STDCE-1) performed in microgravity...
approach: The approach combined archival microgravity data analysis, computational modeling, and ground experiments to study surface tension driven convection (STDC). Video data from the original NASA STDCE-1 e...
detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 19.46 MB PSI-119Version 1 Enhanced Particle Tracking in STDC Data and Its Industrial Application of Marangoni Convection Investigation Submitted Date: 24-Nov-2022 Initial Release Date: 15-Sep-2025 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/dwhy-bb73 Research Area: Fluid Physics SubResearch Area: Capillary flow Related Investigation: PSI-108, PSI-109 License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Ground Investigation Proposal Title Enhanced Particle Tracking in STDC Data and Its Industrial Application of Marangoni Convection Investigation Start Date 11-25-2020 Investigation End Date 11-24-2022 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), PSI Grant NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives The primary objective this grant was to extract and understand the detailed thermo-fluid mechanics of the original NASA Surface Tension Driven Convection Experiment (STDCE-1) performed in microgravity, using modern diagnostic and computational tools. The study aims to revitalize the original video data found in PSI by applying advanced Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV) and Particle Tracking Velocimetry (PTV) methods, which provide higher resolution, sub-pixel accuracy, and robust flow field extraction compared to the limited analyses available in the early 1990s. By systematically comparing velocity and pressure fields obtained from these reanalyzed datasets with theoretical perturbation methods and COMSOL Multiphysics computational models, the project seeks to isolate the fundamental role of Marangoni convection and interfacial curvature in driving oscillatory and steady-state flows. Complementary ground-based experiments incorporating gravitational effects will be conducted to disentangle the relative contributions of buoyancy and surface tension-driven convection. These objectives ultimately support both NASA’s PSI solicitation by expanding the scientific return from legacy datasets and advancing applied understanding for industrial processes that rely on controlled Marangoni flows, such as wafer drying, thin-film coating, and microfluidic device operation. Approach The approach combined archival microgravity data analysis, computational modeling, and ground experiments to study surface tension driven convection (STDC). Video data from the original NASA STDCE-1 experiments were re-analyzed using several modern particle tracking techniques, including four MATLAB-based codes, three ImageJ-based codes, and sub-pixel localization methods, to produce velocity and pressure fields. These flow fields were compared with theoretical models derived from perturbation methods and with computational simulations performed in COMSOL Multiphysics® v5.6 that incorporated boundary conditions and curved free-surface geometries. In parallel, ground-based STDC experiments were carried out to examine gravitational effects and to distinguish buoyancy-driven flows from thermocapillary convection. This combination of data reanalysis, numerical simulation, and experimental testing provided a means to identify the influence of interfacial curvature, surface stresses, and geometry on Marangoni convection. Hypothesis Re-analyzing NASA’s STDCE-1 microgravity video data with advanced particle tracking and computational modeling to reveal previously inaccessible details of thermo-fluid mechanics in surface tension driven convection. These insights, validated against ground-based experiments, aimed to clarify the interplay between Marangoni forces, interfacial curvature, and flow instabilities, leading to improved predictive models of thermocapillary flows. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits Space Benefits: Improves understanding of thermocapillary convection in microgravity, critical for designing reliable thermal management and materials processing systems aboard spacecraft. Provides validated numerical and theoretical models that can guide future ISS and space-based fluid physics experiments, reducing uncertainty from prior low-resolution analyses. Earth Benefits: Supports industrial applications such as semiconductor wafer cleaning, thin-film coatings, welding, and liquid crystal display fabrication. Findings also translate to emerging fields like active matter and micro/nano robotics, where Marangoni flows and surface interactions could be harnessed for medical diagnostics, targeted drug delivery, and microplastics removal. title: Dynamic Response of Particle-Filled Polymeric Fluids in Flows with Complex Lagrangian Time Histories
objectives: The primary objective of this ground investigation is to exploit the unique flight data from the Shear History Extensional Rheology (SHERE, SHERE-II, SHERE-R) investigations to better understand the d...
approach: The investigation combines numerical simulations, theoretical modeling, and SHERE flight data validation. The SHERE experiments measured transient extensional responses of dilute particle suspensions ...
detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 10.06 KB PSI-66Version 1 Dynamic Response of Particle-Filled Polymeric Fluids in Flows with Complex Lagrangian Time Histories Investigation Submitted Date: 06-Dec-2024 Initial Release Date: 15-Sep-2025 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/67jq-z098 Research Area: Complex Fluids - Soft Matter SubResearch Area: Polymer Solutions Related Investigation: PSI-103, PSI-105 License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Ground Investigation Proposal Title Dynamic Response of Particle-Filled Polymeric Fluids in Flows with Complex Lagrangian Time Histories Investigation Start Date 12-07-2022 Investigation End Date 12-06-2024 Sponsoring Agency NASA, PSI grant NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives The primary objective of this ground investigation is to exploit the unique flight data from the Shear History Extensional Rheology (SHERE, SHERE-II, SHERE-R) investigations to better understand the dynamic rheology of particle-filled polymeric fluids in complex flows. These fluids, encountered in manufacturing processes such as fiber spinning, hydraulic fracturing, and roll-to-roll film production, experience alternating regimes of shear and extension in a Lagrangian frame. By using SHERE’s microgravity dataset, the study seeks to isolate the interplay between polymer stresses, particle orientation, and flow disturbances—effects that cannot be cleanly separated in Earth’s gravity. The overarching goal is to develop quantitative predictions and mechanistic insights into how particles alter extensional flow responses, strain hardening, and energy dissipation in viscoelastic suspensions. Approach The investigation combines numerical simulations, theoretical modeling, and SHERE flight data validation. The SHERE experiments measured transient extensional responses of dilute particle suspensions in Boger fluids at moderate extension rates—regimes inaccessible on Earth due to sedimentation and buoyancy. To interpret these data, the project applies finite-difference methods in spheroidal coordinates to resolve inertia-less viscoelastic flows around suspended particles, capturing strong local stress gradients near particle surfaces. Semi-analytical theories are also employed to predict rheology in the limit of small polymer concentrations, allowing parameter sweeps that are computationally prohibitive in full simulations. Three flow classes are studied: (1) sphere suspensions in transient extension with/without pre-shear to directly compare with SHERE data; (2) spheroidal particle suspensions transitioning between shear and extension to mimic fiber-film processing; and (3) alternating shear/extension flows modeling turbulent drag reduction. Together, this multi-method approach bridges PSI experimental data with first-principles rheological predictions. Hypothesis The central hypothesis is that particle-polymer interactions fundamentally alter the transient extensional rheology of polymer solutions in ways that cannot be predicted by simple additive models of particle and polymer stresses. Specifically, the particle-induced velocity disturbances are expected to modify local polymer stress distributions, suppress strain hardening at large deformations, and alter stress development depending on flow history (e.g., pre-shear orientation effects). Furthermore, anisotropic particles such as spheroids will introduce orientation-dependent rheological signatures, leading to different stress responses under alternating shear and extension. By validating these predictions with SHERE microgravity data, the study tests whether advanced numerical and theoretical models can accurately capture the coupled dynamics of particles and polymers across relevant industrial flow regimes. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits In-Space Benefits: For space exploration and on-orbit manufacturing, understanding the rheology of particle-laden polymeric fluids is crucial for the design of efficient life-support systems, in-space fabrication, and thermal management technologies. Microgravity eliminates sedimentation, enabling stable suspensions and novel material processing methods, such as fiber spinning and advanced coatings. Insights from SHERE-based models improve predictability of fluid performance in spacecraft systems where multiphase, particle-laden fluids may be used. Earth Benefits: On Earth, particle-polymer suspensions underpin industries such as hydraulic fracturing, fiber spinning, extrusion molding, roll-to-roll manufacturing, and enhanced oil recovery. Adding particles imparts tailored mechanical or conductive properties but also increases energy demands due to altered rheology. This project provides mechanistic predictions for how particle orientation and polymer stress coupling influence flow resistance, helping optimize industrial processes, reduce energy consumption, and enable development of high-performance materials. By combining SHERE microgravity data with advanced modeling, this work addresses gaps in extensional rheology knowledge that hinder efficient design of complex fluid processing systems. title: Structure and Properties of Pb-Sn and Pb-free Sn-Ag-Cu Solders Produced in Terrestrial vs. Microgravity Environments under Extremes of Elevated and Cryo Temperatures
objectives: This study addresses the reliability of solder joints in space by pursuing two principal objectives: (1) Characterization of solder-joint formation under microgravity conditions aboard the Internation...
approach: The study examined three distinct solder alloys: the ISSI lead-based (40Pb-60Sn) composition, an off-eutectic 50Pb-50Sn formulation, and a lead-free alloy consisting of 95.5Sn-3.8Ag-0.7Cu. Microstruct...
detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 487.38 GB PSI-181Version 1 Structure and Properties of Pb-Sn and Pb-free Sn-Ag-Cu Solders Produced in Terrestrial vs. Microgravity Environments under Extremes of Elevated and Cryo Temperatures Investigation Submitted Date: 17-Apr-2025 Initial Release Date: 20-Aug-2025 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/td9e-cz97 Research Area: Materials Science SubResearch Area: Microstructural Characterization, Terrestrial vs Microgravity Effects, Solder Joints Related Investigation: PSI-77 License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Ground Investigation Proposal Title Structure, Properties, and Performance of Solder Joints in Terrestrial vs. Reduced-Gravity Environments Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 01-01-2020 Investigation End Date 12-31-2022 Sponsoring Agency NASA, PSI grant NASA Center Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) Objectives This study addresses the reliability of solder joints in space by pursuing two principal objectives: (1) Characterization of solder-joint formation under microgravity conditions aboard the International Space Station, specifically examining the impact of suppressed convective flow and buoyancy on 40Pb-60Sn alloys utilized in the In-Space Soldering Investigation (ISSI). (2) Evaluation of the solder’s material and mechanical properties under extreme thermal environments, including elevated and cryogenic temperature exposures characteristic of spaceflight conditions. Approach The study examined three distinct solder alloys: the ISSI lead-based (40Pb-60Sn) composition, an off-eutectic 50Pb-50Sn formulation, and a lead-free alloy consisting of 95.5Sn-3.8Ag-0.7Cu. Microstructural characterization was performed on four solder specimens processed in microgravity from the ISSI investigation, one terrestrial ISSI solder, and a freshly fabricated terrestrial 40wt%Pb-60wt%Sn sample. These analyses elucidated the role of suppressed buoyancy and natural convection in void formation within microgravity environments. Evidence of void-induced Marangoni convection influencing microstructure development was demonstrated using wire-feed solder processed in space. The micromechanical response of solders fabricated under both terrestrial and microgravity conditions was further evaluated across a broad thermal range (–157ºC to +121ºC), simulating the conditions encountered externally on the International Space Station. Investigations under cryogenic conditions focused on the β-to-α phase transformation in Sn below 13ºC, examining associated volumetric expansion, internal stress evolution, and the ductile-to-brittle transition phenomena observed in Sn-based alloys. At ambient temperature, the influence of accelerated aging on both microstructural stability and mechanical performance was assessed. Hypothesis In microgravity environments, fluid dynamics are markedly constrained, predominantly governed by solidification-induced volumetric changes, thermally driven density gradients, and Marangoni convection. This suppression of fluid motion results in diminished mixing, causing voids and gas bubbles to remain entrapped within the solder joint during the solidification process. Such internal porosity critically impairs the solder’s thermal and electrical conductivity, while also compromising the mechanical robustness of the joint. To advance the feasibility of extended space missions, this study seeks to elucidate the fundamental mechanisms, observable phenomena, and process parameters that influence the structural and functional integrity of solder joints fabricated under terrestrial and microgravity conditions. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits The research presented in this project offers significant contributions across multiple space exploration initiatives: (i) The project objectives are closely aligned with ongoing NASA initiatives focused on metal joining techniques in reduced gravity environments. The three solder alloys investigated—selected in collaboration with NASA partners, underscoring the relevance of the study to future space exploration efforts, (ii) The findings are expected to inform the design of future experiments responsive to forthcoming NASA proposal calls, including those associated with the Artemis program, which aims to return humans to the lunar surface, (iii) The insights gained into microgravity fluid behavior and surface tension variation can be extended to a broad range of spaceflight-enabling technologies, such as boiling, heat transfer, combustion, welding, brazing, and soldering. This research enhances the understanding of gravity-driven separation processes—such as gas bubble removal—that must be accomplished via alternative mechanisms in microgravity conditions. (iv) The gravity-level-specific protocols (GLSPs) developed for various soldering configurations serve as practical guidance for future investigations into metal joining techniques under reduced gravity. These protocols may be adopted by scientists and flight personnel for welding, brazing, and soldering applications in spaceflight environments. Contact(s) Siddhartha Pathakemail,Ralph E. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 454.38 GB PSI-177Version 1 Investigating the Structure of Paramagnetic Aggregates from Colloidal Emulsions - 4(InSPACE-4) Investigation Submitted Date: 10-Feb-2025 Initial Release Date: 15-Aug-2025 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/jq1d-x679 Research Area: Complex Fluids - Soft Matter SubResearch Area: Colloids Related Investigation: PSI-74, PSI-75, PSI-76 License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Proposal Title Structural and Rheological Transitions of Field-Responsive Fluids in Microgravity Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 09-01-2016 Investigation End Date 08-31-2023 Sponsoring Agency National Science Foundation (NSF), ISS National Laboratory (ISSNL) NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives The overall objective of the InSPACE-4 investigation was to study the effects of particle shape and toggle duty cycle on the phase separation kinetics of particles in toggled fields. Three specific objectives include: (1) investigation of phase separation kinetics of anisotropic particles in toggled fields, (2) study the effect of toggle duty-cycle on the phase diagram, and (3) perform concurrent ground-based self-assembly experiments using the same magnetic colloids and extend the work to dielectric (insulating) particles driven by toggled alternating current (AC) electric fields.Concurrent ground-based experiments help translate International Space Station (ISS) discoveries to Earth-based manufacture by providing additional insights into the structure of equilibrated phases. Approach This ISS investigation was conducted using magnetic prolate ellipsoids with aspect ratios ranging from 2:1 to 4:1. Experiments involving spheres was also be conducted for comparison purposes. The sample material consisted of randomly oriented nano Fe3O4 coated polymer beads within a fluid filled vial, creating a magnetorheological fluid (MR). The vials were subjected to a pulsed magnetic field, which created a configuration of three-dimensional structures.The particle orientation was determined from birefringence measurements using crossed polarizers. The effects of particle shape, anisotropy, and magnetic field toggling frequency on the phase separation of particles was examined. Relatively short duration, ground-based experiments was conducted using the same magnetic particles to provide additional details about structure formation from particle-level to mesoscale structure. Hypothesis Due to their anisotropic dynamics and interactions, investigators hypothesize that particle shape, in particular anisotropy (having different physical properties along different molecular axes), affects the phase separation kinetics of suspensions in toggled fields. Theoretical and simulation results suggesting that dynamic self-assembly can access a broad range of states analogous to equilibrium phases, even metastable ones, was also tested. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits Discoveries from this work could lead to advanced materials for space applications such as better thermal shields, protection from micrometeorites, materials for energy production, energy-transfer devices, control systems and new mechanical actuators and sensors for robotic and human missions. This investigation helps advance the manufacture of next-generation nanomaterials for applications on Earth such as thermal shields, sound damping devices, shock absorbers, camouflage, medical diagnostic and environmental sensors, display technologies and advanced coatings. The technology also is expanding into larger-scale applications such as building foundation stabilizers for areas prone to earthquakes. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 116.24 MB PSI-186Version 2 Coupled Growth in Hypermonotectics(CGH) Investigation Submitted Date: 25-Jul-2025 Initial Release Date: 12-Aug-2025 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/bmfr-9m70 Research Area: Materials Science SubResearch Area: Solidification License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform Space Shuttle Investigation Start Date 01-01-1993 Investigation End Date 05-31-2005 Sponsoring Agency NASA NASA Center Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) Objectives The overall objective of the Coupled Growth in Hypermonotectics is to understand the fundamental physics controlling solidification in immiscible alloy systems. Specific experimental goals were (1) to show that production of an aligned fibrous microstructure is possible in hypermonotectic alloys by achieving interfacial stability and steady state coupled growth through microgravity processing, (2) to determine the influence of alloy composition and growth velocity on microstructure, and (3) to determine the growth velocity and composition range over which interface stability is possible in a hypermonotectic alloy system. Approach The CGH experiment investigation flew aboard the Life and Microgravity Spacelab (LMS) mission during the summer of 1996. Processing conditions were controlled in an attempt to force the production of an aligned fibrous phase in the microstructure of processed samples. The Advanced Gradient Heating Facility (AGHF) was used to directionally solidify the immiscible alloys. Aluminum (Al)-Indium (In) alloys were studied and specialized aluminum nitride (AlN) ampoules were used in order to control several undesirable effects that are sometimes observed during low gravity processing. Three alloy compositions, namely 17.3 weight % In monotectic, and 18.5 and 19.7 weight percent In hypermonotectic alloys were processed during this mission. A thermal gradient of 67 C/cm was achieved and all flight samples were processes at a translation velocity of 1 micrometer/s. Ground based control samples were subsequently processed under conditions identical to those of two of the flight samples in order to allow a direct comparison of the results. Hypothesis This investigation aimed to answer fundamental unanswered questions concerning solidification of immiscible alloys, namely: (a) is it possible to solidify a hypermonotectic alloy under steady state interfacially stable conditions to produce a fibrous microstructure, (b) can a simple supercooling approach predict stability limits, (c) does extensive diffusion in the liquid phases result in morphological effects not observed in eutectic systems, and (d) what role does surface tension driven flow play at the solidification front. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits Many alloys in immiscible systems show great promise for potential applications in areas that include superconductors, magnetic materials, catalysts, and electrical contacts. For example, some immiscible alloys may be used to produce filters that can remove micron-sized particles for medical applications. Other alloys are expected to exhibit superconducting characteristics or have unusual magnetic properties. Contact(s) J. Barry Andrews (retired)email,Sam R. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 1.47 GB PSI-166Version 2 Unified Support for THERMOLAB - ISS, ICOPROSOL and PARSEC(EML USTIP Batch 2) Investigation Submitted Date: 06-Jan-2025 Initial Release Date: 05-Aug-2025 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/hsz9-cr03 Research Area: Materials Science SubResearch Area: thermophysical properties, nucleation and growth License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 09-01-2010 Investigation End Date 11-15-2015 Sponsoring Agency NASA, ESA NASA Center Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) Objectives Specific objectives of this investigation were as follows: • Plan and develop experiment parameter sets to investigate anomalous nucleation events in zirconium samples during ISS-EML experiments • Analyze cavitation-induced nucleation experiments on zirconium and zirconium-nickel alloys • Analyze fluid flow during ISS-EML experiments to support collaborators investigations • Continue flight preparations and development of experimental parameter sets for upcoming experiments in Batch 3 • Provide magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) modeling support of macroconvection in various materials for three ESA sponsored projects: PARSEC, THERMOLAB - ISS, ICOPROSOL. Approach • The anomalous nucleation events of interest are hypothesized to be caused by cavitation in the melt. Experiments replicated the conditions in which the nucleation events were previously observed and explored similar experimental conditions. • Magnetohydrodynamic modeling of fluid flow is to be used to determine the flow conditions during ISS-EML experiments. Relevant parameters include fluid velocity, shear rates, turbulence intensity, and their distribution. Such data is critical for control of experiments and input to other theoretical and modeling efforts. Hypothesis • Dynamic nucleation is an effect of the fluid flow and not reliant on classical nucleation theory. • Thermophysical property measurements may require appropriate flow conditions, which should be quantified • Flow conditions may affect solidification and nucleation behavior • Oxygen may influence surface tension measurements in metallic melts Research Impacts/Earth Benefits Containerless processing provides access to the deeply undercooled region of metallic melts. Using this unique processing environement we are able to investigate fundamental solidification behaivor and meausure thermophysical properties of metallic melts including density, surface tension, viscosity, thermal expansion, heat capacity, thermal conductivity, and electrical conductivity. More specifically, impacts and benefits are broken out by the 3 associated flight experiments. In PARSEC, the effect of fluid flow on the solidification path of certain alloys is investigated. Control of the solidification path would enable tailoring of the microstructure and properties of metal parts for specific applications. In ThermoLAB, the thermophysical properties of high-temperature materials is investigated. Many of these materials are used commercially. A better understanding of the physical properties will allow more efficient and more reliable production of metallic parts using these alloys. Other alloys are chosen because of scientific interest in their properties, which may illuminate fundamental physics related to the formation of bulk metallic glasses and quasicrystals. The nucleation and growth of quasicrystals, and the effect of atomic-scale order on the macroscopic properties of these alloys is investigated in ICOPROSOL. This fundamental investigation may improve our ability to tailor the microstructure of metals for commercial applications. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 444.65 KB PSI-185Version 1 Testing Analytical and Numerical Models in Phase Coarsening using NASA Physical Sciences Informatics System Investigation Submitted Date: 22-Jul-2025 Initial Release Date: 01-Aug-2025 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/q87k-9f72 Research Area: Materials Science SubResearch Area: Simulation, Microstructure Evolution Related Investigation: PSI-44, PSI-40, PSI-41 License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Ground Investigation Investigation Start Date 09-16-2016 Investigation End Date 09-15-2020 Sponsoring Agency NASA, PSI grant NASA Center Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) Objectives NASA has supported “coarsening in solid–liquid mixtures” (CSLM) experiments, performed in microgravity on the International Space Station (ISS), with greatly reduced sedimentation rate in partially molten alloys. CSLM experimental data are stored in NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI). Microgravity experiments offer a unique opportunity to test existing numerical modeling and theories of phase coarsening. The objective of this research is to test existing numerical modeling methods for simulation of the microstructure evolution that occurs during phase coarsening, using experimental data for Sn-Pb mixtures currently held in PSI. Results from this research can be found in the following publications: Wang, K.G., Glicksman, M.E. Testing Numerical Modeling of Phase Coarsening by Microgravity Experiments. JOM 69, 2825–2830 (2017). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11837-017-2553-x Approach (1) use data archived in NASA's PSI system from the Coarsening in Solid-Liquid Mixtures (CSLM) microgravity experiments to determine mean and maximum particle sizes in each sample processed through the CSLM microgravity experiments; (2) apply a two-dimensional (2-D) phase-field simulation code to allow simulation and evolution of initial microstructures that were observed in the CSLM experiments for Sn-Pb solid-liquid phase mixtures, and which provide input data for our phase-field code to numerically evolve coarsened microstructures over time; (3) calculate particle size distributions (PSDs) from the prior NASA CSLM experiments, our phase-field and multiparticle diffusion simulations, and from diffusion screening theory. Hypothesis Phase-field and multiparticle diffusion numerical methods can be applied to simulate the evolution of the microstructure during phase coarsening, delivering accurate statistical physical quantities such as the particle size distribution (PSD). Phase-field modeling can adequately capture the complexity of the microstructures developed during phase coarsening at large volume fraction. In contrast, multiparticle diffusion modeling can track the evolution of microstructures consisting of nearly spherical particles that develop during phase coarsening at lower volume fraction. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits The contributions from our research activities improved the understanding of fundamental materials phenomena, i.e., phase coarsening. We advanced the state of the art in both theory and simulation. Better understanding of two-phase microstructures will help engineers improve process designs in economically important areas, including liquid-phase sintering for the production of hard tool materials. The theory and simulation tools developed herein that are tested by microgravity experiments, will provide technical pointers for the improvement of important processes, microstructures, and materials properties. The improved knowledge of microstructure evolution in this project will have significant impact on alloy design and service-life strategies for alloy materials. The theory and simulation tools developed will provide guidance toward exploring the structure and properties of alloys. Finally, the theoretical and computational tools will save money and time for alloy modification. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 474.07 MB PSI-148Version 2 Spurious Grain Formation in Alloys Directionally Solidified on the Space Station Due to Marangoni Convection Investigation Submitted Date: 24-Feb-2023 Initial Release Date: 24-Jul-2025 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/dnd8-ke54 Research Area: Materials Science SubResearch Area: Granular Materials License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Ground Investigation Investigation Start Date 09-16-2019 Investigation End Date 02-24-2023 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), PSI Grant NASA Center Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) Objectives Develop a three dimensional solidification model incorporating Marangoni convection and thermosolutal convection which can predict formation of spurious grains during DS. Extract data, such as, fluid velocities along stream lines as a function of distance from the surface-void, angular rotation of the fragmented side arms due to Marangoni flow lines, etc. from PFMI (Pore Formation and Mobility Investigation) videos, and then compare these observations with the simulations in order to quantitatively validate our numerical model. Use that model to predict formation of spurious grains in a totally different alloy, Al-7Si (MICAST), under varying processing conditions, such as, during re-melting prior to DS, after a step increase or decrease in growth speed vs at constant speed, etc. Approach Use the PFMI and MICAST experimental flight data available in PSI to validate a three dimensional solidification model to predict that formation of spurious grains during DS. Hypothesis Columnar and dendritic growth experiments in a predominantly diffusive microgravity environment have shown the presence of voids at the melt-crucible interface which are the likely the source of Marangoni convective flows. It is hypothesized that it is this flow that is responsible for fragmentation of the dendrite-side arm, and its rotation which creates the nucleus for the subsequent growth and formation of spurious grains. This hypothesis was tested by numerically simulating the influence of the Marangoni convection on the trajectory of such a dendrite fragment in the alloy melt and comparing with the experimental observations. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits Results from this research are valuable not only for terrestrial technologies involving solidification, such as repairing gas turbine blade tips by laser cladding, but also for any future space manufacture or repair which involves solidification. objectives: The Ring-Sheared Drop (RSD) is a Microgravity Science Glovebox experiment that launched in July 2019 to the ISS to study shearing flow in the absence of solid walls. The major goals of this project we...
approach: Preflight preparation included refurbishment of all test cells including modification of test cells S/N 101-106 to include the flight tested (both parabolic and ISS with the assistance of NASA MSFC) i...
detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 29.77 GB PSI-160Version 1 Ring-Sheared Drop - Interfacial Bioprocessing of Pharmaceuticals(RSD-IBP-I) Investigation Submitted Date: 23-Dec-2024 Initial Release Date: 05-Jun-2025 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/smat-bb74 Research Area: Biophysics SubResearch Area: Soft Matter License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Proposal Title ISS: Collaborative research: Interfacial bioprocessing of pharmaceuticals via the ring-sheared drop (RSD) module aboard the ISS Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 09-15-2019 Investigation End Date 12-31-2023 Sponsoring Agency National Laboratory - National Science Foundation (NL-NSF) NASA Center Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) Objectives The Ring-Sheared Drop (RSD) is a Microgravity Science Glovebox experiment that launched in July 2019 to the ISS to study shearing flow in the absence of solid walls. The major goals of this project were to adapt and use the RSD module to develop and test predictive models of non-Newtonian flow of high-concentration proteins at the interface. Incorporating non-Newtonian constitutive equations for both interfacial and bulk flows and coupling the interfacial and bulk stresses is essential for mechanistic models that would be capable of predicting behavior under flow conditions of practical interest. The coupled problem is intrinsically nonlinear and there is a need to develop robust and accurate numerical techniques to interrogate flow dynamics and experimentally validate and verify results. The ring-sheared drop interfacial bioprocessing of pharmaceuticals-I (RSD-IBP-I) campaign aimed to study non-Newtonian interfacial hydrodynamics of the blood transport proteins bovine serum albumin (BSA) and human serum albumin (HSA) in microgravity. Specifically, scientific aims focus on the effects of protein primary structure (BSA or HSA), protein concentration (4, 40, or 400 mg/mL), and interfacial shear rate (3, 10, or 30 rpm) on microgravity fluid flow, measured using velocimetry of hollow glass microsphere tracer particles within protein samples. This campaign intended to confer improved understanding of interfacial protein flows in relation to physiology, the environment, and industry relevant to both spaceflight and Earth. Approach Preflight preparation included refurbishment of all test cells including modification of test cells S/N 101-106 to include the flight tested (both parabolic and ISS with the assistance of NASA MSFC) integrated deployment tube and upper ring design by TBE, refurbishment of all test cells used in the previous RSD-BPS campaign by TBE, preparation of protein samples and methodological ground controls. Following sample installation, the RSD drop was deployed by extruding a drop from the deployment tube until pinning is achieved at the far ring. Shearing was then commenced by rotation of the far ring, measurements recorded for startup, steady, and stop flows each at 3, 10, and 30 rpm. Each 1.5 min. image sequence was then compressed to a portable video file and downlinked to the ground computer at RPI. ISS flight campaigns occurred Summer 2022 and Spring 2023, achieving 92% of proposed science objectives with 121.5/132 sample videos successfully collected, meeting the criteria for complete success. Additionally, 27 videos of interfacial aging and 24 micrographs of extra data were collected. The RSD hardware concluded the campaign in a nominal configuration with good health and status after four years in space aboard the ISS. Postflight: Test cells were returned June 30th 2023 on SpX-28 to TBE. Test cells appear to be in nominal pre-refurbishment configuration. RSD hardware remains in nominal configuration and good health. Hypothesis The study of fluid interfaces coupled to bulk flows, including non-Newtonian response of either the interfacial or the bulk fluid can be uniquely advanced through experimentation in microgravity, where surface tension containment can be achieved at relatively large length scales. If the hydrodynamics of concentrated protein solutions are precisely measured, then sufficiently descriptive viscosity constitutive relations can be selected or developed from fundamental physics to describe fluid behavior. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits Coupled bulk and interfacial flow in the RSD, developed under this grant is currently being analyzed to aid in formulating a model of non-Newtonian interfacial hydrodynamics coupled to a Newtonian bulk flow. These results were recently submitted for publication in a special issue of the journal Fluids, entitled ''Non-Newtonian Flow: Interfacial and Bulk Phenomena.'' While all cases examined remain at least weakly coupled to the bulk flow, this investigation established the effective ranges of model parameters. Bulk flow profiles demonstrate moderate sensitivity of the bulk flow to the behavior of the air-liquid interface, in general increasing with higher Boussinesq number Bq (non-dimensionalized surface viscosity) while maintaining interface to bulk flow coupling. Furthermore, investigation of dissipation may be useful for gauging the interchange between the hydrodynamics and energetics of flow constituents. The change in Bq by the shear-thinning model is indicative of a change in structure of an constituent material. As such, changes in the shape of a constituent of a complex fluid induced by flow are reciprocal with the changes that manifest in flow behavior. Describing the stability of such reciprocal changes could lead to a better understanding of natural systems as well as improved control of transport phenomena. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 27.12 GB PSI-179Version 1 Aerosol Sampling Experiment(ASE) Investigation Submitted Date: 16-Apr-2025 Initial Release Date: 05-Jun-2025 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/pdgr-c961 Research Area: Complex Fluids - Soft Matter SubResearch Area: Multiphase Flow License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 09-01-2016 Investigation End Date 10-01-2019 Sponsoring Agency NASA, R.J. Lee Group NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives Aerosols are small particles suspended in the air, and in Earth’s atmosphere, aerosols include soot, dust, pollen and a wide range of other natural and human-made materials. Smoke does not rise and dust does not settle in microgravity the way they do on Earth, causing aerosols to behave differently and pose hazards for crew members breathing the air. The Aerosol Sampling Experiment (ASE) collects airborne particles in the International Space Station’s (ISS) cabin air, and returns them to Earth for scientists to study. The objectives of ASE were: 1- Characterize airborne particulate matter aboard the ISS to assess air quality for crew health and hardware longevity. 2- Identify particle sources (e.g., human skin, equipment wear, biological contaminants) in the spacecraft environment. 3- Improve understanding of particle transport and accumulation in microgravity conditions. 4- Support design of future spacecraft air filtration systems, ensuring they are appropriately targeted for actual airborne particle profiles. Approach The ASE approach involved passive aerosol sampling in multiple ISS modules using filters placed in air ducts and cabin areas (especially near high-traffic zones and vents) by deploying commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) samplers for long-duration exposure (3 months–1 year). The sampled filters were returned to Earth for ground-based analysis using: 1- Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM), 2- Energy-Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDS) and 3- Gravimetric analysis. The ISS samples were compared to terrestrial cleanroom and indoor environments to assess relative cleanliness and particle source uniqueness. Data collected was cross-referenced with previous ISS air monitoring efforts (e.g., TOCA, CCAA) to inform models of contaminant accumulation and mitigation. Hypothesis Airborne particulate matter aboard the ISS exhibits a different size distribution, composition, and transport behavior in microgravity compared to Earth-based environments, and that particles from crew activity and hardware wear contribute significantly to the aerosol burden as well as the assumption that microgravity reduces sedimentation, allowing finer particles to stay suspended longer and accumulate in regions not typically affected by gravity-based settling on Earth. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits Crew members on the ISS are breathing more or less the same fixed volume of air that has been on the ISS for years. There is no chance to get ‘fresh air’ as we do on Earth, but an advanced air revitalization system processes and cleans the air continuously. Crew members in space have complained of allergies and nose and eye irritation, which suggests the ISS cabin air has a high concentration of tiny particles that can be inhaled. The ISS filtration system is designed to remove these particles, but researchers have no way to verify the efficiency or cleanliness of the air. This investigation generates new data to characterize the quality of the air on the ISS, in terms of particles. Future space travelers may benefit from this data, as they can be used in the design and selection of particle detectors appropriate for low gravity. Long-term manned space missions need aerosol measurement capability to ensure crew health and comfort Contact(s) Marit E. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 3.99 MB PSI-12Version 2 Growth of Large, Perfect Protein Crystals for Neutron Crystallography(Perfect Crystals) Investigation Submitted Date: 11-Sep-2024 Initial Release Date: 07-Nov-2024 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/yc1k-qw81 Research Area: Biophysics SubResearch Area: Crystal Growth Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 09-01-2017 Investigation End Date 08-31-2021 Sponsoring Agency NASA NASA Center Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) Objectives The Perfect Crystals investigation uses microgravity environment on the International Space Station to grow crystals of human manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD). This sheds light on how the antioxidant protein helps protect the human body from oxidizing radiation and oxides created as a byproduct of metabolism. For best results, the analysis technique requires large crystals with minimal imperfections, which are more easily produced in the microgravity environment of the space station. Approach The Growth of Large, Perfect Protein Crystals for Neutron Crystallography investigation grows perfect, large-volume crystal suitable for neutron macromolecular crystallography of large unit cell protein crystals in microgravity. The protein of study in this investigation is human manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD or SOD2), which has an enzymatic mechanism that relies on a proton shuttling pattern that has yet to be fully elucidated. Neutron macromolecular crystallography allows for visualization of protons that cannot be achieved by XRay Diffraction or Cryo-EM, but requires large-volume crystals minimal imperfection for best results. Gravity has been implicated as a cause of defects in crystals grown on Earth. The marriage of the liquid-liquid capillary diffusion crystal growth technique to the microgravity environment aboard the International Space Station (ISS) allows for the growth of multiple greater than 1 mm3 crystals with very few defects. Please refer to AccessingPerfectCrystalData.pdf under the Science Documents section. Hypothesis In 2001, the Borgstahl laboratory successfully grew large crystals of SOD using microgravity conditions on the International Space Station (ISS). Using existing crystallization hardware that uses the Granada Crystallization Boxes (GCB) for capillary counter diffusion protocols will be used to achieve microgravity crystallization results for SOD. The principal outcome will be to identify the role of hydrogen atoms in enzymatic activity, discern superoxide from peroxide, and water from hydroxide ion by their protonation state and decipher a structure-based mechanism for human MnSOD more precisely than from previous X-ray crystallographic models determined from Earth-grown crystals. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits Manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD) is implicated in a number of human diseases, including non-Hodgkins lymphoma, lung cancer and colorectal cancer. Understanding how it works is an important step toward developing better prevention and treatment methods for such diseases. In space application, MnSOD could help researchers protect astronauts on future long-term missions. Astronauts receive significantly more exposure to oxidizing radiation than people on Earth, and on long journeys such as to Mars may receive dangerous doses that create Reactive Oxygen Species (ROS). These can damage DNA and other biomolecules, causing diseases such as cancer. The manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD) enzyme converts ROS into molecular oxygen and hydrogen peroxide, which other enzymes can then break down. Studies on MnSOD can help researchers can develop artificial techniques to reduce ROS and help protect astronauts on future long-term missions. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 1.03 TB PSI-4Version 2 Flow Boiling and Condensation Experiment Flow Boiling Module(FBCE FBM) Investigation Submitted Date: 28-Aug-2024 Initial Release Date: 25-Oct-2024 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/s3td-y977 Research Area: Fluid Physics SubResearch Area: Two Phase Flow and Heat Transfer Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Proposal Title Flow Boiling and Condensation Experiment Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 06-01-2017 Investigation End Date 12-31-2021 Sponsoring Agency NASA NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives The proposed research aims to develop an integrated two-phase flow boiling/condensation facility for the International Space Station (ISS) to serve as a primary platform for obtaining two-phase flow and heat transfer data in microgravity. By comparing the microgravity data against those obtained in Earth’s gravity, it will be possible to ascertain the influence of body force on two-phase transport phenomena in pursuit of mechanistic models as well as correlations, and to help determine the minimum flow criteria to ensure gravity independent flow boiling and condensation. This research is a joint effort between the Purdue University Boiling and Two-Phase Flow Laboratory (PU-BTPFL) and the NASA Glenn Research Center. Personnel from the two organizations combine extensive experience in research and development of both flow boiling and condensation systems, and in conducting microgravity experiments. The objectives of the Flow Boiling and the Flow Condensation Experiment (FBCE) in the long duration microgravity environment of the ISS are to: 1. Develop experimentally validated, mechanistic model for microgravity flow boiling critical heat flux (CHF) and dimensionless criteria to predict minimum flow velocity required to ensure gravity independent CHF. 2. Develop experimentally validated, mechanistic model for microgravity annular condensation and dimensionless criteria to predict minimum flow velocity required to ensure gravity independent annular condensation. Also, develop correlations for other condensation regimes in microgravity. 3. Obtain flow boiling data (heat flux, flow visualization, the wall temperature difference) in long duration microgravity environments for a well characterized heating surface as functions of liquid inlet mass velocity and subcooling. 4. Obtain flow condensation data (heat flux, flow visualization, the wall temperature difference) in long duration microgravity environments for a well-characterized condensing surface as functions of inlet quality and flow rate of condensing vapor. Specific tasks for the study will be as follows. Approach The approach used in this project is to perform the following sequential series of tasks: 1. Provide detailed design and instrumentation requirements for the Flow Boiling Module (FBM). 2. Provide design and instrumentation requirements for the entire flow loop. 3. Generate test matrix for operating conditions of the study. 4. Perform initial validation tests in both terrestrial gravity and parabolic flight. 5. Perform tests on board the ISS. 6. Based on both the ISS and terrestrial data, develop a series of predictive tools, including empirical correlations as well as theoretical, computational, and machine learning models. Hypothesis In literature spanning many decades, body force in terrestrial gravity is identified as having a profound influence on two-phase transport behavior. This behavior is drastically altered In the absence of gravity, wherein flow fluid and heat transfer are dictated by flow inertia and surface tension. This implies predictive tools from terrestrial gravity studies are inapplicable for design of NASA's reduced gravity systems. This limitation points to a need for performing two-phase flow and heat transfer experiments on board the ISS as basis for formulating relevant reduced gravity predictive tools. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits The proposed research will lay the foundation for development of advanced high power to weight ratio thermal management systems for NASA's future space vehicles and planetary bases. Purdue University research has also shown tremendous value in findings from this projects to numerous other applications including ultra-fast charging of electric vehicles, fusion reactors, hydrogen storage, avionics, high-Mach turbine engines, and advanced electronics in laser, microwave, and radar systems. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 526.95 GB PSI-1Version 1 Round Robin - Thermophysical Property Measurement(ELF-2 Round Robin) Investigation Submitted Date: 27-Aug-2024 Initial Release Date: 16-Oct-2024 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/8jtx-fx45 Research Area: Materials Science SubResearch Area: Metals Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Proposal Title Round Robin: Thermophysical Property Measurement, Augmented-Program for Levitation Utilization in Space (A-PLUS) Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 04-01-2017 Investigation End Date 02-28-2023 Sponsoring Agency NASA NASA Center Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) Objectives The key scientific objectives are: (a) Conducting baseline space ESL containerless property measurement experiments for two paired classes of levitation-based thermophysical properties:Density/Thermal Expansion, Viscosity/Surface Tension. (b) Selecting materials compatible with both electrostatic levitation (ESL) and electromagnetic levitation (EML) to allow comparison between space facilities. (c) Using modeling to evaluate theories used to predict the influence of gravity on propertymeasurement experiments. (d) Actively encouraging collaboration with existing science teams using other facilities through organizing a Round Robin test consortium Approach The experimental approach involved inserting a sample carousel of 20 individual samples into the JAXA ISS-ELF facility, conditioning the test atmosphere, and conducting individual melt cycles on each sample. The heating lasers were used to precondition the sample when the sample is heated to a desired pre-bake temperature. Following the preconditioning period, the sample was charged by the electrodes and released to achieve stable positioning. The lasers were then used to thermally cycle the sample. The cycle starts by application of the highest laser heating power (activated by a control current setting in the ELF software measured in amps) until the sample is fully molten and achieved the maximum liquid superheat temperature. The heater power was then turned down to maintain the desired isothermal hold. Surface excitation was conducted using varying volage from the electrodes at this temperature. Surface tension and viscosity was measured using the droplet oscillation behavior. The laser power was then turned off to allow the molten sample to cool down. Density and cp/ε evaluations are conducted during the free cooling without any influence from the laser. Once recalescence occurred, the sample was then allowed to become fully solid at room temperature which marks the completion of a thermal cycle. Overall, processing a single melt cycle can take up to 10 - 15 minutes excluding the pre-bake. Following the cycle completion, the sample is retrieved back into the cartridge to end the test on this sample. Using the described experimental approach several thermophysical properties were measured on a variety of metallic melts as described below: 1. Density –One high-speed video camera was used to monitor the sample size as a function of time during the free cooling phase. Sample edge was detected using a custom algorithm for the density measurement. The volume of the sample was calculated using a known calibration of pixels/mm3, which was subsequently correlated with temperature allowing calculation of density and thermal expansion coefficient (from the slope of the density curve). Tracking of sample mass loss was accomplished post-mission using Langmuir’s equation of evaporation. 2. Surface tension – After melting, the heating laser is set to a reduced value such that the sample is held at constant temperature. A sinusoidal modulation of the positioning voltage was applied to both electrodes to excite surface oscillations without changing sample position. The resulting sample deformation was measured by the high-speed linear array. A frequeny sweep was conducted to identify natural frequency. Two method was applied to identify the natural frequency from the sweep: (1) Maximum amplitude method where maximum deformation is observed at the natural frequency and (2) Excitation crossover method where the natural frequency was observed at the linear intersections of the damped and free oscillations. Natural frequencies identified using both methods were used to evaluate the surface tension. 3. Viscosity – In conjunction to surface tension, viscosity was measured from the damped oscillations at the identified natural frequency. The characteristic exponential time decay from a sinusoidal fit was used to evaluate the viscosity. 4. Specific heat capacity and emissivity – The ratio of these two quantities was evaluated from the cooling curve as monitored by the IR pyrometer after correction for conductive mass losses to the gas environment. 5. Evaporation – Integration of the time-temperature profile allows calculation of evaporation assuming a known relationship using Langmuir’s equation for loss as a function of temperature. Pre- and post- measurement of sample mass anchors these predictions. Dynamic mass is crucial for tracking for density, surface tension and viscosity measurement. Hypothesis The experimental hypothesis was that in microgravity environment in the absence of stirring, high quality thermophysical property would be measured compared to the ground-based levitation facility. This was successfully observed for gold samples. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits This research aids in dissemination of an baseline archived dataset allowing researchers to validate models accounting for gravity-induced systematic error in property measurement used for industrial welding, casting and additive manufacturing operations . Industry will be better able to correlate ground and space results to expand the quantity and quality of available information without the requirement for access to space. Advance the understanding of how to best allocate the scant resources available for space-based materials property measurement using levitation. In the future this could lead to development of a model where fidelity and cost can be readily calculated for a given material classification and serve as the basis for prioritization of specific ground and space thermophysical property investigations. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 238.65 GB PSI-3Version 3 NASA Research Under Project Quasi-crystalline Undercooled Alloys for Space Investigation (QUASI) and ESA-Based Investigations, THERMOLAB-ISS and ICOPROSOL(EML B1-QUASI) Investigation Submitted Date: 28-Aug-2024 Initial Release Date: 09-Oct-2024 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/rwgz-es78 Research Area: Materials Science SubResearch Area: Metals Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Proposal Title NASA Research Under Project Quasi-crystalline Undercooled Alloys for Space Investigation (QUASI) and ESA-Based Investigations, THERMOLAB-ISS and ICOPROSOL Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 05-01-2000 Investigation End Date 05-31-2013 Sponsoring Agency NASA NASA Center Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) Objectives The primary objectives are: 1. Investigations of nucleation of crystal phases from supercooled (metastable) liquids as a function of stirring (fluid-flow) conditions. Systematic studies of this under terrestrial conditions are not possible due to the presence of convective flow in the liquid. 2. Measurements of thermophysical properties of metallic liquids under microgravity conditions, including the specific heat, viscosity, surface tension. These are then compared with measurements made under terrestrial conditions, when possible. These data are important for the analysis of the nucleation data, fluid flow calculations; additionally they are important for understanding fundamental connections between liquid dynamics and structure. Approach Measurements of the supercooling are made under controlled stirring conditions. The nucleation rates are derived from the distribution of maximum supercooling following the approach developed by Skripov. By systematically changing the fluid-flow rates by applying controlled voltages to the heater/positioner coils in the ESA electromagnetic levitation facility on the ISS (ISS-EML), the nucleation rates can be studied as function of stirring, allowing the hypothesis to be examined. Hypothesis When the composition of the nucleating crystal phase is different from that of the liquid, long range diffusion can become important for the nucleation process. The potential impact on the nucleation rate depends on the ratio of the attachment rates to the nucleating cluster and the time required for long-range diffusion. This can be investigated by nucleation measurements made as a function of stirring, since fluid-flow can decrease the impact of long-range diffusion. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits Realistic modeling approaches have the potential to greatly improve the efficiency of materials development. However, progress is frequently hampered by the lack of relevant thermophysical property data needed for the modeling. Further, key processes such as crystal nucleation from the liquid or other phase transitions within the liquid, are often poorly understood, making it difficult to realistically model them. In many cases, the experimental data and a deeper understanding of some processes cannot be obtained from terrestrial experiments due to interactions with sample containers at the temperatures of interest. The combination of the containerless based terrestrial methods and the ISS-EML enables these measurements. In addition to their relevance for processes such as additive manufacturing on earth, where nucleation in highly stirred conditions is important, measurements in two different gravitational fields will be important for designing additive manufacturing in space and on the Moon. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 4.14 GB PSI-2Version 1 Multi-Scale Modeling and Experimentation on Liquid Phase Sintering in Gravity and Microgravity Environments(MSRR GEDS) Investigation Submitted Date: 27-Aug-2024 Initial Release Date: 02-Oct-2024 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/pez3-ew29 Research Area: Materials Science SubResearch Area: Liquid Phase Sintering Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Proposal Title Multi-Scale Modeling and Experimentation on Liquid Phase Sintering in Gravity and Microgravity Environments Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 09-29-2010 Investigation End Date 03-32-2023 Sponsoring Agency NASA NASA Center Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) Objectives In this study, the compositions start with W-Ni-Cu-Mn powder mixtures. The solid-liquid ratio is adjusted via changes in the tungsten content from 70 to 90 wt %. Most of the tungsten remains solid during sintering. The liquid is formed from melting the mechanically alloyed Ni-Cu-Mn additive. The liquid dissolves up to 28 wt % tungsten at the sintering temperature, giving the desired semisolid system. In these experiments, changes are also made to the Ni:Cu ratio from 3:2 to 2:3 to slightly adjust the tungsten solubility. Seven cartridges with seven samples each are processed in microgravity. One cartridge is heated to the temperature where first significant densification occurs on Earth, 1180°C, and five of the cartridges are processed for progressively longer times at 1210°C. A seventh cartridge is for backup in case of an aborted run, otherwise it provides a replicate at 34 min at 1210°C. An early part of this research focused on developing a W-Ni-Cu-Mn alloy to allow lower sintering temperatures to accommodate downgraded furnace peak temperatures. The new alloys are tested using ground proof runs to gather ground data. Those results are contrasted with the microgravity data. Extensive testing is documented to show the experimental platform; tests involved thermal overload, vibration, equipment proofing, evaporation, transient runaway, and temperature verification trials. An early failure in the quartz ampoule led to redesign. Subsequent ground runs were conducted without failure. This report emphasizes the development of the experiments and details the densification and distortion data, and provides microstructure data. Modeling ideas were established early and awaited samples for verification. Much effort was directed to developing a time sequence whereby modeling data would be available for rheological variables associated with the solid-liquid-pore structures existing during sintering, namely extraction of the viscosity and strength variations during the 60 min of isothermal hold. The model is implemented in finite element analysis where stress on the sintering body is assessed using variations in the composition, component size, and gravity. Approach The idea of removing distortion during liquid phase sintering has much appeal. Loss of dimensional precision during sintering is a common industrial problem. Forming technologies allow for precise green bodies (green is the term adopted to indicate the component after forming, but prior to sintering). The body force due to gravity acts in the vertical direction and increases with height and density. In these trials, components of 12 mm in height are processed and analyzed for features such as density, dimensional variation (distortion), microstructure, grain size distribution, and pore agglomeration after return to Earth. Gravity normally produces sufficient substrate friction to locally resist shrinkage during sintering, giving an elephant foot geometry. Microgravity trails examine if densification is possible without distortion, the benefit being net-shape processing. For this research on gravity effects on distortion and densification during liquid phase sintering, the two primary metrics are nonuniform dimensional change and the elimination of pores. Along these lines, isotropic right circular cylinders are fabricated for sintering. Both the initial and sintered dimensions are measured over several locations to quantify densification (and shrinkage) and distortion. Densification is measured using dimensional shrinkage (up to 15 %), relying on the change in porosity divided by the initial porosity (37 %). The samples are initially 63 % dense. Distortion is calculated using multiple dimensional measurements over closely spaced locations and is expressed as the coefficient of variation (standard deviation divided by the mean size). For microstructure assessment to help explain the behavior, the samples are sectioned, mounted, and polished. Optical microscopy, quantitative microscopy, scanning electron microscopy, and energy dispersive analysis of X-rays provide information on the microstructure, especially the pore and grain structure. Quantitative microstructure data include grain size, pore size, connectivity, and distributions for these features. The results are compared to models to validate constitutive laws. In prior research microgravity resulted in large pores, extensive distortion, and a low grain connectivity microstructure with smaller grains. Hypothesis The idea of removing distortion during liquid phase sintering has much appeal. Loss of dimensional precision during sintering is a common industrial problem. Forming technologies allow for precise green bodies (green is the term adopted to indicate the component after forming, but prior to sintering). The body force due to gravity acts in the vertical direction and increases with height and density. The distortion problem is most evident in structures with protrusions and unsupported or cantilever features. Accordingly, for some liquid phase sintered components a majority of the production expense is in correcting dimensional issues after sintering, by use of coining, straightening, grinding, or machining. Many powder metallurgy components start with a green density of just 60 % of theoretical. Shaping is possible using a variety of options - die pressing, injection molding, warm extrusion, cold isostatic pressing, or slurry casting. High performance demands a high sintered density, often from 98 to 100 %. The change from 60 to 98 % density comes with about 15 % shrinkage in each dimension. However, as the component height increases gravity induces nonuniform shrinkage. The friction force at the component bottom increases. This friction force resists densification on the bottom surface, resulting in nonuniform dimensions, effectively distorting the green body. The economic attraction for sintering technologies is the delivery of net-shapes, avoiding post-sintering machining if possible. Unfortunately, it is easy to lose dimensional control, necessitating secondary operations that add greatly to the fabrication expense. In the ideal, tooling design would anticipate sintering shrinkage, even nonuniform shrinkage, enabling sintering to directly deliver final size. This would be possible with computer tools to design the tooling in anticipation of shrinkage and distortion. Our initial conjecture suggested that liquid phase sintering in microgravity would remove distortion, since shrinkage and microstructure should be uniform. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits Sintering is a heat treatment applied to powders with the intent of bonding the particles into a solid structure. It is widely applied to forming complex shapes for automotive, computer, metal cutting, oil and gas drilling, hand tools, firearms, and hardware. Tools is designed to shape the powder into a shape that is oversized to allow for shrinkage. With sufficiently high temperature, heat induces atomic motion and repositioning of solid to form bonds between the particles that strengthen the body. Usually that occurs via diffusion along interfaces such as grain boundary liquid films. In industrial production, the powder is shaped prior to sintering, such as by die compaction or injection molding, with subsequent sintering to produce a complex shape. Accordingly, sintering is frequently applied to high performance materials and is applied in practice over a wide range of products and industries from bricks to rocket engines. It is especially useful for high temperature materials, such as the refractory metals, including tungsten. If densification can be acheived without distortion, considerable expense is avoided by net-shape fabrication. In this sense, tremendous industrial benefit is possible using liquid phase sintering with densifcation but no distortion. In the US sintering technologies are responsible for about 60 kg of each automobile, and dozens of parts in each computer and cell phone. Liquid phase sintering is a desirable option, where in an alloy some liquid forms during the heating cycle (between the liquidus and solidus temperatures for the alloy). The idea of liquid phase sintering gained significance attention during the 1920s as a means to consolidate hard powders, such as cemented carbides (WC-Co), into high performance engineering structures, such as metal cutting tools, wire drawing dies, and oil-less bearings. The tungsten heavy alloys emerged at the same time. It is the latter system selected to demonstrate processing gains or losses associated with gravity. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 1.83 GB PSI-83Version 6 Microgravity Investigation of Cement Solidification - Multi-use Variable Gravity Platform(MICS-MVP) Investigation Submitted Date: 15-Sep-2022 Initial Release Date: 01-Oct-2024 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/eqrg-h817 Research Area: Materials Science SubResearch Area: Cement Solidification License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 11-22-2016 Investigation End Date 11-21-2023 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NASA Center Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) Objectives The purpose of the MICS-MVP is to investigate and understand the complex process of cement solidification as a function of variable gravity and to advance the use of concrete materials for extraterrestrial infrastructure. MICS-MVP will identify the differences between the hydration reaction and microstructural formation at the different gravity levels. Approach Two different mixture combinations of with water and gypsum and tricalcium silicate (C3S) with water were hydrated under 5 different gravity levels, namely, Earth's gravity, microgravity, and simulated gravity levels of the Moon, Mars, and a statistical point at 0.7g. The different components were each placed in opposing compartments of a plastic pouch and separated by a middle burstable seal. To burst the seal, the water filled compartment was rolled up from the outside edge towards the middle until enough forward pressure was achieved to burst the seal. The water is then completely moved into the compartment containing the tricalcium aluminate (C3A) or tricalcium silicate (C3S) and the paste is mixed by a rubber spatula and/or kneaded by hand to reach a homogeneous state. A plastic clip is then attached to help consolidate the paste at one end of the pouch. This mixing procedure generally took a few minutes per sample. The ISS itself provides a microgravity environment, whereas the gravity levels of extraterrestrial bodies that are less than Earths were simulated with centrifugal forces within the Multi-use Variable-gravity Platform (MVP). Samples at different gravity levels were hydrated for different lengths of time, following which the centrifuge was shut off and the samples continued to hydrate till they were returned to earth. The samples were characterized for pore size, pore distribution, portlandite size distribution, crystal morphology, and phase content. Hypothesis It is hypothesized that under variable reduced gravity conditions different transport phenomena such as buoyancy, sedimentation, and convection are minimized and a more diffusion dominant transport will lead to varying degree of uniformity in distribution ofphases, porosity, and crystal morphology. A different microstructure is expected to form in at different gravity levels which possibly leads to different physical properties of the reduced gravity hardened cement paste with respect to that hardened in terrestrial gravity (1g). Research Impacts/Earth Benefits The MICS investigation directly addresses the high priority need for lightweight space structures for habitats that protect crew. Results from this investigation enable the characterization of microstructural development in the hardening of cement paste and improve understanding of crystal growth and hydration kinetics, phase formations, pore distribution, and material properties. Also, MICS can increase understanding and control of the crystal growth kinetics, and morphology, to improve concrete properties. Improved cement properties can lead to improved concrete properties, durability, and lower CO2 emission.
