detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 104.14 KB PSI-5Version 3 Plasma Kristall 4(PK-4) Investigation Submitted Date: 28-Aug-2024 Initial Release Date: 27-Sep-2024 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/58f8-6f41 Research Area: Complex Fluids - Soft Matter SubResearch Area: Complex Plasmas Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 09-11-2014 Investigation End Date 03-03-2024 Sponsoring Agency ESA Objectives PK-4 is not an apparatus dedicated for specific experiments but rather a laboratory which shall offer the possibility to perform a large variety of experiments with complex plasmas and to react to new developments in this field in a manner as flexible as possible. The main interest lies in the investigation of the liquid phase and flow phenomena of complex plasmas for which PK-4 is especially suited thanks to a DC-discharge and its geometry (elongated glass tube with a large observational access). The experiments for PK-4 can be divided into research in three classes of fundamental questions: 1. Microscopic properties of complex plasmas This category comprises the charging of the particles, the external forces on the particles (e.g. ion drag), the fundamental interactions between the particles, agglomeration, and particle growth. 2. Macroscopic properties of complex plasmas In this category belong hydrodynamics (e.g. viscosity), thermodynamics (e.g. equation of state), and non-equilibriums aspects (e.g. lane formation, self-organisation) of complex plasmas. 3. Generic properties of classical many-body systems Complex plasmas are ideal model systems for studying various problems of strongly coupled many-body systems in solid state physics, fluid physics, plasma physics, nano-technology and even nuclear physics because complex plasmas can easily be produced and observed in real time on the microscopic and kinetic level. Hence dynamical processes can be investigated on the level of single particles which is not possible in most systems. Therefore new insights in the dynamics of those processes can be provided. Typical examples are crystallization and melting, phonons in plasma crystals, dust waves, Mach cones, nozzles, turbulence, and nano-fluidics. Approach The basic experimental protocol starts with an evacuation of the plasma chamber for several hours (a minimum of 20 hours; base pressure: less than 10-3 Pa) to guarantee good plasma conditions, e.g. no striations. Then neon or argon gas is filled in with a gas flow of typically 2 sccm reaching pressures between 5 and 250 Pa. Afterwards the plasma is ignited by the high-voltage (about 1000 V) of the DC electrodes corresponding to a DC current of the order of 1 mA and a longitudinal electric field of about 2 V/cm. Then the micro-particles are injected. They get quickly charged in the plasma and drift from the cathode to the anode with a typical velocity between 1 and 10 cm/s. In addition, the electric fields from the two RF coils/electrodes or the fast polarity switching can be used to manipulate the particles, e.g. to capture and confine them. Gas flow, modulation of the DC and RF fields, the powerful manipulation laser, the thermal manipulator, and the EM electrode can also be used to manipulate the particles, e.g. to accelerate them or to introduce oscillations. A sketch of the PK-4 experiment is shown in Figure 1. The micro-particles are made visible by illumination with a laser beam, which is widened into a sheet by a cylindrical lens. The scattered light is recorded by one or two CCD cameras (e.g. up to 200 frames per second, with a maximum resolution of about e.g.10 microns/pixel). The light emission (“plasma glow”) from the plasma will be measured using the narrow band IF-filters. The basic measurements comprise the positions of the particles, their velocities (extracted from the track length of the particles or from their positions in consecutive images), and correlations between the particles. These quantities are determined from the images by using a dedicated IDL program or other methods for image analysis. At the end of each experiment run the particles will be removed by gas flow before the plasma is switched off in order to avoid the contamination of the glass walls Research Impacts/Earth Benefits PK-4 enables fundamental investigation of flows and related instabilities, by mimicking molecular mechanisms at a scale which allows for real time in-situ optical observations. This requires on-orbit experiments to be undertaken in order to observe the processes at work, which are obviously disturbed by the influence of gravity on Earth. Even though PK-4 is principally a fundamental experiment, understanding the processes at work and understanding how complex plasmas can be influenced by varying research parameters gives a better understanding of how improvements can be made in areas and industries where plasmas are used. Understanding how dusty plasmas behave in microgravity could shed light on plasma phenomena in space, which could lead to new research methods or improved spacecraft designs. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 355.08 KB PSI-7Version 3 Particle Stabilized Emulsions and Foams(PASTA) Investigation Submitted Date: 28-Aug-2024 Initial Release Date: 26-Sep-2024 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/70cs-xg17 Research Area: Complex Fluids - Soft Matter SubResearch Area: Foams Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Sponsoring Agency ESA Objectives The work proposed in the PASTA project follows the line from characterizing the surface properties of particles via a complex analysis of the properties of layers at liquid/gas and liquid/liquid interfaces to studying the behaviour of liquid films and finally to model real foams and emulsions. The work comprises the application of available knowledge to the preparation and characterization of particle stabilized emulsions, produced by adapting to the Soft Matter Dynamics instrument. The role of gravity on quiescent wet foams can be captured in 2 key questions: Is the growth law for average bubble size R~√ time, such that R dR/dt is a constant? If so, what is the liquid-fraction dependence of this rate? How do the rate and the nature of the bubble rearrangement dynamics change as the liquid fraction is increased to the point of un-jamming (transition solid-like to liquid-like)? PASTA will address the SPECIFIC OBJECTIVES: Evaluate the characteristic time for the droplet coalescence as a function of the formulation Identify and investigate specific dynamic regimes for droplets dynamics (for example Brownian vs. Capillarydriven) during emulsion destabilization. Test and develop models for emulsion stability/destabilization prognosis. Approach The PArticle STAbilised emulsions experiment (PASTA) is placed inside the Fluid Science Rack (FSL) in the European Columbus module of the ISS. Each PASTA sample cell is fitted with a piston that allows to agitate the mixture within the cell at various frequencies and durations to emulsify the mixture. The sample cells are grouped 4-by-4 in sample cell units that can be fitted on a carousel inside SMD. This carousel allows for placing each individual sample cell in the diagnostics position of SMD, where it can be observed with the SMD sensors and several diagnostic tools, like the overview camera that takes microscope image sequences in black and white of the sample cell. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits Emulsions have large relevance for applications in a wide spectrum of technologies, processes, and products in different fields including oil and gas, specialty materials, pharmaceuticals, cosmetics, and foods. Both stable and unstable emulsions are needs that are shared across a variety of applications. For example, efficient de-emulsifiers are needed to facilitate the process of phase separation (breaking) in the crude oil emulsions extracted from the wells, while high stability oil-in-water emulsions are required in the final stage of production of the same well or to facilitate pumping high-viscosity oils through pipelines. In the food industry, many products based on emulsified fats or oils (condiments, sauces, frozen confections, and others) require long term stability. However, destabilizing emulsions are key to processing raw food materials such as milk and vegetable oils. Contact(s) Libero Liggieri,James K Ferriemail,T. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 6.05 MB PSI-6Version 3 Foam Optics and Mechanics(FOAM) Investigation Submitted Date: 28-Aug-2024 Initial Release Date: 26-Sep-2024 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/34m1-4772 Research Area: Complex Fluids - Soft Matter SubResearch Area: Biophysics Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Sponsoring Agency ESA Objectives The objective is to take advantage of microgravity to eliminate drainage and to use imaging and multiple light scattering diagnostics in order to non-invasively measure and elucidate the time evolution of key features of the bubble-packing structure of wet foams – namely, the bubble size distribution and bubble rearrangement dynamics – and how they are affected by degree of wetness by systematically increasing the liquid content for sequences of otherwise identical foams. FOAM is divided into two experiments: FOAM Coarsening and FOAM Stability. Approach Experiment Cells The FOAM-C experimental set-up comprises five segments with a total of 20 small test cells containing a variety of liquid mixtures. The Fluid Science Laboratory on the ISS Columbus module will automatically shake and analyze these mixtures using complex laser optics, highly sensitive photodiodes and high-resolution cameras that can take up to 10,000 images per second. Each test cell weighs only 20 grams and contains less than 2 cm³ of the liquid mixture, while each segment comprises four test cells and weighs a total of 320 grams. Diagnostics - Overview video, - Multiple light scattering spectroscopies (SVS - Speckle Variance Spectroscopy and/or DWS - Diffusing-Wave Spectroscopy) Example of Protocols - First, the foam is made at the time T0. Then the foam is left to age while optical diagnostics measure its dynamics during aging (up to 24 hours foam age). These cycles can be repeated several times. Another cell with a different composition (liquid fraction, concentration) is then subject of a new series of experiments. - Granular matter samples of defined volume concentration shall be agitated until a steady state is reached. Consequently, optical diagnostics measure the grains dynamics in the steady state and after turning the agitation off. Experiment Protocol For each foam sample, there are different sets of measurements that are to be repeated in sequence, for the total run duration. The maximum experiment duration shall be assumed with 24h per experiment run for each sample. At the beginning of a science campaign on orbit replaceable units shall be exchanged (if necessary) and the EC is installed in FSL by the Crew. Each run starts with the foaming process. Data acquisition shall start just at the end of the foaming process. After a run, either the same sample can be processed again, or another sample can be processed. After a run, data post processing and downlink of results can occur. The results can influence the experiment procedure of subsequent runs, and the possibility to change experiment parameters through telecommand shall be provided. At the end of a science campaign selected scientific data is downlinked and then the EC is uninstalled by the Crew. Runs Repetition Each sample shall be tested 3 times (one just needs to “re-foam” the sample after its first period of coarsening). Experiment Duration and amount of Data The measurements (alternatively SVS, DWS, DTS, Camera) shall be performed during the whole run duration. In the following the measurement time is a requirement. On the opposite, the resulting amount of data is based on the required scientific measurements and the specific data production of the instrument, it is an indication but not a requirement. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits This experiment might provide useful insights for the manufacture, use and ageing behavior of foams, which are utilized in a wide range of areas, including in cosmetics and personal-hygiene products, in the food industry, in cleaning products, sealing products and for firefighting. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 16.83 GB PSI-9Version 1 Electrically Driven Liquid Film Flow Boiling in the Absence of Gravity(EHD) Investigation Submitted Date: 29-Aug-2024 Initial Release Date: 25-Sep-2024 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/18fc-8d56 Research Area: Fluid Physics SubResearch Area: Electrohydrodynamics Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Proposal Title Electrically Driven Liquid Film Flow Boiling: A Two-Phase Heat Transport Device Driven by Electric Conduction and Dielectrophoretic Mechanisms Flight Platform Parabolic Flight Investigation Start Date 10-01-2016 Investigation End Date 09-30-2022 Sponsoring Agency NASA NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives a-Provide fundamental understanding of the combined electrically driven (based on EHD conduction phenomenon) liquid film flow and dielectroporetic vapor extraction mechanism in the presence of phase change (liquid to vapor) in the absence of gravity. b-Provide a phenomenological foundation for the future development of electric field based two phase thermal management systems, leveraging EHD engineering advantages to develop systems of arbitrary mass flow requirements and geometries. Approach As vapor bubbles cover the surface and grow or coalesce, the modes of heat transfer will be limited to conduction and possibly radiation. To avoid this and to enable boiling to take place, EHD-driven liquid film will be fed from the condenser section towards the heater. The inertia of liquid film flow along with DEP extraction force will repel vapor bubbles that have formed on the heater surface. In order to study the competing effects of flow inertia/DEP extraction force vs. bubble behavior in zero gravity, one needs to understand EHD generated liquid film flow and the DEP mechanism. The flow inertia is a function of applied EHD potential, electrode design, liquid film thickness and working fluid properties. The DEP extraction force is also a function of its corresponding electrode design, the spacing between its electrode and heated surface, and the applied potential for a given working fluid. Thus, the controlling parameters for this study are applied EHD conduction pumping potential, applied DEP potential, heat flux, and liquid film height for the selected working fluid and electrode designs. The electrode designs for EHD conduction pumping and DEP mechanism are based on our previous numerical and experimental work. Therefore, the electrode dimensions, design or distance from the heater surface will not need to be varied during this study. Hypothesis Boiling is not acceptable in the absence of gravity unless the generated vapor bubbles can be expelled from the boiling surface and fresh liquid can be pumped onto the hot surface through some mechanism. EHD conduction pumping has the capability of pumping thin liquid films toward the heat source where the boiling takes place, with sufficient inertia to begin expelling bubbles from the heated surface at low heat fluxes. Furthermore, applying an EHD Dielectrophoretic (DEP) extraction force near the boiling surface guarantees the repulsion of vapor bubbles away from the heated surface even at high heat fluxes. Finally, the combined EHD driven liquid film flow boiling and DEP extraction force are expected to sustain and enhance the critical heat flux in the absence of gravity. Combining EHD conduction and DEP effects is therefore critical to the success of the ISS experiment. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits This multi-physics proposal will provide basic scientific understanding about competing physical phenomena of flow inertia and bubble dynamics in electrically driven liquid film flow boiling in the presence of electric bubble extraction force (i.e., dielectrophoretic force) in microgravity. The electrically driven liquid film flow boiling data aboard ISS will determine the critical heat flux, onset of boiling, absence of hysteresis, and bubble characteristics in the absence of gravity.There are a number of potential terrestrial and space applications for this electrohydrodynamic (EHD) driven two-phase heat transport device in all scales (from macro-scale to truly micro-scales). For example, this device can be used to effectively remove heat from electronics in micro- and zero-gravity environment for NASA's future space stations and long term missions. It can also be used in satellites (e.g., embedded system into satellite's multi-functional structure).Terrestrially, it can be used in high intensity electronics cooling as well as in various phase change devices. To achieve these applications, the basic scientific understanding about competing physical phenomena of flow inertia and bubble dynamics in electrically driven liquid film flow boiling in the presence of electric bubble extraction force (i.e.,dielectrophoretic force) in microgravity is needed. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 21.23 GB PSI-105Version 4 Shear History Extensional Rheology Experiment(SHERE; SHERE-R) Investigation Submitted Date: 18-Sep-2024 Initial Release Date: 18-Sep-2024 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/ce4g-x578 Research Area: Complex Fluids - Soft Matter SubResearch Area: Polymers Related Investigation: PSI-104, PSI-103 License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 12-18-2003 Investigation End Date 09-30-2007 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives The objective of this investigation was to study the effect of pre-shear on the transient evolution of the microstructure and viscoelastic tensile stresses for monodisperse dilute polymer solutions. The SHERE flight experiment aimed to investigate and quantify, for the first time, the transient extensional stress growth characteristics of a dilute polymer solution after a defined pre-shear history. Following the initial SHERE campaign a re-flight of the investigation was carried out as SHERE-R with additional experimental runs. Approach The test fluid used for this investigation was a dilute solution (0.025 wt.%) of a narrow polydispersity high molecular weight polystyrene (Mw equals 2.25×106 g/mol, PDI ≈ 1.02) dissolved in oligomeric styrene oil. The FM core consists of two endplates and an inner shroud, which is slid back to deploy the fluid column between the two endplates. A steady shear rate between 0 and 50 s-1 is then imposed on the fluid sample by rotating one endplate from 0 to 500 rpm for a predetermined time (5 to 60 s) while holding the other endplate stationary. As soon as the rotation ceased, an elongational deformation was imposed by axially translating one of the endplates in an exponential manner in order to generate constant strain rates ranging from 0.1 to 5.0 s-1. The tensile force and filament shape were monitored during the stretching flow. The position of the moving plate is recorded to verify the imposed displacement profile. By backlighting the test fluid with an electroluminescent panel and viewing the fluid column from above with a video camera, one half of the (symmetric) fluid column shape was recorded for subsequent image analysis in order to determine the evolution in the filament profile during stretching and subsequent relaxation. The fluid and air temperatures were digitally recorded using thermistors for later post-processing and temperature correction. After cessation of the extensional flow, the experiment monitored the subsequent evolution of the midpoint radius (via a laser micrometer), the filament shape, and the tensile force in the column. Hypothesis Constitutive equations for viscoelastic fluids such as dilute polymer solutions generally predict large changes in the extensional rheology of the material as the elongation rate is increased. This investigation attempts to test the validity of this hypothesis by performing experiment with dilute non-Newtonian polymer solutions in extensional flows. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits Understanding the extensional rheology of a complex fluid such as a liquid polymer is key for containerless processing because the absence of the bounding walls of a container or vessel removes the shearing component of the deformation which typically dominates Earth-based processing operations. The resulting flow is thus shear-free or extensional in character. Containerless processing is a central component in the development of in-situ fabrication technology, such as a means of producing new parts on demand or replacing existing parts or tools. This represents a critical element in the evolution of an autonomous exploration capability. In-situ fabricated parts, which may include both new and recycled materials, will be composed of plastics, filled polymers, metals, ceramics and composites. SHERE plays a role in this area by measuring, in microgravity conditions, a material property that has a direct connection to in-situ manufacturing and fabrication of polymeric parts. In-situ manufacturing operations can occur in microgravity or reduced gravity levels (e.g. on the Moon or Mars) and may include for example, the extrusion and processing of thermoplastic elastomer films, which are very resilient and can be made thin and lightweight. These elastomeric materials may form the basis of adhesives and fillers utilized in a wide variety of repair applications, especially under a reduced gravity environment, such as the repair of space suits or other similar materials. Understanding and exploiting the ability to fabricate new parts in-situ from a limited number of precursor components is critical in future space missions where weight plays a critical role in the overall cost of a mission. Additionally, in-situ repair provides a means of maintaining systems during transport and while on the Moon, Mars, and other extraterrestrial bodies. Fundamental understanding and measurement of the extensional rheology of complex fluids also allows Earth-based manufacturing processes to be controlled and improved. Ground-based work using variants of the Filament Stretching Rheometer includes studies of spinnability, and the investigations of cohesive and adhesive instabilities which manifests themselves in adhesion and tackiness of materials. It has lead to the development of a Resin-spinning technology that allows the formation of ultra-fine elastic threads analogous to spider-silks. Control of the fluid shear history and extensional rheology of test fluid is essential to optimizing the ultimate web properties. Extensional rheology is of critical importance in optimization of polymer processing operations that involve complex flows, i.e. flows that contain both shearing (rotation) and elongation (stretching) components. Radiation / Stretch Extinction Using Counterflow Flames Investigation Submitted Date: 18-Sep-2024 Initial Release Date: 18-Sep-2024 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/80qf-vj95 Research Area: Combustion Science SubResearch Area: Spacecraft Fire Safety Related Investigation: PSI-69 License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Ground Investigation Flight Platform Not Applicable Investigation Start Date 08-01-2016 Investigation End Date 07-31-2021 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives By using the Flame Extinguishment (FLEX) experimental data from the Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) system of combustion science, the purpose of this grant was to conduct new simulations and ground-based experiments using ozone-sensitized counterflow flames to: 1) Develop a new diagram of the flammability limits of diffusional cool flames affected by radiation, diffusion, and convection. 2) Bridge the knowledge gap between the flammability limits and extinction limits of hot flames and cool flames. 3) Verify the phenomena observed on the ISS flame extinguishment experiments. 4) Obtain new, quantitative data of extinction limit, flame temperature, and species distribution for the validation of kinetic and radiation models involving cool flames. 5) Extend the cool flame experiments from the original ISS droplet experiments to a more general ground-based combustion system involving radiation, diffusion, convection, and low-temperature chemistry while maintaining a one-dimensional geometry. Approach Using the experimental conditions of FLEX flight, a comparative studies of the oxygen concentration effects on the extinction limits of cool flames was conducted using three different numerical modeling schemes, (a) spark-assisted flame propagation of a n-heptane/air mixture, (b) one dimensional freely-propagating dimethyl ether (DME) flames using an arc-length continuation method and (c) simulated cool flame regimes and burning limits at elevated pressure (up to 20 atm) using DME/air mixtures. Specific research details are outlined in the publication, ''Dynamics of cool flames'' [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pecs.2019.100787]; '' Understanding Cool Flames and Warm Flames'', [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.proci.2020.09.019] and ''Study of the low-temperature reactivity of large n-alkanes through cool diffusion flame extinction'', [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.combustflame.2017.01.028]. Hypothesis This investigation attempts to answer the critical question as to what conditions causes the hot flames transfer to cool flames and how the cool flame flammable region is related to hot flame flammability limit and extinction limit. The investigation hypothesizes that factors such as oxygen concentration, dilution, pressure, diffusion, and convection transport processes affect the cool flame transition. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits Obtaining a fundamental understanding of the warm diffusion flame is particularly relevant to combustion in highly turbulent flow fields and in microgravity environments, owing to the possibility of long residence times. The results showed that the warm flame has a double reaction zone structure and plays a critical role in the transition between cool flames and hot flames. At elevated pressures, it was found that the flammable region of warm flames and cool flames expands due to the increase in low-temperature and intermediate-temperature reactivity with pressure. Since many real engines operate in the 20-40 atm pressure range, therefore, cool flames and warm flames are relevant and important flame regimes for high-pressure near-limit combustion applications. These calculations from this investigation will serve to advance the understanding of near-limit flame dynamics and provide guidance for experimental observation of different flame regimes. title: Surface Tension Driven Convection Experiment-1(STDCE-1)

detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 22.57 GB PSI-108Version 4 Surface Tension Driven Convection Experiment-1(STDCE-1) Investigation Submitted Date: 18-Sep-2024 Initial Release Date: 18-Sep-2024 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/j1z3-bw42 Research Area: Fluid Physics License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform Space Shuttle Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives The main objectives of STDCE-1 are to investigate: -The extent and nature of thermocapillary flows in transient periods as well as under steady conditions. -Temperature distributions along the free surface and in the bulk fluid. -The effect of the heating mode and the heating level on the flows. -The effect of the liquid free surface on the flows -The onset conditions and nature of oscillatory flows Approach The STDCE program employed a comprehensive and multifaceted approach to investigate the complexities of thermocapillary flow. This strategy encompassed a combination of theoretical analysis, numerical modeling, ground-based experiments, and ultimately, microgravity experiments aboard the Space Shuttle. Theoretical Analysis Dimensionless Parameters: Researchers derived and identified the key dimensionless parameters governing thermocapillary flow, including the Marangoni number (Ma), Prandtl number (Pr), aspect ratio (Ar), and the novel surface deformation parameter (S). These parameters facilitated the understanding of the relative importance of different forces and physical mechanisms at play and provided a framework for data analysis and comparison. Scaling Laws: By analyzing the governing equations and boundary conditions, scientists established scaling laws that characterized the behavior of key flow features, such as boundary layer thicknesses and velocity scales. This theoretical groundwork offered valuable insights into the expected flow characteristics under different conditions. Numerical Modeling Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD): Sophisticated CFD models were developed to simulate thermocapillary flow behavior under various conditions. These models accounted for factors such as heat transfer, fluid properties, surface tension effects, and free surface deformation. The numerical simulations provided detailed predictions of flow patterns, velocity distributions, and temperature profiles, serving as a basis for comparison with experimental data and for exploring a wider range of parameters than feasible experimentally. Ground-Based Experiments Reduced-Gravity Simulations: Researchers conducted experiments in drop towers and other reduced-gravity facilities to observe thermocapillary flows under conditions with minimized buoyancy effects. These experiments served as a stepping stone towards the microgravity experiments and provided preliminary data for model validation and refinement. Test Fluid and Hardware Development: Extensive ground-based testing was undertaken to optimize the experimental setup, including the selection of the test fluid (silicone oil), the design of the test cell, and the development of flow visualization and temperature measurement techniques. Microgravity Experiments Space Shuttle Missions: The culmination of the research effort involved conducting the STDCE experiments aboard the Space Shuttle, taking advantage of the extended microgravity environment to study thermocapillary flows over a broader range of parameters and conditions than possible on Earth. This included meticulous execution of the test matrix, encompassing various heating modes, power levels, and free surface shapes, while collecting detailed flow visualization and temperature data. Data Analysis and Model Validation Comparison of Results: The experimental data from both ground-based and microgravity experiments were rigorously analyzed and compared with the predictions from numerical models. This iterative process allowed for the assessment of model accuracy, the identification of areas for improvement, and ultimately, a deeper understanding of the fundamental physics driving thermocapillary flow. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits While the STDCE program was primarily driven by the need to understand and predict thermocapillary flow behavior in microgravity environments, its findings and technological advancements have yielded valuable insights and applications for Earth-based processes as well. Enhanced Understanding of Thermocapillary Flows Fundamental Physics: STDCE significantly advanced the understanding of the fundamental physics governing thermocapillary flows, including the interplay between surface tension gradients, heat transfer, and fluid motion. This knowledge provides a solid foundation for tackling complex fluid flow problems in various terrestrial applications. Numerical Model Refinement: The experimental data from STDCE served as a critical benchmark for validating and refining numerical models used to predict thermocapillary flow behavior. These improved models now offer more accurate and reliable predictions for a wider range of applications, both in space and on Earth. Technological Advancements Non-Intrusive Measurement Techniques: The development and refinement of non-intrusive measurement techniques, such as infrared imaging and particle image velocimetry, for the STDCE have expanded the toolkit for studying fluid flows in various settings. These techniques are now widely employed in research and industrial applications on Earth, including the study of combustion processes, crystal growth, and microfluidics. Flow Visualization and Analysis: The advanced flow visualization and analysis methods developed for STDCE have facilitated the study of complex flow patterns and structures in various terrestrial applications. These tools enable researchers and engineers to gain deeper insights into flow dynamics and optimize processes for improved efficiency and performance. Earth-Based Applications Materials Processing: The insights gained from STDCE have direct relevance to materials processing techniques on Earth, particularly those involving free surfaces and high-temperature gradients, such as welding, crystal growth, and the fabrication of thin films and coatings. Understanding and controlling thermocapillary flows in these processes can lead to improved product quality and reduced defect formation. Microfluidics: The knowledge gained from STDCE is applicable to the burgeoning field of microfluidics, where surface tension forces play a dominant role in manipulating and controlling fluids at the microscale. This has implications for the development of microfluidic devices for applications such as drug delivery, medical diagnostics, and chemical analysis. Overall, the STDCE program, while initially motivated by the challenges of microgravity research, has generated valuable knowledge and technological advancements with far-reaching implications for various Earth-based applications. The enhanced understanding of thermocapillary flow and the development of advanced measurement and analysis techniques have contributed to the advancement of materials processing, microfluidics, and numerous other fields, demonstrating the profound impact of fundamental scientific research on both space exploration and terrestrial technology. title: Capillary Flow Experiment(CFE)

detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 15.14 GB PSI-38Version 3 Capillary Flow Experiment(CFE) Investigation Submitted Date: 18-Sep-2024 Initial Release Date: 18-Sep-2024 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/zj8d-gw61 Research Area: Fluid Physics License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives 1. The primary objective of the CL unit experiments is to identify the extent the role of the boundary condition at the contact line plays in the natural dynamic response of a large capillary interface to a variety of disturbances. 2. The primary objective of the ICF units is to experimentally determine secondary imbibition rates in complex containers due to spontaneous large length scale capillary flows along interior corners in weakly 3-dimensional containers. Secondary objectives of the experiments are to quantify such flows in closed loop cycles, and to identify the passive phase separation characteristics of certain capillary driven multiphase-flows (e.g. bubbly flow) along interior corners. 3. The primary objective of the VG units is to determine equilibrium interface configurations and critical wetting conditions for interfaces between interior corners separated by a gap. A secondary objective is to validate numerical predictions of the large length scale discontinuous or nearly discontinuous wetting phenomena. Approach Without gravity, it is more difficult to control the flow of fluids and this is a challenge for designing spacecraft systems such as liquid propellants/cryogens, thermal control systems, wastewater management and recycling.Capillary forces (the interaction of liquid with solid that can draw a fluid up a narrow tube) continue to act in the absence of gravity and can be exploited to control fluid orientation so that fluid systems on spacecraft perform predictably.CFE uses the low-gravity environment provided by the International Space Station to understand the special dynamics of capillary flow and will aid in the design of fluid transport systems on future spacecraft. Hypothesis The CFE investigations operate under the hypothesis that capillary phenomena in microgravity, specifically contact line dynamics, interior corner flows, and vane-gap wetting, deviate significantly from idealized theoretical predictions based on simplified geometries and boundary conditions. This deviation is anticipated to manifest as measurable differences in dynamic interface response (frequency and damping) for varying contact line conditions, geometry-dependent secondary imbibition rates in complex containers, and distinct critical wetting conditions in vane-wall gaps influenced by gap size and wettability. The CFE experiments are designed to quantify these deviations, providing empirical data to refine existing theoretical models and enhance the predictive capabilities for low-gravity fluid management systems. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits The knowledge gained from this payload has the potential to be instrumental in the design of future fluid systems for spacecraft-impacting fluid bearing containers such as propellant and cryogenic fluids tanks, thermal control system coolant reservoirs, water storage and management systems, liquid state low-gravity materials processing equipment, and biofluids handling instruments for inflight human health systems. By performing this experiment, researchers will gain information that will lead to improvements in system reliability with reductions in system mass and complexity. These applications of CFE are in direct support of NASA's mission to develop safe, reliable, and affordable spacecraft to pursue the greater exploration of our solar system and universe. The results of the flight experiments are also expected to provide insights into terrestrial interfacial phenomena and may lead to models predicting fluid flows in porous media (i.e. ground water transport), complex capillary structures (i.e. high performance wicks for heat pipes employed in electronics cooling), and Lab-On-Chip technologies (i.e., microscale biofluids processing). detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 483.98 GB PSI-35Version 8 Cold Atom Lab - Fundamental Interactions for Atom Interferometry with Ultracold Quantum Gases in a Microgravity Environment(CAL-Fundamental Interactions) Investigation Submitted Date: 18-Sep-2024 Initial Release Date: 18-Sep-2024 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/0pv6-m208 Research Area: Fundamental Physics SubResearch Area: Quantum Interferometry Related Investigation: PSI-31, PSI-32, PSI-33, PSI-36 License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 04-01-2014 Investigation End Date 09-27-2025 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NASA Center Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) Objectives Precision atom interferometers (AI) in space promise exciting technical capabilities with diverse applications of interest to NASA. These quantum sensors are particularly relevant for fundamental physics research, with proposals including unprecedented tests of the validity of the weak equivalence principle, precision measurements of the fine structure and gravitational constants, and detection of gravity waves and dark matter/dark energy. This investigation will utilize the capabilities of NASA's multi-user Cold Atom Laboratory (CAL), in the microgravity environment onboard the International Space Station (ISS), to study mitigation schemes for the leading-order systematics expected to limit future high-precision measurements of fundamental physics with AIs in microgravity. The flight experiments, supported by theoretical investigations and ground studies at Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), will concentrate on the physics of pairwise interactions and molecular dynamics in ultracold quantum gases as a means to overcome uncontrolled AI shifts associated with the gravity gradient and few-particle collisions. A space-based dual-species AI will be further developed and used, which is planned as an on-orbit upgrade to the CAL science module after approximately a year of science investigations, for proof-of-principle tests of systematic mitigations and phase-readout techniques for use in the next-generation of precision metrology experiments based on AIs in microgravity. The proposed studies require the effective position invariance, long free fall times, and extremely low temperature samples uniquely available with the CAL apparatus. It is anticipated that these studies can lead to the unprecedented level of control and accuracy necessary for AIs to explore some of the most fundamental physical concepts in nature. Approach Investigation comprises two main aspects: the creation of ultracold atomic gases and the subsequent manipulation and probing of these gases to study systematic mitigations. For dual-species operations the process is slightly more complicated, especially with the addition of a sympathetic cooling step, however, the general process is fairly standardized. Creation of Ultracold Atomic Gas: -Laser Cooling: Atoms are released into a vacuum chamber and collected into a magneto-optical trap (MOT), where they are initially cooled using laser cooling techniques. This technique cools the sample by essentially ‘pushing’ the laser against the motion of the atoms effectively lowering the momentum, and therefore the velocity, kinetic energy, and temperature, of the sample. This is followed by brief stages of “compressed MOT”, in which the trapping force of the MOT is increased to compress the gas, and then an “optical molasses” stage, during which the quadrupole magnetic field is turned off and the laser frequency is further detuned to minimize the temperature of the gases. -State Preparation: The sample is optically pumped to a low magnetic field-seeking quantum state. The atoms in this state are then subjected to an intermediate quadrupole magnetic field which traps the atoms from the MOT and allows for the transfer from the MOT, located at the bottom of the science region, to an atom-chip-based trap, located at the top of the science region. -Evaporative Cooling: The atoms undergo forced evaporative cooling, using frequency sweeps of either RF or microwave fields, to bring the gases below the critical temperature, leading to the formation of a Bose-Einstein Condensate (BEC). Evaporative cooling cools the sample by removing the highest-energy atom from the trap so that the remaining atoms re-thermalize at progressively lower temperatures. -Decompression and Release: The tightness of the atom trap is adiabatically relaxed to further cool the atoms via decompression colling. After a short hold time in the relaxed trap, the atoms are released by rapidly turning the atom-chip and bias coil currents to zero to allow the atoms to expand in freefall. At this point, investigators can search for the primary signatures of a BECs for confirmation that one was formed. Formation of a BEC is typically associated with the behavior of the velocity distribution, such as the presence of a narrow peak centered at near zero velocity and the low velocity peak growing (greater fraction of atoms in this domain) as the temperature decreases. Manipulation and Probing: -Probing Techniques: The ultracold gas is probed in freefall using laser, magnetic field, radiofrequency, and/or microwave pulses. These techniques are designed to establish atoms in the proper state, perform atom interferometry, or establish and investigate the pairwise interactions and molecular dynamics crucial for mitigating systematics in high-precision measurements. -Time-of-Flight Imaging: After a predetermined time of flight, the sample is imaged using absorption imaging techniques. This process involves shining resonant light on the atoms and taking two images, per atomic species, of the shadow cast in the light: one of the sample and a reference image post-destruction of the sample. As implied, this is the end of the experimental cycle for this specific BEC as the measurement process destroys the sample. This approach is particularly suited for studying mitigation schemes for leading-order systematics that can affect future high-precision measurements with atom interferometers (AIs) in microgravity. By leveraging the unique microgravity environment provided by NASA’s Cold Atom Laboratory (CAL) on the International Space Station, this investigation aims to achieve the level of control and accuracy required for groundbreaking tests of fundamental physics principles, such as the weak equivalence principle, and precision measurements of the fine structure and gravitational constants. The integration of theoretical investigations and ground studies at JPL supports these flight experiments, enabling comprehensive understanding and development of systematic mitigation techniques. Hypothesis This investigation hypothesizes that the control of interactions and association/dissociation of weakly-bound molecules in ultracold quantum gases can overcome uncontrolled Atomic Interference (AI) shifts in space which are caused by the gravity gradient and few-particle collisions. Investigators will interrogate this hypothesis by conducting tests using ultracold quantum gases and exploring Feshbach resonances at new energy regimes. Investigators expect unprecedented levels of control and accuracy in the AI that will enable exploration of some of the most fundamental physical concepts in nature and open up venues for exploration of novel quantum phases in exotic dynamical regimes. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits Our studies are designed to achieve technological advances in precision metrology that can only be realized in the microgravity environment of the Cold Atom Laboratory (CAL). The tools of ultracold atomic and molecular physics are utilized (namely Feshbach resonances) for exquisite control of the differential center-of-mass distributions of the dual-species quantum gases and on methods to use the fundamentals of few-body interactions to maintain coherence in atomic ensembles for enhanced precision sensor capabilities. Subsequent proof-of-principle studies with the dual-species atom interferometer on CAL will further advance the state of the art for precision interferometry with ultracold matter waves. The impact of such research to the field of metrology can be seen through its potential to increase precision for atom-interferometry and also the possibility of engineering highly efficient system-specific devices based on the fundamental nature of few-body interactions. The microgravity environment of the CAL facility strongly favors such explorations and allow for the possibility of uncovering novel effects and quantum phases of matter, a major goal in ultracold quantum gases and other disciplines of fundamental physics. These studies can benefit life on Earth by providing both fundamental understanding of nature in previously inaccessible environments and energy regimes, and by enhancing the tools available for scientific exploration at the highest precision. menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 16.60 KB PSI-57Version 3 Capillary Channel Flow - Critical Velocities Experiment Unit 1(CCF-CV EU1) Investigation Submitted Date: 18-Sep-2024 Initial Release Date: 18-Sep-2024 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/1hdc-0y18 Research Area: Fluid Physics License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Sponsoring Agency German Aerospace Center (DLR) NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives The investigation aims to characterize and quantify critical flow dynamics in open capillary channels of parallel plate and groove geometries. A primary objective is determining the critical flow rates at which free surface destabilization (''choking'') and gas ingestion occur, emphasizing the capillary-inertial regime. The investigation will examine the relationship between critical flow rate and channel length for complete and half-channel configurations. Controlled, low-frequency flow oscillations will be introduced to probe instability onset sensitivity across geometries and lengths. High-fidelity data on free surface shapes and critical velocities will be acquired to validate theoretical models and assess underlying assumptions, refining predictive capabilities for capillary flows relevant to spacecraft fluid management. Approach The CCF experiment was operated on the ISS in the MSG. The CCF hardware consists of two experiment units, experiment unit number #1 for the parallel plate and groove geometry, and experiment unit number #2 for the wedge geometry. Initally, one experiment campaign for each experiment unit was planned. Due to the great success of the first two runs, two more additional runs were performed. The challenge for these runs was the commissioning of the fluid loop. The original design of the hardware did not foresee a commissioning from an undefined state, as it was the case after the first operation of each module. The fluid management technology builtinto the CCF hardware - however - was able to recover from an undefined fluid distribution state and allowed additional runs. Hypothesis The primary hypothesis guiding CCF-CV EU1 is that a limiting flow rate, or 'choking' phenomenon, exists in open capillary channels with parallel plate and groove geometries. A relationship between the fluid velocity, the channel geometry, and the fluid properties governs this limit. Furthermore, it is hypothesized that the introduction of wave oscillations within the flow will impact the critical flow rate, with the amplitude and frequency of these oscillations playing a significant role in the flow behavior and the onset of choking. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits The knowledge of liquid management in space is important for any device which contain liquid and gas, and have one or many free liquid surfaces. The requirements for the device which experiences different acceleration levels down to fully compensated gravity conditions (weightlessness) during its operation may include the phase separation of liquid from gas, gas from liquid, and the transport of liquid through liquid acquisition devices. The results from the CCF experiments may help to design subsystems of future spacecrafts, such as the propulsion subsystem, the thermal control subsystem and the life support subsystem for crewed exploration. The data can be used to build mathematical models which can be applied to real fluids and real dimensions. The data can be used as well to validate computational fluid dynamics software packages which are state-of-the-art tools the design of spacecrafts.
Capillary forces on Earth are masked by gravity, but may become dominant in small scales. This can be encountered when a wetting liquid wicks into a porous structure. It may be a wanted - as in the case of cleaning - or an unwanted - as in buildings - effect. In a wider sense the CCF experiments contribute to this topic. The main difference is that the flow was not driven by the capillary forces. Instead, the capillary forces were used to stabilize the flow path. title: Capillary Channel Flow - Critical Velocities Experiment Unit 2(CCF-CV EU2)
objectives: The investigation aims to determine critical flow rates (choking) for wedge channels across various lengths and wedge angles. It explores choking behavior across capillary-inertial, visco-capillary, a...

detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 18.27 KB PSI-58Version 3 Capillary Channel Flow - Critical Velocities Experiment Unit 2(CCF-CV EU2) Investigation Submitted Date: 18-Sep-2024 Initial Release Date: 18-Sep-2024 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/2tq7-0z45 Research Area: Fluid Physics Related Investigation: PSI-57 License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Sponsoring Agency German Aerospace Center (DLR) NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives The investigation aims to determine critical flow rates (choking) for wedge channels across various lengths and wedge angles. It explores choking behavior across capillary-inertial, visco-capillary, and overlap flow regimes. Bubble transport, migration, and phase separation within wedge geometries will also be investigated, focusing on the influence of flow rate, channel length, and bubble diameter. Approach The CCF experiment was operated on the ISS in the MSG. The CCF hardware consists of two experiment units, experiment unit number #1 for the parallel plate and groove geometry, and experiment unit number #2 for the wedge geometry. Initially, one experiment campaign for each experiment unit was planned. Due to the great success of the first two runs, two more additional runs were performed. The challenge for these runs was the commissioning of the fluid loop. The original design of the hardware did not foresee a commissioning from an undefined state, as it was the case after the first operation of each module. The fluid management technology built into the CCF hardware - however - was able to recover from an undefined fluid distribution state and allowed additional runs. Hypothesis The central hypothesis for CCF-CV EU2 is that a critical flow rate limit also exists in open capillary channels with wedge and gapped-wedge geometries, and it is governed by the interplay of capillary, viscous, and inertial forces. It is expected that the critical flow rate will be a function of the channel geometry, which includes the wedge angle and channel length, and that there will be different flow regimes which are linked to the governing flow forces. Furthermore, it is hypothesized that the nature of bubble transport, migration, and phase separation will depend on the flow conditions, such as flow rate and channel length, as well as bubble properties, such as the size and frequency. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits The knowledge of liquid management in space is important for any device which contain liquid and gas, and have one or many free liquid surfaces. The requirements for the device which experiences different acceleration levels down to fully compensated gravity conditions (weightlessness) during its operation may include the phase separation of liquid from gas, gas from liquid, and the transport of liquid through liquid acquisition devices. The results from the CCF experiments may help to design subsystems of future spacecrafts, such as the propulsion subsystem, the thermal control subsystem and the life support subsystem for crewed exploration. The data can be used to build mathematical models which can be applied to real fluids and real dimensions. The data can be used as well to validate computational fluid dynamics software packages which are state-of-the-art tools the design of spacecrafts. Capillary forces on Earth are masked by gravity, but may become dominant in small scales. This can be encountered when a wetting liquid wicks into a porous structure. It may be a wanted - as in the case of cleaning - or an unwanted - as in buildings - effect. In a wider sense the CCF experiments contribute to this topic. The main difference is that the flow was not driven by the capillary forces. Instead, the capillary forces were used to stabilize the flow path. A variety of applications on Earth may have this requirement as well. Contact(s) Mark M. Weislogelemail,Michael E. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 5.87 GB PSI-101Version 4 Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight(SAME-R) Investigation Submitted Date: 18-Sep-2024 Initial Release Date: 18-Sep-2024 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/2np7-jv14 Research Area: Combustion Science SubResearch Area: Spacecraft Fire Safety Related Investigation: PSI-102 License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 07-01-2010 Investigation End Date 09-30-2010 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives Similar to the original SAME investigation, the primary objective of the SAME-R investigation was to quantify the sizes that the liquid smoke particulate achieves in low gravity and to relate the droplet size distribution to the smoke generation and smoke transport conditions in the experiment. One of the problems encountered during the SAME investigation was that after the thermal precipitators were returned to the ground, it was found that all the TEM grids were severely contaminated with some unidentified foreign particles, making these grids unusable although some of them showed shapes of certain types of smoke particles. Based on that experience the SAME-R investigation employed several modification covering new materials, extended operating conditions, and diagnostic equipments. Approach SAME-R utilized the SAME hardware used on-orbit. Based on the experience gained from SAME, SAME-R included the following modifications: 1) a new test material, Pyrell®, an intumescent fire-retardant foam by Foamex, was introduced to replace DBP samples, 2) test conditions were broadened including higher heating temperatures and no-flow during sample heating time, and 3) a new instrument, M-pass, developed in-house GRC, was used to replace one of the two Commercial Diagnostic Enclosures that includes a DustTrak and an ionization detector used in SAME. SAME-R flight tests were conducted from July 16, to September 9, 2010, successfully completing 66 test points. After SAME-R flight tests, three major post–flight ground tests were performed to improve data reduction process and to validate the lognormal distribution assumption, the key to the moment method employed by SAME and SAME-R. Hypothesis The three hypotheses that motivated the original SAME investigation is also applicable for the reflight SAME-R investigation: In a μg environment, with the absence of the strong buoyancy-induced flows, smoke particle growth from a pyrolyzing/smoldering source, as a result of nucleation, condensation, and coagulation, will lead to larger particles compared to those produced in 1g. The formation of the larger particles is favored by the expected higher vapor concentration and smoke residence times near the source due to the reduced velocities and mixing at μg conditions. In particular, it is hypothesized that liquid aerosol smokes produced in microgravity will exhibit substantially larger droplet sizes than under the same conditions in normal gravity (with a corresponding decrease in the particle number density for the same mass of smoke). The change in the size distribution and number density will, in turn, affect the response of the smoke detectors and possibly result in some detectors not producing an alarm when exposed to this smoke. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits Along with the results from the original SAME investigation, the results from SAME-R can lead to technology for an advanced fire detector for future spacecraft that will be used for long duration missions. SAME will provide quantitative data on the sensitivity of these detectors to reduced gravity smokes that will allow evaluation of the adequacy of these existing technologies using relevant data. The current Fire Prevention, Detection, and Suppression (FPDS) program plan allows for the re-evaluation of future sensor technology, to allow new technology and capability to be utilized. The results from SAME are needed to provide the reduced gravity baseline data against which future detection technology developments can be evaluated. The smoke detectors developed from the results of SAME can also be useful in other extreme environments on Earth, such as submarines or underwater laboratories. Accurate detection of smoke in these environments can save lives. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 42.78 GB PSI-85Version 5 Nucleate Pool Boiling eXperiment(NPBX) Investigation Submitted Date: 18-Sep-2024 Initial Release Date: 18-Sep-2024 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/09ds-3c47 Research Area: Fluid Physics License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives The primary objective of the proposed study is to develop a mechanistic model for nucleate boiling under microgravity conditions. Specific objectives included: - Single bubble dynamics (nucleation, growth, and departure) under microgravity conditions under constant wall temperature. - Effect of liquid subcooling, wall superheat, and system pressure on single bubble dynamics. - Heat flux variation on the heated surface during single bubble evolution. - Lateral merger of bubbles formed at neighboring sites and mechanism of vapor removal from the surface. Approach The research utilized a systematic and comprehensive approach to understand the complexities of nucleate pool boiling in a microgravity environment. The approach was characterized by a strategic ''building block'' strategy, progressing from simpler to more complex scenarios, enabling a gradual and insightful understanding of the underlying physics. Here's a detailed breakdown of the investigation approach: 1. Single Bubble Dynamics: The research commenced by focusing on the behavior of a single bubble nucleating from a pre-fabricated cavity on the aluminum wafer. This fundamental building block allowed for a detailed examination of bubble growth, departure (if any), and the associated heat transfer processes in microgravity conditions. 2. Multiple Bubble Mergers: Building upon the knowledge gained from single bubble studies, the investigation then explored the interactions of multiple bubbles. Experiments were conducted to study the merger of bubbles nucleating from different cavities. This stage investigated how bubbles merge in the lateral direction, the mechanisms of vapor removal from the heated surface after merger, and the impact of these interactions on the overall heat transfer rates. 3. Integral Nucleate Boiling: The investigation then broadened its scope by conducting experiments with boiling occurring over the entire heater surface. This aimed to obtain the boiling curve, which depicts the relationship between heat flux and wall superheat, under microgravity conditions. This provided a macroscopic view of nucleate pool boiling, considering the collective behavior of numerous bubbles. 4. Numerical Simulations: The experimental work was tightly coupled with complete numerical simulations of the boiling process. These simulations employed advanced computational fluid dynamics (CFD) techniques to capture the intricate details of bubble dynamics and heat transfer. The simulations accounted for a range of factors including time-varying system pressure and temperatures, the presence of dissolved gas in the liquid, surface tension effects, and the influence of microlayer evaporation. The numerical model was rigorously validated against the experimental data obtained in the NPBX experiments. 5. Model Development: The ultimate goal of the research was to develop a mechanistic model for nucleate pool boiling heat transfer under microgravity conditions. This model, based on the physical understanding derived from experimental observations and validated numerical simulations, aimed to provide a reliable tool for predicting boiling behavior across a wide range of parameters and conditions relevant to space applications. Hypothesis In microgravity conditions, where buoyancy forces become negligible, it is expected that forces arising from the inertia of the liquid, evaporation, and condensation at the vapor-liquid interface, disjoining pressure, capillary pressure gradient, and the resulting flow field will become more dominant. The study aimed to understand and quantify the effect of these forces and identify the conditions under which quasi-static or steady-state boiling is possible under prolonged microgravity duration. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits While the primary motivation for this investigation was to advance our understanding of boiling heat transfer in the context of space applications, the knowledge gained has significant implications for Earth-based technologies and scientific understanding as well. Here are some key potential impacts and benefits: 1. Improved Understanding of Boiling at Earth Gravity: By studying boiling in a microgravity environment where buoyancy forces are negligible, researchers can gain a clearer understanding of the interplay of other forces and phenomena that influence boiling behavior. This knowledge can, in turn, enhance our comprehension of boiling processes under Earth's gravity, where buoyancy often masks the effects of these more subtle factors. 2. Development of More Efficient Heat Transfer Systems: The insights gained from this research can contribute to the development of more efficient boiling heat transfer systems for a wide range of applications on Earth. Enhanced efficiency translates to reduced energy consumption, lower operational costs, and a reduced environmental footprint. 3. Advancements in Miniaturization of Electronics: As electronic devices continue to shrink in size, effective thermal management becomes increasingly critical. Understanding boiling in microgravity is crucial for developing innovative cooling solutions for miniaturized electronics, as these devices often operate at high heat fluxes and face challenges in dissipating heat effectively. 4. New Insights into Fluid Physics: This research offers valuable insights into fundamental fluid physics phenomena, including the behavior of bubbles, interfacial phenomena, and the dynamics of multiphase flows. This knowledge can lead to advancements in diverse fields, such as materials science, biomedical engineering, and environmental science. Contact(s) Vijay K. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 252.16 MB PSI-115Version 3 Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity Investigation Submitted Date: 18-Sep-2024 Initial Release Date: 18-Sep-2024 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/q0v5-1v28 Research Area: Combustion Science SubResearch Area: Smoke Aerosol, Combustion Simulation Related Investigation: PSI-102 License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Ground Investigation Flight Platform Not Applicable Investigation Start Date 01-30-2017 Investigation End Date 12-31-2019 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), PSI Grant NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives The objective of this investigation was to use numerical simulation to explore the influence of gravity on pyrolysis smoke growth from a fundamental perspective. The intention of this effort is to quantify the differences between microgravity and Earth gravity smoke, and to identify the fluid dynamic mechanisms that cause the differences. Approach The formation and growth of dibutyl-phthalate (DBP) particles in Earth gravity and microgravity environments was simulated. Direct numerical simulation via a Navier-Stokes nodal approach was utlilized. The smoke originates from pyrolysis vapor expelled from a heated sample in a geometry similar to that considered in the SAME experiments. This study considered two cross-flow velocities of sufficiently low speed that buoyancy cannot be neglected in the presence of gravity. Simulations are presented to assess the dependence of particle size distributions on thermophoresis, particle settling, and flow geometry. The final report for this investigation introduces the simulation and modeling methodology, followed by a description of the flow geometry and the parameter space under consideration.The differences in the wake geometry attributable to buoyancy for the lower of two flow speeds was examined. Instantaneous scalar fields were used to describe particle accumulation and growth in the buoyant and non-buoyant wakes that form downstream of the hot vapor source. Hypothesis Without buoyancy, mixing and heat transfer are reduced, the time-temperature history of the combustion vapors (or particle precursors) and particle trajectories are significantly altered, changing the composition of the smoke. The chemical composition of the burning material also affects the characteristics of the smoke generated. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits Models and tools that characterize particles generated as smoke can be used to ascertain how temperature, gravity, and material properties affect the smoke produced. This would directly lead to better smoke detection devices and prevent fires that can lead to loss of materiel and loss of life. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 37.55 MB PSI-113Version 4 Solidification Using a Baffle in Sealed Ampoules(SUBSA) Investigation Submitted Date: 18-Sep-2024 Initial Release Date: 18-Sep-2024 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/ep4n-sg69 Research Area: Materials Science SubResearch Area: Solidification, Crystal growth License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform ISS Investigation Start Date 07-01-1996 Investigation End Date 12-31-2004 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NASA Center Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) Objectives There are both technology demonstration objectives and scientific objectives. The technology demonstration objectives are to test the performance of an automatically moving baffle in microgravity and to determine the behavior and possible advantages of liquid encapsulation in microgravity conditions.The science objectives are to visualize the melt/encapsulant behavior in microgravity and to grow doped InSb without dewetting. The key goal of SUBSA was to clarify the origin of the melt convection in space and to reduce the magnitude to the point that it does not interfere with the transport phenomena. Approach In the space environment, accelerations produce circular motions that affect the solidification of crystal growth/semiconductor materials flight experiments, resulting in a material that is less useful.The objectives of SUBSA are:Test the performance of an automatically moving baffle (used to minimize melt motion).Visualization of the melting process to identify what causes the melt motion.Production of several crystals with reproducible properties.To determine the behavior and possible advantages of liquid encapsulation in microgravity conditions. Hypothesis A baffle placed inside a melt reduces the effective size of the melt and leads to a decrease in the amount of convection. The combined effect of microgravity (reduction of gravitational acceleration by a factor of 10^6 ) and a small zone melt (reduction of the size and temperature differential by a factor of 10^3 ) will generate the effective conditions of “nano-gravity” (the Rayleigh number will be reduced by a factor of 10^9 ). Research Impacts/Earth Benefits The SUBSA furnace, with its capability to control and visualize melting and solidification of semiconductor crystals has increased our understanding of semiconductor crystal growth phenomena. The transparent furnace coupled with the video downlink and real-time commanding capability provided a powerful tool for scientists to watch the motion of the crystal-melt interface as semiconductor crystals were formed. The design of the SUBSA ampoule which includes a baffle and a system that prevents de-wetting resulted in crystals whose properties have not been disrupted by micro-accelerations at the Station, making it possible for future researchers to produce the high-quality semiconductor crystals that are in demand on Earth. objectives: The primary objective of the Strata-1 investigation was to study the mixing and segregation dynamics of regolith on small bodies by exposing a suite of regolith simulants to the microgravity environme...
