Atom interferometry is an ultra-sensitive measurement technique that splits the quantum wave function of an atom into two distinct wave packets that travel separate trajectories and then recombine. This technique, already demonstrated on the ground, should work better in space and could be useful for future space navigation systems. Approach This investigation uses rubidium (87Rb) and potassium (39K and 41K) samples in the Cold Atom Laboratory (CAL) aboard the International Space Station (ISS). The approach for the flight-based investigation comprises two main aspects: the creation of ultracold atomic gases and the subsequent manipulation and probing of these gases to study systematic mitigations. For dual-species operations the process is slightly more complicated, especially with the addition of a sympathetic cooling step, however, the general process is fairly standardized. 1. Creation of Ultracold Atomic Gas: • Laser Cooling: Atoms are released into a vacuum chamber and collected into a magneto-optical trap (MOT), where they are initially cooled using laser cooling techniques. This technique cools the sample by essentially ‘pushing’ the laser against the motion of the atoms effectively lowering the momentum, and therefore the velocity, kinetic energy, and temperature, of the sample. This is followed by a brief stage of “optical molasses” during which the quadrupole magnetic field is turned off and the laser frequency is further detuned. • State Preparation: The sample is optically pumped to a low magnetic field-seeking quantum state. The state is then subjected to an intermediate quadrupole magnetic field which allows for the transferred from the MOT, located at the bottom of the science region, to an atom-chip-based trap, located at the top of the science region. • Evaporative Cooling: The atoms undergo evaporative cooling to below the critical temperature, leading to the formation of a Bose-Einstein Condensate (BEC). Evaporative cooling cools the sample by removing the highest-energy atom from the trap so that the remaining atoms re-thermalize at progressively lower temperatures. • Decompression and Release: The atom trap is slightly relaxed to further cool the atoms, eventually releasing them completely to allow free expansion. At this point, investigators can search for the primary signatures of a BECs for confirmation that one was formed. Formation of a BEC is typically associated with the behavior of the velocity distribution, such as the presence of a narrow peak centered at near zero velocity and the low velocity peak growing (greater fraction of atoms in this domain) as the temperature decreases. 2. Manipulation and Probing: • Probing Techniques: The ultracold gas is probed using laser, radiofrequency, and/or microwave pulses. These techniques are designed to investigate the pairwise interactions and molecular dynamics crucial for mitigating systematics in high-precision measurements. • Time-of-Flight Imaging: After a predetermined time of flight, the sample is imaged using absorption imaging techniques. This process involves taking two images: one of the sample and a reference image post-destruction of the sample. As implied, this is the end of the experimental cycle for this specific BEC as the measurement process destroys the sample. This approach is particularly suited for studying mitigation schemes for leading-order systematics that can affect future high-precision measurements with atom interferometers (AIs) in microgravity. This investigation utilizes the atom interferometry equipment aboard the CAL instrument for precision measurement experiments. The BEC formed according to the steps laid out in the Creation of Ultracold Atomic Gases section is split using an off resonance standing wave laser. The split waves packets will travel different trajectories, and then recombine after a secondary laser beam is applied. After the recombination, the atomic interference pattern can be collected. The flight-based results can be compared to theoretical investigations and ground studies done at JPL, enabling comprehensive understanding and development of systematic mitigation techniques. Hypothesis This investigation hypothesizes that, combined with the current atomic cooling techniques, the implementation of expansion cooling will produce atoms with temperatures on the order of a trillionth of a degree above absolute zero (10^-12 K). With the unique settings provided by Cold Atom Laboratory (CAL) the maximum expansion and low temperature limits are able to be probed. Atomic interferometry can be used to measure the acceleration of cold atoms relative to the International Space Station, allowing investigators to explore using ultracold atoms as part of an inertial navigation system. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits The development of precision inertial sensing techniques is useful for Earth-based as well as space-based navigation. Besides using direct sensing for inertial navigation, rotation sensing can also be useful for north-finding while gravity sensing can be used to tabulate local gravity variations and form a type of three-dimensional map for navigating. These techniques also have many applications in geophysics. Gravity sensing can be used for oil and mineral exploration, while rotation sensing can detect dynamics in the Earth's core. Gravity sensing also has defense applications such as locating underground tunnels and potential screening cargo for high-density contraband or weapons. Other precision measurement applications have less direct impact, but advance scientific knowledge. For instance, precision tune-out spectroscopy measurements of atomic matrix elements can be used to improve the interpretation of atomic parity violation experiments. These in turn impact our understanding of the standard model of particle physics and thus the nature of our universe. Direct benefits of such understanding can be hard to trace, but in general the continued advance of technological applications builds on advances in our fundamental knowledge. Contact(s) Charles A. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 471.26 GB PSI-51Version 5 Electromagnetic Levitation Flight Support for Transient Observation of Nucleation Events(EML B1-ELFSTONE) Investigation Submitted Date: 18-Sep-2024 Initial Release Date: 18-Sep-2024 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/t7nh-x768 Research Area: Materials Science License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Proposal Title Batch 1 Processing of Sample #09 FeCrNi Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 09-20-2010 Investigation End Date 11-30-2015 Sponsoring Agency NASA NASA Center Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) Objectives The objective of this project is to understand phase selection in structural alloys and to investigate the effects of convection on time-dependent nucleation phenomena during rapid solidification from the melt. The ELFSTONE investigation involves a collaboration with the European Space Agency's (ESA) Thermolab Experiment which focuses on thermophysical properties data measurement of industrial alloys in the liquid phase as a function of temperature. The property values obtained are used to increase the accuracy of numerical modeling of casting and solidification processes of metal alloys. For access to data relating to the Thermolab Experiment, please consult ESA's HRE Data Archive (hreda.esac.esa.int) Approach The samples are processed in the Electromagnetic Levitator (ISS-EML), a facility that has been operational since 2015 and is located in the Columbus module. The investigation is part of Sample Batch 1 - the first of six proposed 18-sample multi-user cartridges uploaded to the ISS. For the ELFSTONE Sample #09, a ternary FeCrNi analog steel sample, a process cycle is defined as (1) the melting of the sample, (2) the gathering of science data, and (3) the subsequent undercooling and rapid solidification of the sample. The next cycle starts with the re-melting of the sample. In any particular cycle, stirring may be induced at different levels to study the effect of convection on rapid solidification behavior. After all cycles are complete, final microstructure is preserved for return to earth. Hypothesis The experimental hypothesis was that melt convection would significantly decrease the nucleation kinetics for transformation of metastable ferrite to stable austenite in ferrous structural steel alloys. The was successfully observed. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits The value of this research is that the results have application to the design of industrial welding, spray forming, and casting operations for a commercially important class of structural materials. In addition, this research addresses fundamental issues relating to rapid solidification behavior, metastable phase selection, and analysis of the processes governing microstructural evolution. Experiments focus on the use of convection as a processing control parameter. title: Characterization of Biofilm Formation, Growth and Gene Expression on Different Materials and Environmental Conditions in Microgravity(Space Biofilms)
objectives: 1. To use microbial strains that are relevant to human spaceflight, and nosocomial infections that have also occurred in spaceflight, and substrata materials that are relevant to (i) spacecraft struct...
approach: The Space Biofilms project, performed at the International Space Station, contributes to the understanding of microbial communities in space by characterizing the morphology and gene expression of bac...
detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 114.30 GB PSI-8Version 2 Characterization of Biofilm Formation, Growth and Gene Expression on Different Materials and Environmental Conditions in Microgravity(Space Biofilms) Investigation Submitted Date: 28-Aug-2024 Initial Release Date: 29-Aug-2024 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/tz48-ng44 Research Area: Biophysics SubResearch Area: Biofilms Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Proposal Title Characterization of Biofilm Formation, Growth and Gene Expression on Different Materials and Environmental Conditions in Microgravity Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 01-03-2017 Investigation End Date 12-31-2022 Sponsoring Agency NASA NASA Center Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) Objectives 1. To use microbial strains that are relevant to human spaceflight, and nosocomial infections that have also occurred in spaceflight, and substrata materials that are relevant to (i) spacecraft structures and surfaces, (ii) life support systems, (iii) space biology research hardware, and (iv) medical instrumentation. We are meeting this objective by the use of the same fungal strain that was isolated from a bio-damaged Mir window (Penicillium rubens), and an uropathogenic bacterial strain (Pseudomonas aeruginosa). 2. To culture the selected microbial strains in a way that enables biofilm formation, during an up- to-6-month experiment. To achieve this goal, we used BioServe’s already spaceflight- proven hardware and conducted preliminary testing during the first year of the experiment. 3. To quantify potential changes on biofilm mass, thickness, and overall morphology (including the formation of the “column-and-canopy structures) on the spaceflight cultures with respect to matched ground controls. This was achieved by acquiring post-flight (samples fixed in paraformaldehyde) morphological data through confocal laser scanning microscopy. 4. To elucidate the molecular mechanisms behind the observed morphological changes. This was done with the bacterial samples by acquiring post-flight transcriptomic data (samples fixed with RNA Later II) and conducting differential gene expression analyses between spaceflight cultures and matched ground controls. 5. To assess differential expression of genes associated with conferring microbes with oxidative, acidity, and antimicrobial resistance. This was done through RNA Sequencing and comparative gene analysis. 6. To determine physical mechanisms of material/microorganisms interaction in biofilms and their associated molecular basis. The morphological and transcriptomic data was utilized to identify potential correlation in between the differential gene expression and altered material/microorganism interaction in space, with respect to matched ground controls. Different topographic structures were assessed to provide further insight into this aspect (topographical patters with periodicities, same size, as the microbial size). Approach The Space Biofilms project, performed at the International Space Station, contributes to the understanding of microbial communities in space by characterizing the morphology and gene expression of bacterial and fungal biofilms formed in microgravity with respect to ground controls. The project has two big branches, the bacterial and the fungal side. Pseudomonas aeruginosa was used as model organism for the bacterial side and both morphology and transcriptomic (selected samples) studies were performed with bacterial samples, while Penicillium rubens was used as model organism for the fungal side and a morphology study was performed for fungal samples. Bacterial biofilm formation was characterized at one, two, and three days of incubation (37°C) over six different materials: stainless steel 316, passivated stainless steel 316, a lubricant impregnated surface (LIS), catheter grade silicone with and without a linear microtopography, and cellulose membrane. Fungal biofilm formation (mold) was characterized at 10, 15, and 20 days of incubation (25°C) over seven different materials: stainless steel 316, aluminum alloy (Al6061), titanium alloy (Ti-6Al-4V), quartz, catheter grade silicone, carbon fiber, and a superhydrophobic surface “nanograss”. Bacterial samples: 144 flight and 144 ground samples were prepared for the Space Biofilms bacterial experiment. The experiment independent variables were two gravitational regimes (Earth gravity and microgravity), three incubation times (1, 2, and 3 days), six material-media combinations (LBK media was used for samples grown over SS316, pSS316, and LIS; while mAUMg-hi Pi media was used for samples grown over cellulose, silicone, and silicone DLIP), two types of fixative/preservative (PFA and RNAlater), and replicates (four). To provide the necessary levels of containment, each sample was prepared in a Fluid Processing Apparatus (FPA) and eight FPAs were integrated into a Group Activation Pack (GAP). Once in microgravity, samples were activated by introducing the bacterial inoculum into the sterile medium and placing the samples at 37°C for the corresponding incubation time. After the incubation time the samples were terminated by introducing the fixative (for morphology samples) or the preservative (for transcriptomic samples). The morphology samples were stained (one dye for lipids and one dye for nucleic acids) and imaged with a confocal microscope. The resulting 3D images of the biofilms (.nd2 files) were processed and analyzed using the COMSTAT2 software to quantify biofilm mass, biofilm thickness, and biofilm surface area coverage. The transcriptomic samples had their RNA extracted and sequenced. The resulting transcriptomic data files (fastq files) were processed and used for gene expression analysis using DeSeq2. For more information on the bacterial sample preparation see section 4, and for information about the experiment performance in space see section 5 of the following paper: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actaastro.2022.07.015 For more information on the bacterial morphology and transcriptomic analyses see the Methods section of the following paper: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41526-023-00316-w Fungal samples: 288 flight and 288 ground samples were prepared for the Space Biofilms fungal experiment. The experiment independent variables were two gravitational regimes (Earth gravity and microgravity), three incubation times (10, 15, and 20 days), seven material substratum (stainless steel 316, aluminum alloy Al6061, titanium alloy Ti-6Al-4V, quartz, catheter grade silicone, carbon fiber, and a superhydrophobic surface “nanograss”), two types of fixative/preservative (PFA and RNAlater), and replicates (6-12 depending on the specific set). To provide the necessary levels of containment, each sample was prepared in a well of a 24-well plate and sealed with a gas permeable membrane. Additionally, four 24-well plates were integrated into a Plate Habitat (PHAB). Once in microgravity, samples were activated by wetting pads inside the PHAB to increase the environment humidity and by placing the samples at 25°C for the corresponding incubation time. After the incubation time the samples were terminated by introducing the fixative (for morphology samples) or the preservative (for transcriptomic samples)*. *The transcriptomic samples were not analyzed as part of this project. The morphology samples were stained (one dye for chitin and one dye for extracellular matrix proteins) and imaged with a confocal microscope. The resulting 3D images of the biofilms (.nd2 files) were processed and analyzed using the COMSTAT2 software to quantify biofilm mass, biofilm thickness, and biofilm surface area coverage. For more information on the bacterial sample preparation, the experiment performance in space, and the fungal morphology analyses see section 2 of the following paper:- https://doi.org/10.3390/life13041001 Hypothesis It is hypothesized that, in comparison to matched ground controls: a) Biofilm mass and thickness in microgravity will be increased for all bacterial and fungal species, growth medium, and substratum material; b) Gene expression will vary as a function of growth medium, substratum material, and gravitational regime; c) A systematic increase in expression of the genes that confer microorganisms with oxidative, acidity, and antimicrobial resistance will be observed in space (becoming more pronounced with time in space); and d) The formation of the “column-and- canopy” bacterial biofilm architecture and the material/microorganism interaction mechanisms in space will vary from one microbial species and material to the other, and will be associated with the differential expression of specific genes. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits This project is relevant to the space program and the “Biophysics – Biomaterials” emphasis of this NRA as it investigates biofilm formation (which can increase the risk of astronaut infection and equipment failure) on spacecraft-relevant materials. This work is relevant to the Space Biology Program and the Human Research Roadmap as it utilizes human pathology-associated bacterial species (uropathogenic Pseudomonas aeruginosa), growth media (e.g. modified artificial urine media), and materials (e.g. silicone from catheters).The knowledge produced may help address Gaps Micro-01, -02, -03, and -04 by characterizing bacterial and fungal responses to spaceflight, by interrogating the expression of genes associated with drug resistance, and by elucidating the governing mechanisms behind the observed phenomena. Furthermore, due to our proposed approach, the knowledge derived from this project may be translatable to biofilm-associated illnesses on Earth. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 393.75 GB PSI-13Version 6 Advanced Colloids Experiment- Microscopy(ACE-M1) Investigation Submitted Date: 30-Nov-2023 Initial Release Date: 30-Nov-2023 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/vcgk-a071 Research Area: Complex Fluids - Soft Matter SubResearch Area: Colloids License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 12-01-2021 Investigation End Date 11-30-2023 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives The ACE-M1 investigation aims to study the behavior of microscopic particles in colloidal mixtures such as gels and creams. Objectives include the study of the physics of colloidal coarsening and the role of polydispersity (variation in particle size) in determining the stability of colloidal systems. Previous Earth-based experiments show that polydispersity dramatically affects the time it takes for these gels to collapse. The imaging goal was to observe crystallites and resolve particle centroid positions with less than 20% error. Approach The ACE-M1 investigation utilized a Sample Cartridge disk with 10 Sample Wells for 10 samples. Samples were colloidal fluids of small and large particles in varying concentration over .5 to 2.0 mg/ml. Protocols included Homogenization and microscopic Observation and Imaging. A crew member used magnetic stir bars embedded in the sample well to homogenized each sample. Fluorescent microscopy and Imaging of the colloidal crystallites in each well as they developed over time allowed observation of particle movements and interactions to characterize and quantify rates of growth of structures formed. Hypothesis Polydispersity significantly affects the time scale and dynamics of coarsening. It is believed that polydispersity can lead to a substantial difference in the collapse time of weak gels, and understanding this effect in a microgravity environment can provide critical insights into product design and stability. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits Space Benefits: By conducting colloidal research in microgravity, the ACE-M1 experiment can obtain clearer data on the dynamics of liquid mixtures, free from the effects of gravitational forces. This research can improve the manufacturing processes for creating new, longer-lasting products for use both in space and on Earth. Earth Benefits: Understanding the behavior of colloidal mixtures and the coarsening process can help materials scientists design products with longer shelf lives. This has significant implications for a wide range of products, including food, medicine, cosmetics, gels, and cleaning solutions, potentially leading to reduced waste and enhanced product performance​. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 2.37 GB PSI-84Version 8 Microgravity Investigation of Cement Solidification(MICS) Investigation Submitted Date: 21-Nov-2023 Initial Release Date: 21-Nov-2023 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/zqtn-8g63 Research Area: Materials Science SubResearch Area: Cement Solidification License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Proposal Title Microgravity Investigation of Cement Solidification (MICS) Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 11-22-2016 Investigation End Date 11-21-2023 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NASA Center Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) Objectives The objective of the proposed investigation is to better understand the complex process of cement solidification by conducting experiments in the microgravity environment aboard the International Space Station (ISS) and further the development of an in-situ lunar concrete material. Approach Several different mixture combinations of tricalcium aluminate (C3A), tricalcium silicate (C3S), ordinary portland cement (OPC), superplasticizer (SP) and ratios of cement to water were packed in commercially available plastic bags (Burst Pouches®) with separate compartments divided by an internal, burstable seal which allowed mixing of materials under sealed conditions in microgravity and terrestrial conditions. Space and ground samples were mixed simultaneously and at the same conditions of 20 ºC ± 2 ºC, 1 ATM and 35% RH. As such, gravity is considered the only variable between the space and ground experiments. After a specific period of hydration samples were subjected to a wide variety of characterization techniques such as image analysis and mercury intrusion porosimetry (MIP) to assess porosity and pore size distribution, thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) to estimate degree of hydration, x-ray diffraction (XRD) for crystalline phase identification, energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) and electron microprobe analysis (EMPA) for compositional analysis. Phase distribution, pore structures, and crystal morphology as a function of composition and gravity level was documented. Hypothesis The research hypothesis for the ISS experiments is that minimizing gravity-driven transport phenomena, such as buoyancy, sedimentation, and convection results in a purely diffusion-controlled hydration process. Without the physical effects induced by gravity, diffusion will lead to a more uniform distribution of phases. As such, the dissolving cement particles will disperse in the aqueous solution, resulting in greater uniformity of features such as pore structures and crystal morphology in the hardened cement matrix. A different microstructure is expected to form in microgravity (µg), which possibly leads to different physical properties of µg-hardened cement paste with respect to that hardened in terrestrial gravity (1g). Research Impacts/Earth Benefits The MICS investigation directly addresses the high priority need for lightweight space structures for habitats that protect crew. Results from this investigation enable the characterization of microstructural development in the hardening of cement paste and improve understanding of crystal growth and hydration kinetics, phase formations, pore distribution, and material properties. Also, MICS can increase understanding and control of the crystal growth kinetics, and morphology, to improve concrete properties. Improved cement properties can lead to improved concrete properties, durability, and lower CO2 emissions. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 137.39 GB PSI-48Version 9 DEvice for the study of Critical LIquids and Crystallization Directional Solidification Insert-Reflight(DECLIC DSI-R) Investigation Submitted Date: 31-Oct-2023 Initial Release Date: 31-Oct-2023 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/wc3d-md27 Research Area: Materials Science SubResearch Area: Solidification, Dendritic Growth License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 10-01-2017 Investigation End Date 11-01-2018 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NASA Center Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) Objectives The main objective of the DSI-R investigation was to quantitatively establish the fundamental physics controlling the spatiotemporal organization of the secondary sidebranch structure and its interaction with the array structure of primary branches under directional solidification conditions. This investigation particularly focused on the origin of sidebranches that occur when columnar solidification patterns transform from cellular to dendritic as a function of thermal gradient and solidification velocity and study the potential for the formation of an intermediate multiplet pattern. The dynamics and stability of cellular and dendritic growth patterns, and the relationship between the tip geometry and growth pattern were also to be investigated as well. This intent of this investigation was to directly address outstanding issues that remain open in the understanding of complex dendritic microstructures. Approach The DSI-R investigation utilized a Bridgman type furnace and an experimental cartridge containing the organic transparent alloy of succinonitrile (SCN) - camphor. The nominal concentration was 0.46 wt% camphor. A single crystalline solid seed with a 100 direction parallel to the pulling axial direction is kept unmelted during all experiments. Solidification is performed by pulling the experimental cartridge containing the alloy inside a thermal gradient G at a pulling rate V. The G and V were the primary variable for each experimental run. Images obtained by the direct axial observation, providing top-view interface images, and transverse observations, providing side-view interface images, were analyzed. Hypothesis Bridgman solidification of transparent binary alloys in a diffusion controlled growth regime can yield benchmark data required for establishing the detailed dynamics of interface pattern selection. The ''SPAtiotemporal evolution of three-dimensional DEndritic array Structures'' (SPADES) investigation conducted during the reflight of the Directional Solidification Insert (DSI-R) campaign targeted the columnar dendritic growth regime to quantitatively establish the fundamental physics controlling the spatiotemporal organization of the secondary sidebranch structure and its interaction with the array structure of primary branches under directional solidification conditions. SPADES focused on the origin of sidebranches that occur when columnar solidification patterns transform from cellular to dendritic as a function of thermal gradient and solidification velocity. The “Effects of Curvature and Unsteady Dynamics on Alloy Solidification Patterns” (CUSP) investigation extended the DSIP and SPADES project into a new direction that addressed the critical effects of the macroscopic curvature of the solidification front and the unsteady dynamics that occurs in response to changes of growth conditions or that is associated with side-branching. A weak macroscopic interface curvature can have a major effect on both the array pattern evolution and grain structure. The convex and concave interfaces lead to a continuous increase and decrease of the average primary spacing, respectively, and it only attains a stationary value for a flat interface. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits By providing a reduced gravity environment where fluid convection is suppressed, space enables the direct experimental observation of the solid-liquid interface dynamics during the solidification process under long-duration and purely diffusive conditions. The acquired benchmark data will make it uniquely possible to critically test computational models of alloy microstructures by quantitative comparisons of modeling predictions and experimental observations, thereby contributing to the development of Integrated Computational Materials and Engineering (ICME) tools for both space and earth applications. Those tools are expected to “shorten development time, optimize designs and reduce costs relative to more traditional strategies involving building prototypes, testing and redesigning philosophies. In addition, understanding alloy solidification in the microgravity environment of space is important to improve in-space processing (manufacturing, joining, and welding) of structural materials that will be used for future space exploration. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 1.82 TB PSI-21Version 4 Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame(ACME CLD Flame) Investigation Submitted Date: 15-Sep-2023 Initial Release Date: 15-Sep-2023 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/23e1-9950 Research Area: Combustion Science SubResearch Area: Flames of gaseous fuel License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Proposal Title Fuel Dilution Studies of Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flames in a Microgravity Environment Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 10-01-2006 Investigation End Date 05-31-2022 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives In order to provide the experimental data needed to allow rigorous testing of computational models at the extremes of the fuel dilution spectrum, we have the following objectives: A) Characterize the behavior of weak coflow diffusion flames of methane and ethylene, as a function of velocity and fuel dilution, through measurement of flame shape, lift-off heights, temperatures and extinction limits. B) Characterize the sooting tendencies of diffusion flames with long residence times, as a function of velocity and fuel dilution, through measurement of flame shape, gas temperatures in the soot-free portion of the flame, soot luminosity, soot temperatures, and soot volume fractions. Approach ACME CLD Flame project goals include the generation of improved computational models with improved soot sub-models that are effective for both dilute flames and sooting flames that vary from low to high soot loading levels. The enhanced time and spatial scales in a microgravity environment will be important for achieving both goals. Experimentally, we plan to study methane and ethylene diffusion flames over a wide range of test conditions. For the more dilute flames, measurements will be made of flame chemiluminesence of OH* and CH* to observe variations in lift-off height and flame shape as extinction limits are approached. The sooting tendencies of the more fuel-rich flames will be investigated using soot luminosity and laser extinction measurements to determine soot temperatures and soot volume fractions. Flame temperatures in non-sooting regions will be measured using thin-filament pyrometry. Based on observations, modifications can be made to the kinetics and soot model to match better the experimental results. If the overall agreement of the measurements and computations is good, the results of the computations can be “mined” to provide insight on species (and hence chemical processes) that cannot be measured directly using the diagnostics available for the proposed experiment. Hypothesis This investigation was focused on gathering bench mark data to validate the hypothesis of computation models, the details of which are available within the following publications: 1) Smooke, M.D., Hall, R.J., Colket, M.B., Fielding, J., Long, M.B., McEnally, C.S., and Pfefferle, L.D., Investigation of the transition from lightly sooting towards heavily sooting co-flow ethylene diffusion flames. Combustion Theory and Modelling, 2004. 8(3): p. 593-606. https://doi.org/10.1088/1364-7830/8/3/009 2) Luque, J., Jeffries, J.B., Smith, G.P., Crosley, D.R., Walsh, K.T., Long, M.B., and Smooke, M.D., CH(A-X) and OH(A-X) optical emission in an axisymmetric laminar diffusion flame. Combustion and Flame, 2000. 122(1/2): p. 172-175. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0010-2180(00)00112-7 3) Walsh, K.T., Fielding, J., Smooke, M.D., and Long, M.B., Experimental and computational study of temperature, species, and soot in buoyant and non-buoyant coflow laminar diffusion flames. Proceedings of the Combustion Institute, 2000. 28: p. 1973-1979. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0082-0784(00)80603-7 4) Walsh, K.T., Long, M.B., Tanoff, M.A., and Smooke, M.D., Experimental and computational study of CH, CH*, and OH* in an axisymmetric laminar diffusion flame. Proceedings of the Combustion Institute, 1998. 27(Vol. 1): p. 615-623. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0082-0784(98)80453-0 Research Impacts/Earth Benefits Diffusion flames are the flame type of most practical combustion devices. The ability to predict the coupled effects of complex transport phenomena with detailed chemical kinetics in such systems is critical in the modeling of turbulent reacting flows and in understanding the processes by which soot formation and radiative transfer take place. In addition, an understanding of those factors that affect flame extinction in diffusion flames is critical in the suppression of fires and in improving engine efficiency. While normal gravity combustion studies can provide important information on combustion processes, the effects of gravitational forces often complicate the interpretation of both computational and experimental results. Momentum effects dominate most practical combustion devices, but the contribution of buoyancy forces is hard to eliminate in normal gravity. A goal of the study will be to apply sophisticated numerical tools and quantitative diagnostic techniques to the study of hydrocarbon diffusion flames in a microgravity environment. This will lead to a more detailed understanding of the interaction of convection, diffusion and chemistry under momentum-dominated conditions. Contact(s) Marshall B. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 1.34 TB PSI-17Version 3 Advanced Colloids Experiment - Temperature 6(ACE-T6) Investigation Submitted Date: 15-Sep-2023 Initial Release Date: 15-Sep-2023 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/4gj8-d687 Research Area: Complex Fluids - Soft Matter SubResearch Area: Colloids Related Investigation: PSI-16, PSI-18, PSI-19 License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 03-28-2008 Investigation End Date 07-01-2015 Sponsoring Agency Center for the Advancement of Science in Space (CASIS) NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives ACE-T6 studies the microscopic behavior of colloids in gels and creams. Consumer products are often required to be ‘structured’ by colloidal gels to prevent instability - or bulk separation of dispersed benefit actives. Benefit actives are generally dispersed as micron-size drops in liquid products to impart a consumer benefit, such as fabric softness. This leads to a fundamental challenge- how do you preventing bulk separation of the actives (i.e. maintain shelf life) while at the same time maintaining the relative ease-of-flow characteristics of the products. The objective of ACE-T6 is to use confocal microscopy to study the 3D behavior of microscopic particles in gels and creams, to advance knowledge of the fundamental physics associated with gel coarsening to improve the shelf-life stability of products. The microgravity environment on ISS was required to detach phase separation from coarsening. Approach The ACE-T6 investigation utilized a single Sample Module (SM) having 3 temperature controlled capillary cells with 20 ml colloidal sample fluid and each having differing particle concentration. The capillary cells were situated on the temperature gradient stage (typical range: 20 – 60 °C, 10 °C temperature differential over the full length). The experiment employed confocal microscopy, which uses a 532-nm frequency-doubled Nd:YAG laser, a confocal scanner, and an 8- to 12-bit digital CCD camera. The scanner allowed 30 frames per second of confocal images to be taken by the CCD camera. A sample’s 3D crystal structure was reconstructed by assembling individual slices with an image analysis program, from which colloidal growth, structure, and dynamics can be observed and measured. To obtain statistically meaningful data, at least ten colloidal structures in each capillary was imaged, for at least ~400 minutes of observation on each capillary. Hypothesis ACE-T6 addresses the effect of polydispersity on coarsening in colloidal systems. It is hypothesized that polydispersity in the polymer makes order-of-magnitude differences in the time scale of collapse of weak gels. The investigation attempts to make benchmark microgravity measurements and advance theories that allow a more comprehensive understanding of the role of polydispersity in the coarsening process. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits This research will have significant impact in two areas. First, in the scientific community, there is a large disconnect between microscopic structure and dynamics of these mixtures to the macroscopic changes in the structure which lead to collapse. This work will significantly enhance the knowledge necessary to advance this important area of science. Second, understanding this relationship should enable us to anticipate instability in products, directly impacting the development of multi-billion dollar products and initiatives which improve the lives of 4.8 billion people on Earth per day from products originating from Procter and Gamble alone. Understanding the behavior of mixtures and coarsening can help materials scientists to make colloidal mixtures with longer shelf lives. This has great potentials in creating a wide range of products from food, medicine, cosmetics, gels, and cleaning solutions which do not expire quickly. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 124.32 GB PSI-16Version 4 Advanced Colloids Experiment - Temperature 1(ACE-T1) Investigation Submitted Date: 15-Sep-2023 Initial Release Date: 15-Sep-2023 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/sb1s-3m71 Research Area: Complex Fluids - Soft Matter SubResearch Area: Colloids Related Investigation: PSI-17, PSI-18, PSI-19 License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 08-15-2016 Investigation End Date 11-22-2023 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives The ACE-T1 investigation seeks to answer fundamental questions about behaviors of colloids, helping scientists to understand how to control, change, and even reverse interactions between tiny particles. The objective is to build a fundamental understanding of the behavior of antisotropic (directionally dependent) Janus particles and their 3D self-assembly in microgravity. For decades, important advances have been reported in the literature regarding the effects of directionally dependent particles, both the chemical and morphological aspects, that provide the potential to extend the complexity of the self-assembled structures. Approach The ACE-T1 investigation was executed in 2 phases and utilized 3 Sample Modules (SM), each having 3 temperature controlled capillary cells with 20 ml sample fluid each. Phase 2 was a re-run of the T1-103 SM and employed confocal microscopy, which uses a 532-nm frequency-doubled Nd:YAG laser, a confocal scanner, and an 8- to 12-bit digital CCD camera. The scanner allowed 30 frames per second of confocal images to be taken by the CCD camera. A sample’s 3D crystal structure was reconstructed by assembling individual slices with an image analysis program, from which colloidal growth, structure, and dynamics can be observed and measured. To obtain statistically meaningful data, at least ten colloidal structures in one capillary cell was imaged, at least ~400 minutes of observation on each capillary. Hypothesis Fundamental science and colloidal engineering can be pursued and understood directly at a particle level. Microscopy enables scientists to directly observe what is happening at a colloid particle level - one no longer requires a theoretical model to hope to connect macroscopic experimental observations to microscopic ones (as when observing experiments at the size scale seen with a photograph taken of a BCAT or PCS sample). Research Impacts/Earth Benefits SPACE APPLICATIONS Observing colloidal interactions without the influence of gravity provides new insight into how unhindered particles form network and structures. Results from ACE-T1 lay a foundation for understanding this mechanism. Very small scale self-assembly of materials can be an efficient method to build new materials and equipment in space. EARTH APPLICATIONS The ACE-T1 investigation seeks to answer fundamental questions about behaviors of colloids, helping scientists to understand how to control, change, and even reverse interactions between tiny particles. This knowledge is crucial for developing self-assembling, self-moving, and self-replicating technologies for use on Earth. It is anticipated that this novel fabrication approach can be applied to produce novel functional material in various applications such as self-assembly, photonics, diagnostics, and drug-delivery. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 15.84 GB PSI-87Version 4 Pool Boiling Experiment(PBE) Investigation Submitted Date: 15-Sep-2023 Initial Release Date: 15-Sep-2023 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/nc4b-jz16 Research Area: Fluid Physics License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform Space Shuttle Investigation Start Date 09-01-1987 Investigation End Date 11-30-1998 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Objectives The program described here seeks to improve the understanding of the fundamental mechanisms that constitute nucleate pool boiling. The vehicle for accomplishing this is an investigation, including experiments to be conducted in microgravity and coupled with appropriate analyses, of the heat transfer and vapor bubble dynamics associated with nucleation, bubble growth or collapse, and subsequent motion. Certain effects that can be neglected at normal Earth gravity, such as surface tension and vapor momentum, can become quite significant in microgravity. Momentum imparted to the liquid by the vapor bubble during growth tends to draw the vapor bubble away from the surface, depending on the rate of growth, which in turn is governed by the temperature distribution in the liquid. Thermophoretic forces, arising from the variation of the liquid-vapor surface tension with temperature, on the other hand, tend to move the vapor bubble toward the region of higher temperature. The bubble motion will be governed by which of these two effects prevail. The elements of nucleate boiling, for which research conducted under microgravity would advance the basic understanding, are: 1. Nucleation or onset of boiling. Indications are that both heater surface temperature and temperature distribution in the liquid are necessary to describe nucleation. 2. The dynamic growth of a vapor bubble in the vicinity of the heater surface. This includes the shape as well as motion of the liquid-vapor interface as growth is taking place. These are influenced by the liquid temperature distribution at the initiation of growth. 3. The subsequent behavior of the vapor bubble. This includes the motion, whether departure takes place or not, and the associated heat transfer. Approach The approach encompasses a comprehensive experimental methodology designed to dissect the nuances of the boiling process in an environment where gravity's influence is minimal. This approach aims to isolate and analyze the core mechanisms that drive nucleate pool boiling, offering insights that are obscured under normal Earth gravity conditions. Here is an outline of the investigation's methodological approach: 1. Experimental Setup in Microgravity: a. The investigation utilizes a specially designed experimental apparatus capable of accurately controlling and measuring heat flux, liquid subcooling levels, and temperature distribution within the liquid and at the heater surface. This apparatus is deployed in a microgravity environment provided by space-based platforms to ensure the minimization of gravity's influence on the boiling process. 2. Controlled Heat Flux Application: a. A key component of the approach involves applying a controlled heat flux to a pool of liquid, initiating the boiling process. The heat flux is carefully modulated to explore a range of boiling conditions, from gentle nucleation to vigorous boiling, under varying levels of liquid subcooling. 3. High-Resolution Data Acquisition: a. To capture the dynamics of bubble formation, growth, and departure, the investigation employs high-resolution, high-speed imaging techniques, along with precise temperature and heat flux measurement tools. This data acquisition setup allows for the detailed observation and analysis of bubble behavior and heat transfer phenomena during the boiling process. 4. Parameter Variation: a. The investigation systematically varies key parameters, including the heat flux magnitude, the degree of liquid subcooling, and the pressure within the system, to study their effects on the nucleation process, bubble dynamics, and heat transfer rates. This parameter variation helps in identifying the critical factors that influence nucleate pool boiling under microgravity. 5. Data Analysis and Model Development: a. The collected data undergoes rigorous analysis to elucidate the fundamental mechanisms of nucleate pool boiling, focusing on nucleation criteria, bubble growth rates, and heat transfer characteristics. Insights gained from the analysis are used to develop and refine predictive models that can accurately describe boiling behavior under a variety of conditions. 6. Cross-Comparison with Earth Gravity Data: a. Findings from the microgravity experiments are compared with data obtained from similar experiments conducted under Earth gravity conditions. This cross-comparison aids in isolating the effects of gravity on the boiling process and contributes to the development of generalized models that can predict boiling behavior across different gravitational environments. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 193.29 GB PSI-109Version 4 Surface Tension Driven Convection Experiment-2(STDCE-2) Investigation Submitted Date: 15-Sep-2023 Initial Release Date: 15-Sep-2023 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/ehpd-h527 Research Area: Fluid Physics Related Investigation: PSI-108 License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform Space Shuttle Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives The main objectives of the present work are to investigate: 1. The onset conditions and nature of oscillatory flows. 2. The effect of the heating mode and the static free surface shape on the oscillations. 3. The shape and motion of the free surface during oscillations. 4. The coupling among the free surface deformation, the surface temperature distribution, and the velocity field. Approach The STDCE-2 investigation employed a systematic approach to explain the role of free surface deformation in oscillatory thermocapillary flows under microgravity conditions. This approach comprised: Controlled Variation of Key Parameters: -Container Size: Utilizing three chamber diameters (1.2 cm, 2.0 cm, 3.0 cm) allowed researchers to examine the influence of scale on the onset of oscillations and assess potential inertial effects. -Heating Mode: Employing both submerged heater (CT mode) and CO2 laser (CF mode) systems enabled the comparison of flow behavior under constant temperature difference and constant heat flux boundary conditions, respectively. -Free Surface Shape: Tests were conducted with flat, concave, and convex free surfaces to explore the interplay between surface curvature and flow dynamics. Advanced Diagnostic Techniques: -Flow Visualization: The use of tracer particles enabled the visualization and qualitative characterization of flow patterns, including the three-dimensional, time-dependent structures observed during oscillations. -Infrared Imaging: An infrared scanner captured the temperature distribution across the oil's free surface, providing insights into the thermal gradients driving the thermocapillary flow and their evolution during oscillations. -Optical Deformation Measurement: A Ronchi system was employed to measure the free surface deformation and motions, allowing researchers to quantify the dynamic changes in surface shape and correlate them with observed flow behavior and temperature variations. Interactive Operation: The experiment was conducted interactively, allowing the researchers on the ground to communicate with the astronauts onboard the Spacelab, observe the downlinked video images in real-time, and adjust test parameters based on the observed phenomena. This flexibility facilitated the exploration of unexpected results and the fine-tuning of the experimental conditions to optimize data collection. The STDCE-2 investigation gathered comprehensive data aimed at complex dynamics of oscillatory thermocapillary flows and verifying the hypothesized role of free surface deformation in their onset. Hypothesis The onset of oscillatory thermocapillary flow, particularly in microgravity environments, is significantly influenced by free surface deformation, which acts in conjunction with the Marangoni number (Ma). • Buoyancy masks the true oscillation mechanism in Earth- based experiments: The experimental data on oscillatory thermocapillary flows taken in normal gravity environments are often confusing or contradictory due to the presence of buoyancy. This suggests that buoyancy may obscure the role of free surface deformation in the oscillation process. • Marangoni number alone is insufficient to predict oscillations in microgravity: The unexpected stability observed in the prior STDCE microgravity experiments, even at Marangoni numbers exceeding the critical threshold observed in ground-based tests, indicates that Ma is not the sole determinant of oscillatory onset in the absence of buoyancy. • Free surface deformation is a key factor: The interaction between thermocapillary forces and free surface deformation plays a key role in the oscillation mechanism. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 1.21 TB PSI-89Version 4 Packed Bed Reactor Experiment - Water Recovery(PBRE-WR) Investigation Submitted Date: 15-Sep-2023 Initial Release Date: 15-Sep-2023 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/4bs6-af73 Research Area: Fluid Physics Related Investigation: PSI-88, PSI-90 License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives The objective of the flight experiment was to study the hydrodynamics of packed beds in microgravity and under different gas and liquid flow conditions. The hydrodynamics consists of the pressure drop inside the packed bed and the liquid hold-up. The different regimes are the results of different liquid and gas flow rates, and different initial conditions embodied by gas and liquid pre-flow or flushes prior to beginning of the runs. Another objective of the experiment was to understand transient flow rates and the hysteresis in the pressure drop as a function of the flow rates. Approach The PBRE-WR investigations employed a systematic and comprehensive approach to study the hydrodynamics of two-phase flow in packed bed reactors under microgravity conditions. The approach can be summarized in the following key steps: 1. Ground-Based Research and Model Development: Prior to the spaceflight experiments, extensive ground-based research was conducted to develop theoretical models and establish a foundation for understanding two-phase flow in packed beds. This included: Literature review: A thorough review of existing literature on single-phase and two-phase flow through porous media, focusing on pressure drop, flow regimes, and the influence of various parameters. Development of hydrodynamic models: Formulation of mathematical models, such as the modified Ergun equation, to predict pressure drop and flow regime transitions in microgravity. Ground-based experiments: Conducting experiments in reduced gravity environments, such as parabolic flights and drop towers, to gather preliminary data and validate initial model predictions. 2. Design and Development of Spaceflight Experiment: A dedicated experimental facility was designed and developed for operation on the ISS. This involved: Test facility design: Engineering a flow control system, test section, and data acquisition system capable of operating reliably in microgravity and meeting the specific requirements of the investigation. Selection of packing materials: PBRE-WR used 3.5 mm Alumina packing, a common inert material used in reactor beds such as water purification systems. Definition of test matrix: Developing a comprehensive test matrix encompassing a wide range of gas and liquid flow rates, pre-flow conditions, and transient flow scenarios. 3. Execution of Spaceflight Experiments: The PBRE-WR experiments were conducted on the ISS, following the defined test matrix and procedures. This involved: Preflow procedures: Implementing the chosen pre-flow treatment (liquid flush or gas flush) before each test run. Flow control: Precisely controlling and varying the gas and liquid flow rates according to the test matrix. Data acquisition: Collecting data from pressure sensors, temperature sensors, and high-speed cameras throughout each test run. Downlinking data: Transmitting the acquired data to the ground for analysis. 4. Data Analysis and Interpretation: The downlinked data was meticulously analyzed to: Characterize flow regimes: Identify and classify the different flow regimes observed in the experiments based on pressure traces and video recordings. Evaluate pressure drop: Analyze the pressure drop data and compare it with model predictions to assess the validity and accuracy of the models. Investigate flow regime transitions: Determine the conditions and mechanisms leading to transitions between different flow regimes. Assess the influence of packing properties and pre-flow conditions: Analyze the impact of packing material wettability, size, and pre-flow treatments on the flow behavior and pressure drop. 5. Dissemination of Results: The findings of the PBRE-WR investigations have not been completed and disseminated yet. Hypothesis While the overarching principles of two-phase flow in porous media apply, the specific material properties of alumina will cause unique flow phenomena, and models can be modified to account for such. Furthermore, this unique data is specifically relevant to the design and operation of reactors used in space-based water recovery systems, and the data can be used to improve and optimize such systems. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits Fundamental understanding the impact of reduced or zero gravity on the hydrodynamics (pressure drop, as well as distribution and holdup of each phase) is relevant to systems that involve two-phase flow such as life support systems, fuel cells, in-situ resource utilization, heat pipes, materials processing, production of pharmaceutical-grade water, and transport of nutrients in soils. Design and operation of many chemical and biological processing systems require this fundamental understanding of two-phase gas-liquid flows through porous media because many of these space-based systems or unit operations involve gas-liquid flows through porous media. Some examples of current space systems involving two-phase flow through fixed porous media include the Volatile Removal Assembly (VRA), the Integrated Advanced Water Recovery System (AWRS), and IntraVenous Water GENeration system (IVGEN). The ability to predict flow regimes and corresponding pressure drop in a particular system involving two-phase flow is crucial to the design of the fluid system and the pumping requirements. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 76.63 GB PSI-52Version 3 Advanced Colloids Experiment - Temperature Control and Gradient Sample 11(ACE-T11) Investigation Submitted Date: 15-Sep-2023 Initial Release Date: 15-Sep-2023 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/vkw0-me50 Research Area: Complex Fluids - Soft Matter SubResearch Area: Colloids License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 09-01-2019 Investigation End Date 08-31-2024 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives ACE-T11 studies the design and assembly of complex 3D structures from small particles suspended within a fluid medium with control of particle density, phase and behavior. Objectives included study of nucleation and growth of crystals within colloidal samples by varying the size and concentration of colloids and depletant, exploring the effect of temperature gradients, and demonstrating control of particle shape and density which is essential for creating high performance materials for 3D printing and advanced optical materials. The research goal is to produce various colloidal structures and study the dynamics of crystal nucleation and growth. The imaging goal is to observe crystallites and resolve particle centroid positions with less than 20% error. Approach The ACE-T11 investigation used 2 Sample Modules (SM), each containing 3 capillary cells for a total of 6 samples. Confocal microscopy was employed for 3D imaging of non-spherical colloids, with phases controlled by adding depletants, adjusting spatial temperature changes, and applying temperature gradients. The size and concentration of both the particles and depletants were varied across different samples. After homogenization using a magnetic stirrer, the particles were left undisturbed to crystallize. Preliminary observations were made with a 2.5X objective, followed by detailed imaging using 10X, 63X, and 100X objectives. Hypothesis Under microgravity conditions, colloidal particles would exhibit unique crystallization and self-assembly behaviors that differ from those observed under Earth's gravity. Researchers believed that without the effects of sedimentation, they would better understand the fundamental mechanisms governing colloidal phase transitions and self-organization​. This hypothesis also included the idea that controlling external factors like temperature and depletant concentration would enable precise manipulation of colloidal structures, allowing for the creation of more complex and functional materials. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits Future space missions will require self-assembly and self-replication technologies for self-repairing materials and devices, essential for long-duration travel. 3D printing and additive manufacturing are crucial for creating replacement parts, with research focusing on developing particle slurries and pastes suited for both micro and regular gravity environments. This research advances soft matter science, with applications in medicine, electronics, and photonics. Self-assembly techniques will enable new devices for energy and communication, while 3D printing and additive manufacturing rely on optimizing high-density slurries and pastes with diverse mechanical properties. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 3.18 GB PSI-112Version 6 Solidification Using a Baffle in Sealed Ampoules - Effect of Convection on the Columnar-to-Equiaxed Transition in Alloy Solidification(SUBSA - CETSOL) Investigation Submitted Date: 15-Sep-2023 Initial Release Date: 15-Sep-2023 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/gx1w-bk91 Research Area: Materials Science SubResearch Area: Solidification License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Proposal Title Effect of Convection on Columnar-to-Equiaxed Transition in Alloy Solidification Flight Platform International Space Station Investigation Start Date 10-01-2010 Investigation End Date 07-31-2023 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NASA Center Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) Objectives The objective of the proposed investigation is to better understand the columnar-to-equiaxed grain structure transition (CET) in solidification of metal alloys. By performing solidification experiments both on earth and in a microgravity environment, the effects of gravity-driven melt convection and sedimentation/floatation of unattached dendrite fragments and equiaxed crystals on the CET will be examined. The origin of equiaxed grains in non-refined alloys is of particular interest in the proposed experiments. The benchmark data from these experiments can be used to test theoretical models and computer simulations. Approach Experiments were conducted in the Solidification Using a Baffle in Sealed Ampoules (SUBSA) furnace to investigate the CET for stationary samples without an imposed temperature gradient. Most experiments with aluminum-copper (Al-Cu) alloys, namely, Al-4wt%Cu, Al-10wt%Cu and Al-18wt%Cu alloys. The reason is that Al-Cu alloys are better suited for the duplicate ground-based experiments. If solidified upward (low temperature at the bottom, high at the top), thermosolutal natural convection of the melt will generally be minimized. The sedimentation or floatation of dendrite fragments and small equiaxed grains can be controlled by the solute concentration. For smaller solute concentrations, the solid is heavier than the melt and will sediment, while for higher solute concentrations the solid is lighter and will float. Hence, dendrite fragments and equiaxed grains in the Al-18wt%Cu alloy will float upwards ahead of the columnar front, and a CET can be expected. On the other hand, for the Al-4wt%Cu alloy, the fragments will sediment and remain between the primary columnar trunks, and a CET may not occur. For Al-10wt%Cu alloys, the solid is approximately neutrally buoyant in the melt. An additional experiment with an unrefined Al-7wt%Si alloy was also conducted. No grain refiner was used. In all proposed CET experiments, the samples were first fully melted and then solidified by decreasing the temperature of the SUBSA furnace at a controlled rate. The samples were not moved, and no temperature gradient were explicitly imposed. Corresponding flight and terrestrial experiments were conducted. Samples were analyzed by measuring the grain structure and any macrosegregation. Hypothesis The primary hypothesis of this investigation is that fragmentation of columnar dendrites can lead to a CET in non-grain-refined alloys. The secondary dendrite arms that detach from the primary columnar trunks are a potent source of new (equiaxed) grains. However, for a CET to occur the growth of the primary columnar trunks must be blocked by equiaxed grains. This can only be accomplished if the secondary dendrite fragments are transported to the columnar front, rather than remain between the primary columnar trunks. Due to natural convection of the melt and sedimentation or floatation of the fragments, such transport can be expected to readily occur in the gravitational field of earth. In the absence of gravity, it is not clear if fragmentation alone, without fragment transport, is sufficient to cause a CET. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits The CET refers to the transition between the elongated grains in the outer portions of a casting and the more rounded grains in the center. Understanding this transition is fundamental to determining what type of grain structure forms in castings of most metal alloys (steel, aluminum, copper, etc.). Often, a fully equiaxed structure is preferred, but the fully columnar structures of many turbine blades are an important exception. In addition to its high practical significance, the CET represents a “holy grail” in the area of modeling and simulation of casting. This is because in order to realistically predict the CET, almost every physical phenomenon at every length scale must be taken into account simultaneously. This investigation will not only provide an improved understanding of the CET, but also models and computer simulations of the grain structure formation in metal castings that can be used by industry to better industry to better understand and optimize their casting processes.
