title: Cold Atom Lab - Zero-G Studies of Few Body and Many-Body Physics(CAL - Few Body Physics)
objectives: Zero-G Studies of Few-Body and Many-Body Physics (Cold Atom Lab - Few-Body Physics) investigates the dynamics of interacting ultracold atoms under varying conditions. The dynamics of few-body systems ...
approach: The Zero-G Studies of Few-Body and Many-Body Physics investigation uses rubidium (87Rb) and potassium (39K and 41K) samples in the Cold Atom Laboratory (CAL) aboard the International Space Station (IS...
detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 94.58 GB PSI-36Version 4 Cold Atom Lab - Zero-G Studies of Few Body and Many-Body Physics(CAL - Few Body Physics) Investigation Submitted Date: 15-Sep-2023 Initial Release Date: 15-Sep-2023 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/rqkw-df69 Research Area: Fundamental Physics SubResearch Area: Many Body Systems Related Investigation: PSI-31, PSI-32, PSI-33, PSI-35 License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 04-01-2014 Investigation End Date 09-27-2025 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NASA Center Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) Objectives Zero-G Studies of Few-Body and Many-Body Physics (Cold Atom Lab - Few-Body Physics) investigates the dynamics of interacting ultracold atoms under varying conditions. The dynamics of few-body systems comprised of just three or four atoms can strongly influence the collective behavior of quantum gases and play an important role in development of quantum gas applications. Modern laser cooling techniques are used to chill atoms to near absolute zero temperatures. At these temperatures, atoms behave like matter waves, according to the laws of quantum mechanics. Fully automated data runs, each lasting about one minute, acquire images of ultracold atom clouds under varying conditions. The acquired data fills a critical need for the development of detailed and precise atomic physics models. The development of these models is performed in theoretical studies accompanying the data gathering campaigns with the CAL instrument. Studying the behavior and interaction of few atoms in microgravity could provide important data for developing a precise theory describing quantum gases on a microscopic level. The knowledge gained in this study also aids in the development of future quantum technologies for which a detailed microscopic understanding of few-body physics is essential. Examples of future quantum technologies include, among others, atom interferometers for inertial navigation or precision measurements of gravity and sensitive Terahertz (THz) detectors for astronomy. Approach The Zero-G Studies of Few-Body and Many-Body Physics investigation uses rubidium (87Rb) and potassium (39K and 41K) samples in the Cold Atom Laboratory (CAL) aboard the International Space Station (ISS). The approach for the investigation comprises two main aspects: the creation of ultracold atomic gases and the subsequent manipulation and probing of these gases to study few-body physics and exotic quantum states. Modern laser-cooling techniques are used to cool atoms to near absolute zero temperatures. At these temperatures, atoms behave like matter waves, according to the laws of quantum mechanics. Fully automated data runs, each lasting about one minute, acquire images of ultracold atom clouds under varying conditions. 1. Creation of Ultracold Atomic Gas: • Laser Cooling: Atoms are released into a vacuum chamber and collected into a magneto-optical trap (MOT), where they are initially cooled using laser cooling techniques. This technique is based on the rapid scattering of light off atoms and can cool a cloud of atoms to temperatures below 1x10-3 K. An additional magnetic field applied in conjunction with the lasers concentrates the cold atoms in a specific region of the vacuum apparatus, called the source chamber. The MOT is the starting point for further cooling and experimental preparation. • State Preparation: Using further laser manipulations, the atoms are then prepared in a state that seeks to occupy regions of low magnetic fields. By applying a suitable magnetic field geometry with a moving magnetic minimum, the cloud of atoms is transported to a so-called “science region.” Magnetic fields generated by a chip with current-carrying traces provide a trap for the atoms in the science region. • Evaporative Cooling: With the atoms trapped in the science region, evaporative cooling is performed by selectively removing the hottest rubidium atoms from the cloud. The remaining atoms then rethermalize at a lower temperature. The selective removal of the hottest rubidium atoms is achieved by applying suitably tuned radiofrequency radiation. Potassium atoms are cooled by being in thermal contact with the actively cooled rubidium atoms, in a process called sympathetic cooling, where rubidium atoms act as a cold bath of atoms. With sufficient evaporative cooling, the clouds of rubidium and potassium atoms can undergo a phase transition to a Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC), providing a macroscopic, quantum mechanical object. However, pronounced quantum mechanical effects can already be observed before reaching this phase transition. • Further sample preparation: After the preparation of the ultracold sample, further preparation steps are employed for the proposed studies. These steps include changes to the trapping strength, changes of the internal states of the atoms, and the application of suitable homogeneous magnetic fields. 2. Manipulation and Detection: • Manipulation Techniques: The ultracold gas is manipulated using laser, radiofrequency, and/or microwave pulses. In addition, homogeneous magnetic fields are used to shift internal energy levels of the atoms. These techniques are designed to adjust the pairwise interactions as needed for the preparation of exotic quantum states. • Time-of-Flight Imaging: After a predetermined time-of-flight during which the cloud is released from the trap and can expand freely, the sample is imaged using absorption imaging techniques. For this, a short laser pulse is flashed onto the atoms, and the shadow cast by the atoms is imaged on a CCD camera using a custom microscope setup. This imaging process typically destroys the “quantumness” of the sample and concludes an experimental cycle. The apparatus then starts over with the preparation of a new sample. Many cycles are performed during a typical data-taking campaign, with a time scale of approximately one minute per run. Hypothesis Ultracold atoms in microgravity provide a unique environment for the study of complex few-body phenomena. One of the surprising predictions for quantum mechanical few-body systems is the existence of universality, i.e. the idea that highly intricate phenomena can be governed by underlying principles that are agnostic to specific microscopic realizations. As a concrete example, Efimov physics predicts the emergence of an infinite series of exotic three-body bound states when the interactions between the atoms are made stronger and stronger. It is predicted that these Efimov states are connected by universal scaling relations governing their energy and their size. Our experiments aim to provide essential benchmark data to test this universality hypothesis. By measuring two members of this infinite series, scaling relations can be probed and can be compared to some of the most advanced few-body theories to date. This will be a steppingstone towards the investigation of a plethora of associated few-body phenomena, with the ultimate goal of significantly advancing the boundary of our understanding and paving the way for the development of new quantum technologies. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits Physics is the discipline that provides understanding of biology and chemistry at the most microscopic level, and the area within physics most relevant to chemistry and biology is “few-body physics.” It is an often neglected portion of physics, because it is so difficult to do. An important way to make progress is to simplify, simplify, simplify: to come up with model systems in which we can make progress that can later be applied to human-centric disciplines like biology, and develop exotic and useful new materials. A promising way to simplify is to study matter at lower temperature, and lower densities. The Cold-Atom Lab (CAL) flying in the International Space Station (ISS) is where we will reach the lowest possible temperatures, and low densities, to perform studies of simple, yet intricate (think “snowflakes”) clusters of three or four atoms. Ultracold atomic gases are a key platform for a broad range of future quantum technologies, including ultraprecise sensing and timekeeping, novel medical imaging methods, secure communication schemes, high-performance computing, and development of exotic materials. A precise knowledge of few-body physics is necessary to fully realize the potential of quantum technologies. This project supports development of a detailed understanding of quantum mechanical few-body physics at the microscopic level, which may open new avenues for quantum gas applications in future space exploration. Such applications include inertial navigation and precision measurements using atom interferometry, or calibration standards for detectors used in astronomy. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 67.31 GB PSI-19Version 5 Advanced Colloids Experiment with Temperature Control - R [Ellipsoid](ACE-TR) Investigation Submitted Date: 15-Sep-2023 Initial Release Date: 15-Sep-2023 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/h43z-ae86 Research Area: Complex Fluids - Soft Matter SubResearch Area: Colloids License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 09-17-2020 Investigation End Date 02-10-2021 Sponsoring Agency Center for the Advancement of Science in Space (CASIS), National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), National Institutes of Health (NIH) NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives The objective of the ACE-TR (Ellipsoid) experiment was to image and document the self-assembly of complex 3D structures formed from small elliptical colloidal particles suspended in a fluid. Temperature gradients were varied with the objective to explore the effect of thermophoresis on colloidal crystallization. The goal was to crystallize a metastable colloidal liquid to study how the orientation and periodicity in particle arrangement evolves in different regions of the phase diagram of elliptical colloidal particles. The objective was to understand the effects of gravity on colloidal self-assembly, test predictions of current theories for soft materials, and develop novel techniques that can be applied to combine materials with different densities in additive manufacturing. The expected outcome has the potential to make novel colloidal materials in a Low-Earth orbit and return them to Earth. Approach ACE-TR will view collections of temperature-controlled, fluorescent-core micron-sized colloidal particles. It uses two different sets of ellipsoids, each in their own sample cells. These have aspect ratios of either 1x2.8 or 1x4.5 microns. The particles are small enough that 50 of them could be placed end to end across the width of a fine human hair; yet big enough that the particles and the structures they form can be photographed with visible light of a confocal microscope. The observations will be done using a 3D confocal microscope at the particle level for sufficiently high particle concentrations; in some samples, we will attempt to control the desired concentration by applying a temperature gradient, to see if the particle number density will adjust itself as a function of temperature throughout the sample cell. ImageJ software and internally developed MATLAB functions and scripts were used for processing and quantification of images collected. Hypothesis Despite the fundamental and technological importance, the understanding of colloidal crystallization is still elusive. This investigation hypothesizes that there is interrelation between processes driving orientation and periodicity in particle arrangement. Comparing the outcome of the ACE-T11 (Hard Spheres) and ACE-TR (Ellipsoids) experiments should help elucidate this interrelation. This will enable a better understanding at the particle level of how a disordered arrangement of elliptical particles self-organizes into a 3D ordered structure. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits ACE-TR reveals several fundamental and practical aspects of soft matter science with potential applications on Earth. Self-assembly processes are crucial to making functional materials and devices from small particles. Improved design and assembly of structures fabricated in microgravity may have use in a variety of fields from medicine to opto-electronics on Earth. Ultimately, the ability to design and build functional structures based on colloids will allow new devices for chemical energy, communication, and photonics, including photonic materials to control and manipulate light. The rapidly growing fields of 3D printing and additive manufacturing rely on the assembly and sintering of particle aggregates and the preparation of high-density slurries and pastes of different colloidal materials and with different rheological and mechanical properties. These ellipsoids may behave like liquid crystals when they self-assemble and their possible defects (hedgehogs) may also be visible. Contact(s) Boris Khusidemail,Paul M. Chaikinemail,William V. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 9.68 GB PSI-97Version 4 Ring-Sheared Drop - Amyloid Fibril Formation(RSD-AFF) Investigation Submitted Date: 31-May-2023 Initial Release Date: 31-May-2023 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/d4jq-pv07 Research Area: Biophysics SubResearch Area: Proteins License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Proposal Title Amyloid Fibril Formation in Microgravity: Distinguishing Interfacial and Flow Effects Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 09-01-2013 Investigation End Date 12-31-2023 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NASA Center Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) Objectives This campaign centered on four main objectives: (i) engineering the RSD to flight proven hardware, (ii) testing measurement and instrumentation methods aboard the ISS, (iii) studying protein kinetics under interfacial shear, and (iv) measuring and modeling protein solution rheology. The primary obective of this investigation is to quantify the effects of flow on fibrillization in the bulk and at interfaces, specifically at the air/water interface. This includes studying protein kinetics under interfacial shear, and measuring and modeling protein solution rheology. The overall objective is project to advance the mechanistic description of fibrillization by determining how shearing flow affects each of the stages of amyloid formation process − protein unfolding and nuclei formation, growth into protofibrils, and elongation and intertwining into mature fibrils and fibril growth − without any influence from solid boundaries. Approach The Ring Shear Drop (RSD) is used to facilitate amyloidogenesis and study flow dynamics without solid wall interactions. It uses surface tension to contain fluids in a microgravity environment. Techniques like Particle Tracking Velocimetry (PTV) are used to measure fluid dynamics and protein interactions. This information was used to create high-fidelity computational models. Formation and flow of protein aggregates on the surface of the drop will be imaged by the microscope as a function of time. The RSD imaged the surface of a 2.50 cm diameter drop of protein solution with shear imposed by the rotation of one of the two sharp-edged rings (essentially knife edges) that constrain the drop. A separate measure of the turbidity quantified by the extinction of a light beam through the center of the drop provided an independent signal for fibril formation. A variable degree of shear was imposed on the drop with a negligible contact with solid boundaries. Velocity of the fluid on the surface of the drop will be determined by standard cross-correlation techniques from images obtained by the microscope. Details regarding sample composition and experimental parameters can be found in RSD Experimental Table. Hypothesis The absence of gravity in a microgravity environment will significantly alter the amyloid fibril formation process in proteins.The hypothesis tested was that if protein solutions in microgravity are seeded with fibrils and subject to steady interfacial shear, then amyloidogenesis will occur with the extent of gelation depending on total protein concentration. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits Amyloid fibril formation in proteins is of great interest because of its role in diseases such as Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s. For example, the waxy plaque choking off neurons in Alzheimer’s patients consists of the A-beta protein that has formed into amyloid fibrils. The microgravity environment aboard the ISS was utilized to study the biophysics of protein amyloidogenesis. The absence of gravity allows surface tension to provide fluid containment so that wall nucleation and other complications associated with solid containers can be avoided. Flow effects on protein fibrillization was studied at fluid interfaces similar to physiological processes, as all brain tissue consists of interfaces with fluidity, being comprised of cell membranes. The goal is to advance mechanistic descriptions of amyloid fibril formation. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 255.77 GB PSI-25Version 4 Burning and Suppression of Solids - II(BASS-II) Investigation Submitted Date: 31-Dec-2022 Initial Release Date: 31-Dec-2022 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/4qc4-de67 Research Area: Combustion Science SubResearch Area: Spacecraft Fire Safety Related Investigation: PSI-26 License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 01-01-2010 Investigation End Date 12-31-2022 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives BASS-II results contribute to the combustion computational models used in the design of fire detection and suppression systems in microgravity and on Earth. Objectives Include: 1) Study the ignition, flame growth, flame spread, and extinction limits for solid fuels burning in low-velocity forced flows in microgravity. 2) Begin to bridge the gap between the normal gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test #1 method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual material flammability in microgravity. 3) Provide SoFIE PIs with preliminary data to refine Science Requirements. 4) Practical, realistic (thicker) fuels in typical geometries will be examined, including slabs, cylinders, and spherical sections. The primary variables include: • Forced flow velocity (speed and direction) • Ambient oxygen concentration (via working volume nitrogen vitiation) • Sample geometry (rods, spherical section, slabs, films, and fabric sheets Approach To summarize, BASS-II's approach, microgravity combustion tests were performed aboard the International Space Station. Active crew support for real-time “lab partner” operations. The wind tunnel was installed in the Microgravity Science Glovebox which supplied power, imaging, and a level of containment. Fuel samples were mounted inside a small wind tunnel which could impose airflow speeds up to 40 cm/s. Main variables are airflow speed and oxygen concentration (oxygen varied below 21% by adding nitrogen). Flame appearance, flame growth, and spread rates were determined in both the opposed and concurrent flow. Hypothesis BASS–II tests the hypothesis that materials in microgravity, with adequate ventilation, burn as well if not better than the same material in normal gravity with other conditions being identical (pressure, O2 concentration, temperature, etc.). NASA tests and controls materials from a flammability perspective using an upward burning test in normal gravity, which is considered to be the worst-case geometry for flammability of the material on Earth. However, it may not be conservative for flammability in space. Testing at constant O2 mole fractions permits studying flame spread and extinction at low and high flow speed. We are interested in finding the fundamental limit for a given material. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits A primary goal of BASS-II is improved spacecraft fire safety, improved understanding of combustion in space and how to avoid it. If you’re on a mission far from Earth, a fire can be catastrophic. BASS-II helps engineers select the safest materials and improve firefighting methods on future space missions. In outer space, fuels burn as oval balls rather than with an upward pointed cone flame as they do on Earth. This simpler combustion process enables researchers to evaluate computer models of fuel burning. These models can then be used to more accurately study flames on Earth, such as in wildfires, building fires, energy recapture from waste recycling, and other combustion problems. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 1.62 GB PSI-111Version 7 SUBSA Brazing of Aluminum Alloys IN Space(BRAINS) Investigation Submitted Date: 30-Nov-2022 Initial Release Date: 30-Nov-2022 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/g6v6-rx24 Research Area: Materials Science SubResearch Area: Brazing, Capillary Forces License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform ISS Investigation Start Date 04-Nov-2016 Investigation End Date 30-Nov-2022 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NASA Center Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) Objectives The primary scientific goal of the proposed terrestrial and planned microgravity molten metal capillary flow experiments is to better understand the physics of the flow of molten metals over the topographically modified surfaces (e.g., filling in the holes, flow over sharp edges and/or flow over surfaces having variable curvatures). By performing capillary flow tests both on Earth and in a microgravity environment, the effects of microgravity on the kinetics of the larger masses of melt flow, and ultimate equilibrium shape of the meniscus will be closely examined. The objective of the microgravity experiments is to provide benchmark data against which theoretical models and computer simulations can be tested. The BRAINS project’s primary pragmatic/engineering obective is that a capillary flow of braze under microgravity conditions would enable a repair or bonding of larger and/or more irregular mating surfaces defects, compared to the terrestrial conditions. This would be important for future development of advanced brazing techniques with applications to both damage repair and construction in space. Approach Before being assembled into the ampoule, the samples were always ultrasonically cleaned in the sequence of (i) soapy water, (ii) water, (iii) 190 proof ethanol, and then dried in air or a compressed air. A double nitrogen purge was done before sealing the ampoule. Three configurations of the Al alloy filler and corresponding substrates were considered as relevant for the intended study: (i) HOLE, (ii) PIN and (iii) Hollow Pin. Solidification Using a Baffle in Sealed Ampoules” (SUBSA) furnace, which was designed for operation in the ISS’s Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) was used for this investigation. All samples were placed in the isothermal region of the furnace instrumented with thermocouples. The furnace was heated to the dwell temperature (600 - 605 °C ± 2K) at a rate of 5 K/minute (optimal 10K/minute). A dwell time was maintained for completion of capillary flow and establishing of the equilibrium meniscus shape. Subsequent cooling of the samples was performed at the maximum cooling rate allowed by the facility. Capillary topography identification and microstructure evaluation was performed on all samples. Hypothesis A series of space (ISS) and terrestrial experiments, integrated with modeling and analysis are expected to answer the following practical and fundamental questions: (1) How can the absence of gravity and dominance of capillary forces be take advantage of in transporting the molten braze? (2) Which brazing alloy and the brazing technique will enable strong and efficient bonding of selected proxies of structural elements and facilitate a repair. That is, can brazing be done in space and/or on board of space vehicles by using flux-less braze? Specifically: A comparison between flux and flux-less brazing under space and terrestrial conditions can answer underlying scientific questions related to molten metal flow kinetics, specifically wetting and spreading of liquid clad/filler over topographically modified surfaces. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits A brazing process may be used to mitigate the consequences of high velocity micro meteoroids’ and/or space debris’ impacts, and possible catastrophic penetration of aluminum man-made objects in space. Second, construction in space would necessitate joining complex assemblies, e.g., habitat systems, with brazing being one meaningful manufacturing option of permanent bonding. Validation fundamental models including phase field models will allow prediction of terrestrial brazing quality. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 1.85 TB PSI-20Version 4 Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator(ACME BRE) Investigation Submitted Date: 15-Sep-2022 Initial Release Date: 15-Sep-2022 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/vb93-3y72 Research Area: Combustion Science SubResearch Area: Flames of Gaseous Fuels License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Proposal Title Experimental Investigation of Emulated Burning Rate at Various Gravity Levels Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 01-01-2010 Investigation End Date 02-08-2025 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives The BRE flight program seeks to establish the burning conditions in a quiescent microgravity ambient in terms of material properties. The specific flight objectives are as follows. 1. Observe burning behavior in long-duration microgravity for CH4/N2 and C2H4/N2mixtures on porous circular burners of 25 and 50 mm diameter. Consider O2/N2 ambients with various pressures and ambient O2 concentrations and pressures. NASA - considered atmosphere for human space missions will be examined: 14.7 psia, 21 % oxygen: 10.2 psia, 26.5 %; and 8.2 psia, 34 % oxygen. Emphasize fuel conditions that can be related to a diverse range of condensed fuels. 2. Consider the conditions of Objective 1 for ambients of O2/CO2 (desired). 3. Consider the conditions of Objectives 1 – 2 for extinction limits. Approach To accomplish the above objectives, flight experiments are proposed. Additionally, preliminary flight tests will be performed to verify the experiment operations and for comparison with ground-based tests. For each test, conditions will be established for the chamber contents, namely choice of diluent, oxygen concentration, and pressure. Fuel flow will commence followed by ignition. The flames will initially be observed without varying the fuel flow rate. Because burner surface temperature and heat flux will vary, this will allow a broad range of conditions to be observed during a single test. As the surface temperature of the burner increases, and the flame remains steady, a continuous set of data is produced for the flammability map. Eventually either the flame will extinguish, the surface temperature of the burner will equilibrate, or the temperature limit of the heat flux sensor will be reached. At this time the fuel flow will be terminated. So a test should terminate for a given flow rate at extinction, and for continued burning when the burner surface temperature has steadied or the temperature limit of the heat flux sensor is neared. The extinction limit could be found once the burner temperature has steadied, and the heat flux sensor has not exceeded its limit. At that state, the flow rate can be reduced in small increments, until extinction is observed and the flow rate shut off. Again, in this process, new data is being produced for the flammability map. Ignition limit tests are not proposed for microgravity, but we will explore these under normal gravity. We believe there is better control on Earth-based ignition testing and that these results should carry over to microgravity conditions. In addition to the flight experiments, in normal gravity testing will continue. These tests will involve gaseous, liquid, and solid fuels. These experiments will further establish the validation of the BRE for 1-g applications and show its usefulness to establish 1-g ignition and extinction limits. As available, drop facility testing will be used to refine procedures, test instrumentation, and help to establish viable flow conditions. We will also pursue a CFD model for the quiescent microgravity burning. This will also guide us in the flight experiments, and potentially provide a predictive methodology. Hypothesis The BRE investigation hypothesizes that there can exist a regime of quasi-steady burning in microgravity as a function of materials properties. Steady burning may never be achieved, and only slowly changing unsteady flames are possible. The proposed tests aboard the ISS aims to query this hypothesis by establishing a range of quasi-steady burning conditions for condensed fuels in the microgravity environment. It is hypothesized that BRE can determine a range of burning conditions in microgravity as a function of heat of gasification, reradiation heat flux, applied radiant heat flux, heat of combustion and smoke point. This could enable the Cone Calorimeter (NASA Test 2) test as a basis for establishing flammability maps for real materials. The key hypothesis is that the heat of combustion, smoke point, and heat of gasification of the fuel mixture will represent a real solid fuel (or liquid fuel absorbed in an inert matrix). Thus achieved steady burning would represent the potential for real solid fuels to achieve steady burning in microgravity. Other than a candle flame, this has not been shown before. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits BRE yielded important data relevant to spacecraft fire safety. Quasi-steady burning corresponding to various condensed-phase materials (such as PMMA and Nylon) was observed in microgravity despite the absence of air flow, where the cessation of ventilation is an established step in putting out spacecraft fires. The ongoing combustion without air flow was notably seen in elevated-oxygen atmospheres which are being considered for use in future spacecraft, whereas such flames in a normal atmosphere of 21% oxygen self-extinguished in a short time. While BRE’s results are still preliminary, they suggest that NASA may want to increase use of its alternative flammability Test 2, with the cone calorimeter, where that test can measure material properties corresponding to the microgravity flames observed with the BRE burner. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 1.00 TB PSI-15Version 2 Advanced Colloids Experiment-Microscopy 2 Reflight(ACE-M2R) Investigation Submitted Date: 15-Sep-2022 Initial Release Date: 15-Sep-2022 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/5mh8-k670 Research Area: Complex Fluids - Soft Matter SubResearch Area: Colloids License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 11-01-2013 Investigation End Date 07-31-2020 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives Sometimes its hard to tell a gas from a liquid. ACE-M2R observes the microscopic behavior of liquids and gases separating from each other. The investigation examines the behavior of model (colloid rich) liquids and model (colloid poor) gases near the critical point, or the point at which there is no distinct boundary between the two phases. ACE-M2R uses a new microscope to record micro-scale events on short time scales, while previous experiments observed large-scale behavior over many weeks. Liquids and gases of the same material usually have different densities, so they would behave differently under the influence of gravity, making the microgravity environment of the International Space Station ideal for these experiments. This investigation is a re-flight of the original ACE-M2 with the intent to resolve issues from the original flight. Approach The ACE-M2 investigation utilized 2 Sample Modules (1 is duplicate for back-up) with 15 Sample Wells each for a total of 30 samples, 15 flight and 15 slight identical for back-up. Samples were colloidal fluids varying concentrations of two different types of fluorescent dye and particle size; large and small. Magnetic stir bars embedded in each sample well were used to homogenized each sample. Fluorescent microscopy and Imaging of the colloidal crystallites in each well as they developed over time allowed observation of particle movements and interactions to characterize and quantify rates of growth of structures formed. Hypothesis Near the critical point, variations in density and effective temperature will significantly influence particle interactions, leading to observable changes in phase stability and transition behavior. These changes are expected to reveal underlying mechanisms governing critical phenomena in colloidal systems, enhancing the predictability of particle dynamics in similar environments. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits Space Applications: On Earth, gravity plays a big role in how liquids and gases interact: The heavier liquid phase settles beneath a lighter gas phase, and these differences in density enable easy separation. But the flow and behavior of complex fluids and phase separation where there is little or no gravity is not well understood. A greater understanding of liquid-gas interaction in microgravity could benefit a wide range of fluid storage, transport and processing systems for future spacecraft. Earth Applications: Particle separation and behavior in liquids, gels, and creams is important for developing consumer and household products, which are worth billions of dollars annually to the U.S. economy. Many consumer products are complex fluids, combining microscopic particles in gel or liquid, which are similar to the model colloidal system used in the ACE investigations which give insight into product formulations that could be used to maximize stability and shelf life. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 13.99 GB PSI-24Version 4 Advanced Structurally Embedded Thermal Spreader II Oscillating Head Pipes(ASETS II OHP) Investigation Submitted Date: 15-Sep-2022 Initial Release Date: 15-Sep-2022 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/jnp9-vc34 Research Area: Fluid Physics License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform X-37B Investigation Start Date 04-13-2016 Investigation End Date 06-17-2019 Sponsoring Agency U.S. Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL) NASA Center Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) Objectives The three primary science objectives are to measure the initial on-orbit thermal performance, to measure long duration thermal performance, and to assess any lifetime degradation. Flight data will be used to validate microgravity portions of an OHP operating limits model recently published by members of the team. Returned flight experiment hardware will be subjected to post-flight testing to assess the presence of any non-condensable gas that may have formed on orbit. Approach The ASETS-II experiment is made of three low-mass, low-cost OHPs and an electronics experiment control box. The three OHPs are of varying configuration (center heating with single- and double-sided cooling) and working fluids (butane and R-134a) in order to isolate specific performance parameters of interest. In addition to serving as a science experiment, the ASETS-II flight experiment serves as a pathfinder for incorporating high performance OHP-based thermal spreaders into flat plate structures such as electronics chip carriers, thermal ground planes, and spacecraft panels. Microgravity influence on fluid flow, especially two-phase flow, is significantly different than in a terrestrial environment. This is true for steady-state operations, but is more important for transient operation. In addition, the combined effects of the space environment (e.g. thermal Cutaway of an oscillating heat pipe (OHP) showing its microchannel pattern cycling, high vacuum, charging, vibration) are required to verify the performance of the system on orbit for long durations. Hypothesis Oscillating heat pipes will exhibit consistent and stable thermal performance in a long-duration microgravity environment, comparable to their performance in a terrestrial setting. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits Potentially shift the way NASA designs its future deep space craft and extraterrestrial human habitats, providing safer, more reliable temperature regulation for the human occupants and the sensitive technology housed inside Cooling electronics. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 878.96 GB PSI-88Version 5 Packed Bed Reactor Experiment - 2(PBRE-2) Investigation Submitted Date: 15-Sep-2022 Initial Release Date: 15-Sep-2022 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/h0z4-0547 Research Area: Fluid Physics Related Investigation: PSI-89, PSI-90 License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 03-01-2017 Investigation End Date 12-24-2021 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives The objective of the flight experiment is to study the hydrodynamics of packed beds in microgravity and under different conditions that lead to different flow regimes. The hydrodynamics consists of the pressure drop inside the packed bed and the liquid hold-up. The different regimes are the results of different liquid and gas flow rates, and different initial conditions embodied by gas and liquid pre-flows or flushes prior to beginning of the runs. Another objective of the experiment was to understand transient flow rates and the hysteresis in the pressure drop as a function of the flow rates. Approach The PBRE-2 investigations employed a systematic and comprehensive approach to study the hydrodynamics of two-phase flow in packed bed reactors under microgravity conditions. The approach can be summarized in the following key steps: 1. Ground-Based Research and Model Development: Prior to the spaceflight experiments, extensive ground-based research was conducted to develop theoretical models and establish a foundation for understanding two-phase flow in packed beds. This included: Literature review: A thorough review of existing literature on single-phase and two-phase flow through porous media, focusing on pressure drop, flow regimes, and the influence of various parameters. Development of hydrodynamic models: Formulation of mathematical models, such as the modified Ergun equation, to predict pressure drop and flow regime transitions in microgravity. Ground-based experiments: Conducting experiments in reduced gravity environments, such as parabolic flights and drop towers, to gather preliminary data and validate initial model predictions. 2. Design and Development of Spaceflight Experiment: A dedicated experimental facility was designed and developed for operation on the ISS. This involved: Test facility design: Engineering a flow control system, test section, and data acquisition system capable of operating reliably in microgravity and meeting the specific requirements of the investigation. Definition of test matrix: Developing a comprehensive test matrix encompassing a wide range of gas and liquid flow rates, pre-flow conditions, and transient flow scenarios. 3. Execution of Spaceflight Experiments: The PBRE-2 experiments were conducted on the ISS, following the defined test matrix and procedures. This involved: Preflow procedures: Implementing the chosen pre-flow treatment (liquid flush or gas flush) before each test run. Flow control: Precisely controlling and varying the gas and liquid flow rates according to the test matrix. Data acquisition: Collecting data from pressure sensors, temperature sensors, and high-speed cameras throughout each test run. Downlinking data: Transmitting the acquired data to the ground for analysis. 4. Data Analysis and Interpretation: The downlinked data was meticulously analyzed to: Characterize flow regimes: Identify and classify the different flow regimes observed in the experiments based on pressure traces and video recordings. Evaluate pressure drop: Analyze the pressure drop data and compare it with model predictions to assess the validity and accuracy of the models. Investigate flow regime transitions: Determine the conditions and mechanisms leading to transitions between different flow regimes. Assess the influence of packing properties and pre-flow conditions: Analyze the impact of packing material wettability, size, and pre-flow treatments on the flow behavior and pressure drop. 5. Dissemination of Results: The findings of the PBRE-2 investigations were disseminated through: Peer-reviewed publications: Publishing research papers in scientific journals to share the results with the broader scientific community. Presentations at conferences: Presenting the research findings at relevant scientific conferences and workshops. Hypothesis It is hypothesized that in microgravity two-phase packed bed flows, pressure drop will be a function of surface tension (captured by a modified Ergun equation), packing wettability and size, and pre-flow conditions. Furthermore, bubble removal will depend on bubble volume and liquid flow rate, and distinct flow regimes will emerge, with transitions governed by specific gas and liquid flow rate combinations. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits Fundamental understanding the impact of reduced or zero gravity on the hydrodynamics (pressure drop, as well as distribution and holdup of each phase) is relevant to systems that involve two-phase flow such as life support systems, fuel cells, in-situ resource utilization, heat pipes, materials processing, production of pharmaceutical-grade water, and transport of nutrients in soils. Design and operation of many chemical and biological processing systems require this fundamental understanding of two-phase gas-liquid flows through porous media because many of these space-based systems or unit operations involve gas-liquid flows through porous media. Some examples of current space systems involving two-phase flow through fixed porous media include the Volatile Removal Assembly (VRA), the Integrated Advanced Water Recovery System (AWRS), and IntraVenous Water GENeration system (IVGEN). The ability to predict flow regimes and corresponding pressure drop in a particular system involving two-phase flow is crucial to the design of the fluid system and the pumping requirements. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 156.73 GB PSI-31Version 5 Cold Atom Lab - Microgravity Dynamics of Bubble-Geometry Bose-Einstein Condensates(CAL-BEC Bubble Dynamics) Investigation Submitted Date: 15-Sep-2022 Initial Release Date: 15-Sep-2022 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/e8mt-aj63 Research Area: Fundamental Physics SubResearch Area: Quantum Matter Related Investigation: PSI-32, PSI-33, PSI-35, PSI-36 License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform ISS Investigation Start Date 04-01-2014 Investigation End Date 09-27-2025 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NASA Center Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) Objectives Microgravity Dynamics of Bubble-geometry Bose-Einstein Condensates (Cold Atom Lab - BEC Bubble Dynamics) aims to study Bose-Einstein Condensates (BECs) and degenerate Fermi gases (DFGs) confined to a the surface of an experimentally-controlled topologically-connected ''bubble.'' The limitations of gravitational sag have prevented terrestrial exploration of a quantum gas confined to such as surface. This investigation aims to test fundamental ideas in quantum mechanics, statistical mechanics, and strongly-correlated many-body physics in condensed matter. Studying the behavior of quantum gas bubbles could provide insights for next-generation quantum sensors and simulators. Approach This investigation uses rubidium (87 Rb) and potassium (39K and 41K) samples in the Cold Atom Laboratory (CAL) aboard the International Space Station (ISS). The approach for the investigation comprises two main aspects: the creation of ultracold atomic gases and the subsequent manipulation and probing of these gases to study systematic mitigations. Creation of Ultracold Atomic Gas: Laser Cooling: Atoms are released into a vacuum chamber and collected into a magneto-optical trap (MOT), where they are initially cooled using laser cooling techniques. This technique cools the sample by essentially ‘pushing’ the laser against the motion of the atoms effectively lowering the momentum, and therefore the velocity, kinetic energy, and temperature, of the sample. This is followed by a brief stage of “optical molasses” during which the quadrupole magnetic field is turned off and the laser frequency is further detuned. State Preparation: The sample is optically pumped to a low magnetic field-seeking quantum state. The state is then subjected to an intermediate quadrupole magnetic field which allows for the transferred from the MOT, located at the bottom of the science region, to an atom-chip-based trap, located at the top of the science region. Evaporative Cooling: The atoms undergo evaporative cooling to below the critical temperature, leading to the formation of a Bose-Einstein Condensate (BEC). Evaporative cooling cools the sample by removing the highest-energy atom from the trap so that the remaining atoms re-thermalize at progressively lower temperatures. Decompression and Release: The atom trap is slightly relaxed to further cool the atoms, eventually releasing them completely to allow free expansion. At this point, investigators can search for the primary signatures of a BECs for confirmation that one was formed. Formation of a BEC is typically associated with the behavior of the velocity distribution, such as the presence of a narrow peak centered at near zero velocity and the low velocity peak growing (greater fraction of atoms in this domain) as the temperature decreases. Manipulation and Probing: Probing Techniques: The ultracold gas is probed using laser, radiofrequency, and/or microwave pulses. These techniques are designed to investigate the pairwise interactions and molecular dynamics crucial for mitigating systematics in high-precision measurements. Time-of-Flight Imaging: After a predetermined time of flight, the sample is imaged using absorption imaging techniques. This process involves taking two images: one of the sample and a reference image post-destruction of the sample. As implied, this is the end of the experimental cycle for this specific BEC as the measurement process destroys the sample. The manipulation and probing aspect is particularly important for this specific investigation as the ultracold atomic gas must be treated with certain fields to achieve the bubble topology. To do this, a locally harmonic spin-dependent trapping potential originating from inside an applied magnetic field is combined with a near-resonance oscillatory magnetic field with a certain radiofrequency. Together these two magnetic fields produce atoms in spatially dependent dressed atomic states that experience dressed or adiabatic dressed potentials. These potentials can then be manipulated via tuning the radiofrequency field so that the atoms take on an ellipsoid or bubble-like geometry. Hypothesis This investigation hypothesizes that radiofrequency dressing can be used to create a trap formed by a spherical or ellipsoidal shell structure capable of confining quantum gases to a “bubble” topology. Due to gravitational sag and trap distortion present in terrestrial experiments this trap topology has not been explored, and further, it is only able to be explored in the microgravity environment unique to the Cold Atom Laboratory (CAL). The low-energy excitations of such systems, as well as various theories on the physics of phase transitions will be investigated using this bubble-geometry. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits This work, while focused on the fundamental physics of ultracold atoms and not directly connected to human life, has a similar impact to life on Earth as that of all fundamental physics; it broadens our understanding of the physical world and helps us further cement our collective picture of quantum mechanics as ''the way the world works.'' It explores the limits of how large Bose-Einstein condensates can be made, and to what extent the gravity-well of terrestrial labs render certain investigations difficult or impossible. The observations made aboard CAL through this project are a clear demonstration that physical insight can sometimes require microgravity facilities to be fully developed, and that space borne atomic physics experiments can be valuable contributions to our collective scientific efforts. Additionally, insight into fundamental laws of quantum mechanics can have many applications in many on Earth. Quantum computers continue to exponentially accelerate as a field of study and in industry, and research into these fundamentals can support scientific workforce development, public science outreach and research and development. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 15.20 GB PSI-80Version 4 Light Microscopy Module Biophysics-3(LMMBIO-3) Investigation Submitted Date: 15-Sep-2021 Initial Release Date: 15-Sep-2021 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/yyfd-8m39 Research Area: Biophysics SubResearch Area: Proteins License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Proposal Title Growth Rate Dispersion as a Predictive Indicator for Biological Crystal Samples Where Quality Can be Improved with Microgravity Growth Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 01-24-2014 Investigation End Date 01-23-2021 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NASA Center Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) Objectives The primary objectives of this investigation are: 1. Use molecular biology to produce closely related protein constructs that display differences in growth rate dispersion during crystallization. Measure the intermolecular ‘attractiveness’ of each construct, then model the inter-particle forces, diffusion and convection. 2. Measure and compare the growth rate dispersion of ground and microgravity grown crystals. Growth rate dispersion will be measured for ground control crystals using routine crystallization apparatus. In addition, growth rate dispersion will be measure for ground and microgravity grown crystals using the flight apparatus. 3. Characterize the quality of both ground and microgravity grown crystals. Sophisticated X-ray analysis along with X-ray structural data collection will be used to quantify and characterize crystal quality. 4. Link the knowledge about inter-particle forces, measured acceleration levels, calculated flow rates and the resultant X-ray analysis to develop a model and predictive ground-based tests to identify those samples producing crystals on the ground that would be improved in microgravity. Approach Approach: Several cassettes were configured with cassettes identically configured containing three samples, one set in capillaries 1-6, another sample in capillaries 7-12, and the third in capillaries 13-18. Six constructs and the T4 wild type (WT) were loaded into the capillaries at various concentrations and frozen to -80C. The samples were thawed and observed in the LMM facility on board the ISS. Several cassettes were identically configured containing three samples, one set in capillaries 1-6, another sample in capillaries 7-12, and the third in capillaries 13-18. The capillaries were loaded so that capillaries 1-6 contained theWT* construct, capillaries 7-12 the S44E WT* construct and finally, capillaries 13-18 the S44F WT* construct. The cassettes were kept at -80°C until moving to the space station microscope facility. The capillaries were filled as follows: • Capillaries 1-6 with 50 mg/ml WT* in 0.1 M Zn(C 2 H3 O2 )2 , 0.1 M Tris, pH 8, 35% PEG 8K, and 0.1 M NaCl • Capillaries 7-12 with 64 mg/ml S44E WT* in 0.05 M NaC 2 H3 O2 0.1 M Tris, pH 8 30% PEG 8K and 15% glycerol • Capillaries 13-18 with 53 mg/ml S44F WT* in 0.2 M Zn(C 2 H3 O2 )2 , 0.1 M NaC2H3O2, pH 5 and 20% PEG 20K. On return to earth X-ray analysis of samples took place using the IMCA (Industrial Macromolecular Crystallography Association) beamline of the Advanced Photon Source. Hypothesis Removing or greatly reducing the effects of buoyancy-driven convection and sedimentation in microgravity will result in slower, diffusion-controlled molecular transport that can yield larger crystals with fewer defects. It is postulated that growth rate dispersion is reduced in microgravity due to the diffusive rather than convective flow regime that delivers macromolecules to the crystal. Based on previous experimental observations it is hypothesized that the presence of growth rate dispersion in macromolecular crystals grown on the ground is an indicator of crystals that can be improved when grown in microgravity. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: X-ray crystallography is the main method scientists use to study the molecular structures of biology, but it is difficult to crystallize proteins, with only a poor success rate even in the best laboratories. This investigation uses ground and microgravity-based observations to predict which proteins would benefit from crystallization in microgravity, improving the information that may be obtained from them. Long-duration protein crystal growth experiments on the ISS with photo documentation, and subsequent analysis of the comparisons between 1g and μg crystals, will enable a more complete understanding of why proteins and other macromolecules often form more perfect crystals in microgravity than they do on earth. If it could be predicted which macromolecular samples could be improved by crystal growth in microgravity, then the true potential of this medium could be exploited in an efficient manner. Structural biology of protein-protein complexes and integral membrane proteins are currently a high NIH priority due to their importance for systems biology, disease mechanisms and structure-guided drug development. Hauptman Woodward Medical Research Institute has a data archive of millions of time-resolved crystallization images (from over 14,000 different biological macromolecules) that could be used to identify candidates likely to benefit from crystallization in microgravity. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 20.75 KB PSI-125Version 2 Light Microscopy Module Biophysics-2,5(LMMBIO-2) Investigation Submitted Date: 20-Jan-2021 Initial Release Date: 20-Jan-2021 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/y7c0-ha11 Research Area: Biophysics License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Proposal Title Solution Convection and the Nucleation Precursors in Protein Crystallization Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 10-01-2013 Investigation End Date 01-20-2021 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NASA Center Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) Objectives The primary objective of this investigation was to understand why protein crystallization experiments in microgravity have generated unexpectedly low or high numbers of crystals. Each outcome may cause experiments designed to obtain a small number of well-separated crystals to fail. The objective of the proposed investigations is to explore the effects of a hitherto unstudied factor for the nucleation of protein crystals: solution shear flow. Besides providing a novel tool for nucleation control for protein crystallization experiments, the correlation between solution flows and protein crystal nucleation, to be tested in the proposed investigation, will shed light on one of the major mysteries of current space biophysics: the finding that in many cases the number of crystals nucleated in microgravity was greater or smaller than those nucleated on earth. Approach Three cassettes containing five capillaries each were loaded with one of three proteins; (1) Lysozyme, (2) p53, and (3) hnRNPA-LC. The observation of these protein clusters were observed with a newly developed technique, called differential dynamic microscopy (DDM). DDM improves a recent method used to study and quantify the dynamics of sub-micrometer particles in solutions from fluctuations in intensity in optical micrographs. All samples were frozen to a temperature of -80C before flight to the ISS. The proteins were thawed and observed over several weeks in the ISS LMM module where they were filmed and photographed. Sample details and experimental parameters are summarized in LMMBio2_Experimental Table in the science document section. Hypothesis Hypothesis: The behavior of dense liquid clusters at different rates of convection will have a profound effect on crystal growth. The main hypothesis underlying the proposed investigations consists of two parts: 1. The existence of nucleation precursors and the correlation between their properties and the nucleation rate can be used to control protein crystal nucleation via solution flow. 2. Enhancement or suppression of nucleation via solution flow, i.e., independently of solution supersaturation, can be used to achieve higher perfection of the grown crystals. 3. A very small fraction of the protein exists in a dense liquid phase in the form of Brownian particles, each a cluster of roughly 105 protein molecules undergoing liquid-like dynamics. 4. Crystal nucleation occurs when a small, ordered domain forms within the highly concentrated liquid-state environment of one of these particles. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits These images provide data that help scientists and engineers understand the forces that control organization and dynamics of matter at microscopic scales. The organization and movement of matter on the microscopic level profoundly affects the macroscopic world and understanding such processes contributes to development of more efficient materials and machines for application on Earth. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 7.59 GB PSI-91Version 4 Physics of Colloids in Space(PCS) Investigation Submitted Date: 31-Jul-2020 Initial Release Date: 31-Jul-2020 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/72a8-5032 Research Area: Complex Fluids - Soft Matter SubResearch Area: Colloids Related Investigation: PSI-94 License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 12-18-2007 Investigation End Date 07-31-2020 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives The primary objectives of the PCS investigation were to successfully grow binary colloidal crystal alloy structures to monitor their nucleation and growth kinetics with static and dynamic light scattering, determine their structures using laser light crystallography and the properties of the superlattices using dynamic light scattering. In addition, the structure and dynamics of gel-like structures formed by colloid-polymer mixtures will be measured using static and dynamic light scattering and the ultimate equilibrium structures behavior of the mixture will be determined. Finally, large scale fractal colloid aggregates and gels will be grown to measure their mechanical properties using dynamic light scattering, and potentially the cell oscillation techniques. Approach For binary colloidal crystal alloy the samples will consist of polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) particles, stabilized by a thin coating of poly-12-hydroxystearic acid, and suspended in a mixture of decalin and tetralin adjusted to exactly match the index of refraction of the PMMA. Once in orbit, the samples will be homogenized by rapidly spinning each sample cell and suddenly stopping it. Subsequent to homogenization, the nucleation and growth of the binary colloidal alloy crystallites will be monitored by static light scatter in the forward direction. The small angle light scattering will be complemented by larger angle scattering examining the Bragg reflections of the crystals. For the colloidal-polymer mixture part of the investigation the colloidal particles will again be PMMA spheres suspended in an index matched fluid. The volume fractions of these samples will range from about 1% to 30%. The polymer will be polystyrene, with a molecular weight ranging from about 100,000 to 1,000,000. The colloid-polymer mixtures will be homogenized using the same procedure used for the binary colloid mixtures. Immediately after they are homogenized, the small angle scattering will be monitored to measure the formation of the gel-like structure. Dynamic light scattering will be performed concurrently as the gel forms to obtain a sensitive indication of the final formation of the gel. Once equilibrium is achieved, if colloidal crystals are formed in one of the phases the growth and structure of the crystals will be studied using both powder average Bragg scattering and dynamic light scattering. For the fractal colloidal aggregate and gels the aggregation of the colloidal particles will be initiated by mixing the colloidal suspension with another chemical that causes aggregation. Upon initiation of the aggregation, the growth of the colloidal aggregates will be monitored by both dynamic and static light scattering. In addition to the light scattering measurements, small amplitude oscillations of the gel structure will be performed to measure the shear modulus of the gel directly and compare with the light scattering measurements. Hypothesis The availability of microgravity will allow binary colloidal superlattices to be formed from different materials providing new insights into the nucleation and growth kinetics of binary colloidal crystal alloy and thereby establish the new field of “colloid engineering.” This work will unambiguously determine the equilibrium phase diagram for attractive colloidal particles where the attraction is induced by depletion effects through the addition of polymer. It will also provide important new insight into the transition between equilibrium and kinetically limited behavior, in the absence of sedimentation. Further, this investigation will also lead to the fabrication of fractal colloidal structures that extend over the largest range of length scales ever produced, providing a critical test of our understanding of the formation of these structures. With such extended structures, it will be possible to study their physical properties and determine the consequences of the scale invariance on the properties. It will determine the fundamental limits of the range over which fractal structures can exist. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits The long term goal of this research is to establish a new method of fabricating materials, “Colloid Engineering,” where novel materials are fabricated using colloidal particles as precursors. With appropriate choices of the sizes of the particles, it should be possible to form colloidal alloy crystals of higher volume fraction than can be made with monodisperse particles. These colloidal alloys may form the precursors for very high quality ceramics. Alternatively, the particles could be made from different materials, forming colloidal superlattices with novel properties. Then, for example, one set of particles could be plastic and the other set of particles could be a metal or a semiconductor. Alternatively, these structures may be useful in forming materials with reduced phase space available for radiation, allowing a much simpler way of fabricating structures which possess photonic band gaps. Colloid engineering may offer a simple method for making these materials that completely bypasses the difficulties faced by traditional lithography techniques. The superlattices could also be used as novel optical switches or displays. Contact(s) David A. Weitzemail,Peter N. Puseyemail,William V. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 15.56 GB PSI-79Version 4 Light Microscopy Module Biophysics-1(LMMBIO-1) Investigation Submitted Date: 31-Jul-2020 Initial Release Date: 31-Jul-2020 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/d8cc-rg70 Research Area: Biophysics SubResearch Area: Protein Crystal Growth License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Proposal Title Effect of Macromolecular Transport on Microgravity Protein Crystallization Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 08-20-2013 Investigation End Date 07-31-2020 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NASA Center Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) Objectives Specific objectives of this investigation were 1. On the ISS and concurrently in earth control experiments, compare incorporation of protein aggregates (monomers versus dimers, trimers, etc.) into growing protein crystals. Detection of aggregates in the crystal will be qualitatively assessed via LMM’s and laboratory fluorescence confocal microscopes and quantitatively measured using mass spectrometry (ion spray and/or MALDI). Based on the percentage incorporation of larger aggregates within the crystal, the effect of molecular filtering based on differences in diffusion rates will be assessed. 2. Measure crystal growth rates in 1g versus μg for different size aggregates of proteins with molecular weights ranging from less than 20kDa to more than 1,200kDa. 3. Compare the defect density and crystal quality via mass spectroscopy and x-ray diffraction quality of crystals grown at different rates in a 1g environment. Approach A total of four cassettes were sent to the ISS, containing eight samples each. Each sample could contain either; (1) Lysozyme, (2) pfGST, (3) BSA, or (4) XptA1. For each protein investigated, preparative size exclusion chromatography (SEC) was used to fractionate protein monomers from the naturally occurring protein aggregates. The aggregates were then segmented into small, medium, and large categories. Fluorophores (excitation wavelengths: 594 and 488) were chosen and attached to the macromolecules, producing a bright fluorescent signal (red and green) and each exhibited a slow photo-bleach so that fluorescence was maintained for the duration of the proposed crystallization experiments. The samples were upmassed frozen at -80C and thawed to ambient temperature (~20C). After thawing nucleation of the proteins were observable within 24 – 96 hours. Observations were conducted with a confocal fluorescent microscope where the total fluorescence observed for each crystal (after normalizing for the different crystal volumes) provides an estimation of the relative amount(s) of aggregated (containing the fluorophore) versus monomeric (no fluorophore) protein incorporated within the growing crystal. Hypothesis This investigation addresses the hypothesis that improved quality of microgravity-grown protein crystals is the result of two macromolecular characteristics that exist in a buoyancy-free, diffusion-dominated solution: • Slower crystal growth rates, due to slower protein transport to the growing crystal surface • Predilection of growing crystals to incorporate protein monomers versus higher protein aggregates due to differences in transport rates Research Impacts/Earth Benefits Using three-dimensional protein structure information, researchers can determine how proteins function and in cases where these proteins are involved in disease processes, the structure is often used to design new drugs that specifically interact with the protein. Many leading drugs today are the product of structure-based drug design. While enormous strides have been made in the last decade, there remain a large number of important proteins where the difficulty of obtaining crystals of sufficient quality is the chief barrier to their structural analysis. The impact of this investigation is for one important class of proteins, membrane proteins, comprises a number of targets identified by the pharmaceutical industry as high-value commercial opportunities (membrane proteins were the targets for approximately 67% of all past marketed drugs and it is estimated that they will comprise targets for an equal percentage of all future drugs). Membrane protein crystallization represents one area where the onset of space commercialization can maximize the impact of the microgravity environment in space-based research applications for the academic, government and pharmaceutical industries. Other areas include high-value aqueous proteins and protein complexes (based on their functional importance in biological systems) many of which yield crystals of poor quality under 1g laboratory conditions. Access to unique data optimized in microgravity could have great relevance for understanding protein structures and advancing new drugs into the pharmaceutical market. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 3.35 GB PSI-45Version 3 Constrained Vapor Bubble-2(CVB-2) Investigation Submitted Date: 31-Dec-2019 Initial Release Date: 31-Dec-2019 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/d05x-4505 Research Area: Fluid Physics Related Investigation: PSI-46 License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 10-01-2013 Investigation End Date 12-31-2019 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives The primary objective of CVB-2 is to determine the overall interfacial stability, characterize the hydrodynamics, measure heat transfer coefficients, and determine the overall conductance of a complex fluid (94% Pentane/6% Isohexane) in a microgravity environment. Approach The Constrained Vapor Bubble (CVB) Experiment was conducted on the International Space Station (ISS) and the temperature data have been used to analyze the heat transfer mechanisms operating within the quartz cuvette for 40 mm and 30 mm modules. Even with the large millimeter dimensions of the CVB, interfacial forces dominate in these exceedingly small Bond Number systems with small viscous losses. A comparison of the modeling results obtained using a simple one-dimensional analysis of the temperature fields found with the dry and partially liquid pentane filled cuvettes allowed the phase change and radiation fields to be determined in both microgravity and earth gravity. Unique visual observation of the shape of the liquid flow field through a microscope enhanced the understanding of the temperature and vapor pressure [1],[2] measurements. The internal heat transfer processes were very complicated, multidimensional, and the length of the closed system strongly affected the average internal heat transfer processes. Internal radiation was shown to be more significant than originally anticipated as well as the effect of Marangoni convection. The competing processes of capillary flow driving liquid from the cold to the hot end and Marangoni flow driving liquid from the hot end to the cold end resulted in the formation of a central drop and a pinch point in the film thickness profile. The results also indicate that the study of the constrained vapor bubble in an open loop heat pipe configuration would allow the passive bubble more freedom to respond. Hypothesis In microgravity environments, the introduction of a higher boiling point, higher surface tension component into a low-boiling-point fluid within a constrained vapor bubble suppresses temperature-induced Marangoni convection, thereby enhancing heat transfer performance and system stability. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits Most liquids have a surface tension that decreases as temperature rises. This causes fluid to flow in the direction of higher surface tension, a phenomenon known as Marangoni flow. This reduces the effectiveness of a heat pipe, because liquid cannot return to the hot end. CVB-2 investigates whether a mixture of two fuels (pentane and isohexane) that can reduce Marangoni flow and improve the efficiency of the CVB system on the International Space Station. In addition, the investigation provides insight into how heat transfer functions in microgravity. Most satellites use heat pipes to keep critical parts cool, and improved understanding of fluid mixtures could enable future heat pipes that are smaller, lighter and less expensive to launch. A wide range of high-performance devices must be perpetually cooled in order to function, from supercomputers to personal laptops and LED light bulbs. Fluid mixtures circulating through heat pipes can passively dissipate heat, using less energy than fans or cooling systems. But heat pipe transport systems are sensitive to small differences in temperature, pressure, and gravity. Studying how fluid mixtures and heat pipes function in microgravity provides insight into the fundamental principles of thermodynamics. This also provides insight into how mixtures of fluids behave during boiling, condensation, evaporation, distillation, and stripping. These processes are used in a variety of industries and environmental cleanup. Contact(s) Joel L. Plawskyemail,Peter C.
