detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 329.64 MB PSI-67Version 5 Enhancement and Verification of Quantitative Phase-Field Crystal Modeling using NASA-PSI Coarsening in Solid- Liquid Mixtures Experiments Data Investigation Submitted Date: 31-Dec-2019 Initial Release Date: 31-Dec-2019 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/7606-sw68 Research Area: Materials Science SubResearch Area: Solidification, Coarsening License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Ground Investigation Investigation Start Date 01-01-2017 Investigation End Date 12-31-2019 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), PSI Grant NASA Center Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) Objectives The key objectives of this investigation were to develop 1) a binary Molecular Dynamics (MD) interatomic potential for Pb-Sn system, 2) Phase Field Crystal (PFC) models for coarsening of solid-liquid mixtures; 3) a highly-parallel semi-implicit spectral and operator splitting numerical algorithm to use on high performance computing facilities that will enable the necessary large-scale PFC simulations (comparable to CSLM data length-scale); (4) Data mining of NASA-PSI Coarsening in Solid-Liquid Mixtures (CSLM), CSLM-2, CSLM-2R, and CSLM-3 experiments and using them in series of simulations in the developed computational tool for enhancement and verification of the proposed modeling framework. Approach The proposed multi-scale modeling framework is established around two atomistic computational material model of phase-field crystals (PFC) and molecular dynamics (MD). PFC is a unique computational model at diffusive time scale with the capability of simulating solid-liquid processes with atomistic resolutions while MD acts on the time scale of atomistic vibrations. A novel approach of modified-embedded-atom (MEAM) interatomic potential was adopted to obtain reliable interatomic potentials for Pb-Sn binary systems near or at the melting point (MP). The potentials were used to calculate relevant properties such as latent heat, expansion in melting, liquid structure factor, solid-liquid interface stiffness, solidus and liquidus lines, and solid-liquid interfacial free energy. The kinetics of coarsening in solid-liquid mixtures (Ostwald ripening of solid domains in the liquid phase) was simulated using a one mode phase field crystal (1PFC) model. The simulation results were compared to experimental data previously obtained in a microgravity environment. Simulations were carried out as a function of the difference in chemical potential between Pb and Sn. Please the data layout document (DLD) describing the data organization in folders for each delta chemical potential and underlying files as per temperature of simulation and each time step. Hypothesis Modified-embedded-atom (MEAM) interatomic potential and a one mode phase field crystal (1PFC) model can be utilized to simulate the kinetics of coarsening of solid phases in solid-liquid mixtures. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits The proposed computational tool verified/quantified based on CSLM data will establish a virtual laboratory that can be used to study coarsening as well as other material processing phenomena on Earth involving with solid-liquid coexistence; e.g., rapid solidification and grain growth. Since computational models are highly repeatable at lower cost, the proposed modeling framework will result in accelerated material process development and certification. Solid-liquid coexistence is the initial step in many manufacturing technologies such as casting, liquid infiltration, and additive manufacturing. Hence, this modeling framework can be used to investigate the relations between these manufacturing processes and the material properties in order to optimize/control the manufacturing processes parameters. In addition, the results of this research will be disseminated to the public in forms of peer-reviewed articles, scientific reports, a project-specific website, and data uploaded to NASA-PSI website. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 1.11 TB PSI-68Version 6 Flame Extinguishment Experiment - 2(FLEX-2) Investigation Submitted Date: 30-Sep-2019 Initial Release Date: 30-Sep-2019 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/byp8-h018 Research Area: Combustion Science SubResearch Area: Spacecraft Fire Safety License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Proposal Title The Fundamental Studies in Droplet Combustion and Flame Extinguishment in Microgravity Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 08-12-2016 Investigation End Date 09-30-2019 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives The primary goal of the FLEX-2 flight experiments is to extend the results of FLEX-1 to fuels and environmental conditions that mimic real combustor conditions, as well as, provide benchmark experimental data on bi-component droplet combustion over a wide range of initial conditions in order to validate numerical simulations and to develop new theoretical models. Detailed experimental objectives can be further itemized as: 1. Investigate the role of liquid-phase mixing on the burning characteristics of bi-component fuel droplets. 2. Examine the steady and unsteady liquid and gas-phase phenomena in pure fuel combustion. 3. Study flame extinction mechanisms and their boundaries. 4. Analyze the soot formation process, including soot volume fraction soot-shell dynamics. 5. Determine the influence of droplet interactions on the flammability limits and extinction behavior of droplet arrays. 6. Validate theoretical models of droplet combustion through comprehensive experimental data collection in microgravity environments. Approach The chamber was filled with the appropriate atmosphere, which was varied in pressure between 0.5 atm to 3.0 atm and O2 concentration between 0.1 to 0.4 mole fraction with the diluent gas making up the balance. A settling time of approximately 2 minutes elapsed prior to initiating the test in order to ensure that the temperature and pressure of the chamber gases have stabilized. This settling time was followed by the dispensing of a predetermined amount of fuel (based on the target droplet size) onto the support fiber for those tests in which the droplet is not freely deployed. When sufficient fuel has been dispensed the dispensing needles were retracted and a dwell period of at least 10 seconds was allowed for the droplet internal fluid motion induced by deployment to subside. This was then followed by initiating power to the ignitor for a selectable amount of time ranging from 1 second to 5 seconds after which the ignitor was retracted from the field of view. If the flow field is to be generated by translating the droplet then droplet motion would commence at the same time that the ignitor is retracted. A near real-time download of the color camera video was employed in order to verify successful droplet deployment, ignition, and overall progress of the experiment. Pressure and temperature data of the chamber environment was also recorded in near real time. The overall investigation approach can be summarized as: 1. Test parameters are determined, including pressure, temperature, fuel mixture, and humidity. 2. Fill the combustion chamber with the selected gas mixtures. 3. Deploy the droplet(s) carefully controlling the droplet diameter. 4. Allow the droplet to stabilize in the microgravity environment. 5. Ignite the droplet in a uniform and controlled fashion. 6. Monitor combustions and track flame evolution using high speed photography. 7. Monitor and adjust experimental conditions as needed. 8. Analyze data. The independently varied experimental parameters during FLEX-2 experiments were 1) Fuel type 2) Ambient gas composition 3) Ambient Pressure 4) Droplet initial diameter 5) Droplet translation velocity (and acceleration) 6) Droplet spacing and initial size in a binary linear array. Hypothesis Fairly sophisticated numerical simulations of convective droplet combustion have been developed in the last decade where the key contribution is the inclusion of full Navier-Stokes equations for the gas-phase flow field. However, due to the inherent complexity of the problem, varying degrees of approximations have been made in treating the chemistry, radiation, and the coupling between the gas and liquid phases. The validity of the assumptions or the hypothesis used in these simulation have not been confirmed by using benchmark data. By conducting these experiments in a microgravity environment, the effects of buoyancy are minimized, and the droplet can be characterized only as a function of thermocapillary or solutalcapillary stresses allowing for a clear observation of the fundamental combustion processes, The present FLEX-2 experiments using bi-component mixtures. In addition, the microgravity environment allows study of such phenomena as the transitions between radiative and diffusive extension of the flame. The primary goal of the flight experiments is to provide benchmark experimental data on bi-component droplet combustion over a wide range of initial conditions that could be used to validate numerical simulations and to develop new theoretical models. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits The combustion of liquid fuels is the overwhelming energy source in the transportation sector. Insights gained from these studies can lead to more efficient and cleaner combustion technologies which are crucial for reducing pollution and greenhouse gas emissions. By improving fuel efficiency and developing better fuels, these experiments can contribute to: 1) More sustainable energy production. 2) Future combustor designs with minimal carbon footprint, maximum fuel efficiency and less pollutant emissions. 3) Allow quantitative evaluation of the performance of future fuels in combustors through the development of surrogates (mixtures of pure fuels that simulate the behavior of real fuels). 4) Validation of jet engine models by engine manufacturers with support from prior droplet results. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 175.97 MB PSI-96Version 6 Pore-Mushy Zone Interaction during Directional Solidification of Alloys: Three Dimensional Simulation and Comparison with Experiments Investigation Submitted Date: 15-Sep-2019 Initial Release Date: 15-Sep-2019 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/0cdm-r472 Research Area: Materials Science SubResearch Area: Solidification License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Ground Investigation Investigation Start Date 09-16-2016 Investigation End Date 09-15-2019 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), PSI Grant NASA Center Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) Objectives The primary objective of this research was to develop a numerical 3D model capable of simulating the pore-mushy zone interaction during directional solidification of Succinonitrile -Water alloys in microgravity and test the simulation results against the Pore Formation and Mobility Investigation (PFMI) microstructural observations, quantitatively and qualitatively. Approach This investigation exploited forefront methods in microscale solidification and developed models based on phase filed (PF), cellular automaton (CA) and Lattice Boltzmann (LB) to simulate pore formation and its motion during directional solidification. The results from the Pore Formation and Mobility Investigation (PFMI) experiments were conducted in the microgravity environment aboard the Space Station with the intent of better understanding the role entrained porosity/bubbles play on microstructure during controlled directional solidification (DS). Several sets of time-temperature-interface-bubble interaction data were extracted and analyzed from the PFMI videos. The simulation results were tested against the PFMI microstructural observations. Hypothesis Previous real time observations in transparent analogues of interactions between a bubble and an array of primary dendrites are essentially “two-dimensional” (2D) and are affected by the “wall” effects. Contrary to earlier belief, it is now recognized that the basic premise of such experiments, i.e. 2D dendrites represent morphology of a three-dimensional (3D) array, is false. This investigation hypothesizes that understanding pore-mushy zone interaction in real castings requires both the experimental observations and also the theoretical/numerical modeling with 3D array of dendrites. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits This investigation helped to explain fundamental aspects of the mechanisms that regulate the formation of microporosities. The formation of these defects depends on microstructure features that cannot be properly captured by current meso- and macro-scale models based on averaging techniques. The direct numerical simulation of bubble dynamics in a dendritic network can provide a relation between macroscopically observable variables like cooling rate or temperature gradient and difficult to measure dynamic microscopic features like microporosity distribution, interdendritic permeability, solute redistribution, and dendrite arm spacing. This research not only provided valuable contribution to the understanding of pore-mushy zone interaction during solidification in the absence of gravity, which would be helpful for future in-space fabrication processes involving solidification, but it was a first step to quantitatively simulate such 3D interactions during terrestrial directional solidification in realistic size sample domains. Although much observation has been done in pictures of static microstructures at different stages of solidification, it has never been possible to capture the dynamic response of these features in an evolving mushy zone. This information is critical to assess, validate, and improve macroscale mushy zone models used in current casting and welding codes. objectives: The primary objective of this investigation was to develop and validate a numerical model for further investigation of nucleate pool boiling problems under microgravity conditions.

detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 2.01 GB PSI-50Version 2 Development and Verification of a 3D Nucleate Pool Boiling Simulation Model Using PSI Data Investigation Submitted Date: 14-Aug-2019 Initial Release Date: 14-Aug-2019 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/m65x-pp03 Research Area: Fluid Physics SubResearch Area: Modeling Related Investigation: PSI-85 License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Ground Investigation Flight Platform Not Applicable Investigation Start Date 08-15-2016 Investigation End Date 08-14-2019 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives The primary objective of this investigation was to develop and validate a numerical model for further investigation of nucleate pool boiling problems under microgravity conditions. Approach The moment-of-fluid (MOF) procedure is employed to reconstruct the interfaces of any number of material interfaces in a computational cell. The salient features of the overall approach includes: (i) Multi-material interfaces are represented by the piecewise linear moment-of-fluid (MOF) reconstruction, (ii) the time derivative part of the heat equation is discretized using the backward Euler method which is a discrete maximum principle preserving time discretization scheme, (iii) the spatial derivatives part of the heat equation is discretized using the finite volume method, (iv) the temperature field is discretized on a multi-material “supermesh” in which there is just one temperature variable per material per cell, (v) the discrete location for a given variable is at the materials' centroid, (vi) “connected centroid” method is used in order to approximate fluxes, (vii) at Dirichlet or Neumann embedded interfaces, a linear exact correction term is prescribed so that the method approximates the temperature gradient with second order accuracy. Hypothesis It is hypothesized that the developed model will have the following advantages which can lead to a more accurate prediction: (1) the method can better resolve thermal boundary layers (away from triple points) using adaptive mesh refinement, (2) a novel Moment of Fluid multiphase flow algorithm will straightforwardly prescribe a microlayer model in 3D general geometries, (3) the moment of fluid interface capturing algorithm will enable better handling of 3D problems such as bubble merging, (4) the modeling method can better conserve the boiling mass flow rate by directly exploiting the moment-of-fluid (sharp) interface reconstruction for approximating the interface heat flux in the vicinity of multiple (greater than 2) materials. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits The verified model can be used to further study scenarios not investigated on ISS such as vapor bubble departure and collapse. It can also be used to identify optimal heated surface configuration for better heat transfer characteristics. In addition, the model can be used to study other problems under microgravity such as packed bed reactors. The development of nucleate pool boiling simulation tool in microgravity based on the Navier-Stokes equations from this proposed work can be used to study other boiling problems in Earth gravity such as engine cooling and cooling in electronic devices. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 884.95 GB PSI-22Version 7 Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames(ACME E-FIELD Flames) Investigation Submitted Date: 15-Apr-2019 Initial Release Date: 15-Apr-2019 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/se5a-8c73 Research Area: Combustion Science SubResearch Area: Laminar Flames Related Investigation: PSI-23 License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 11-18-2016 Investigation End Date 11-17-2020 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives The objective of this investigation is to better understand the relationship between electric field voltage and chemi-ion current, analyze the dynamic response of flames to electric field changes, evaluate soot formation, and characterize stabilized near-limit lifted flames. Approach The E-FIELD flames experiment investigates how electric fields influence the behavior of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity. This unique environment is ideal for isolating electric field effects from buoyancy forces. The experiment is conducted with gas-fueled flames, both with and without a coflow of air. In the former case, the tests are conducted using the same coflow burner used by the Coflow Laminar Diffusion (CLD) Flame experiment. An electric field is generated by creating a high voltage (up to 10 kV) differential between the burner and a flat circular mesh suspended above (i.e., downstream of) the burner. Measurements, as a function of the field strength and fuel, are taken of the ion current through the flame and the flame’s response time to electric forcing. The gas-jet burner is used to create a small, focused flame for detailed ion-driven convection studies while the coflow burner surrounds the fuel jet with a weak synthetic air flow to enable flame stability and soot behavior analysis. A high-voltage copper mesh electrode positioned above the burner tip generated an electric field with controlled polarity and strength. The electric field interacts with ions generated through chemi-ionization during combustion, driving ion-driving convection and influencing flame behavior. Methane and ethylene were used as fuels and diluted with nitrogen to control flame strength. Dilution levels were varied to explore a range of combustion dynamics, from highly stable to near-extinction flames. Voltage-current curves were recorded to assess the relationship between electric field strength and chemi-ion current, revealing ion-driven convection effects. High-resolution cameras captured flame shape, luminosity, and soot distribution. Spectral imaging with filters measures chemiluminescent emissions and soot volume fraction. There were thermopile detectors to measure flame radiant emissions. All experiments were conducted in the combustion integrated rack (CIR). Tests were administered with Glenn Research Center (GRC) directing astronaut actions. Parameters such as fuel flow rate, coflow velocity, and field polarity are were varied to isolate specific effects on ion production, flame stability, and soot behavior. Hypothesis The application of electric fields in microgravity environments will significantly influence laminar diffusion flames by enabling precise manipulation of flame stability, soot behavior, and combustion dynamics through ion-driven convection and chemi-ionization processes. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits The E-FIELD Flames research is not being conducted to serve any space applications, but it is possible that its findings could aid the development of future space-based combustion devices (e.g., for solid waste processing). The use of electric fields to control flames can reduce the production of harmful pollutants in practical terrestrial combustion. The combustion of fossil fuel is the primary human source of greenhouse gas and acid rain and furthermore creates soot, which can be beneficial but is also a health hazard. Combustion using electrical fields may also allow for more efficient combustion, reducing fuel consumption in addition to unwanted emissions. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 116.97 GB PSI-18Version 4 Advanced Colloids Experiment - Temperature 7(ACE-T7) Investigation Submitted Date: 08-Nov-2018 Initial Release Date: 08-Nov-2018 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/9vax-q769 Research Area: Complex Fluids - Soft Matter SubResearch Area: Colloids Related Investigation: PSI-16, PSI-17, PSI-19 License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 05-08-2018 Investigation End Date 11-08-2018 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives The ACE-T7 experiment involves the design and assembly of complex 3D structures from small particles suspended within a fluid medium. These so-called “self-assembled colloidal structures”, are vital to the design of advanced optical materials and active devices. The objective of ACE-T7 was to utilize confocal microscopy for time- and space-resolved, 3D imaging of non-spherical colloids whose phases can be controlled by adding depletants and/or adjusting spatial temperature changes around a particular location. The research goal is to produce cubic colloidal structures, and study the dynamics of crystal nucleation and growth. ACE-T7 varied the size of the depletant in different samples with the goal of seeing the effect on crystallization. The imaging goal was to observe crystallites and resolve particle centroid positions with less than 20% error. Approach The ACE-T7 experiment used the Fluids Integrated Rack (FIR) and the Light Microscopy Module (LMM) with enhancements. ACE-T7 utilized two sample cartridges, each having three temperature-controlled capillaries for a total of six samples; each capillary volume has 50 mm length, 2.0 mm ID width, and 0.2 mm ID height, with automated mixing capabilities using magnetic stir bars embedded in the capillaries. Each sample volume was about 20 μl. Each cartridge could be heated or cooled uniformly via Peltier temperature control. The concentrations of hollow silica microcubes and silica nanoparticle depletants are varied to study the effect that each of these parameters have on the dynamics of crystal nucleation and growth in microgravity. In total, six capillaries are prepared, numbered C1-C6. In capillaries C1-C4, the depletant concentration is kept constant at a concentration that produces cubic crystals in a timely manner on Earth (within 1 hour), while the concentration of hollow silica cubes is varied. In capillaries C5 and C6, the depletant concentration is increased and two different concentration of hollow silica cubes are used. After homogenization of each sample using the magnetic stirrer, the particles are left undisturbed to crystallize. Samples were preliminarily observed with a 2.5X objective, followed by measurements with 10X, 63X (air), 63X (oil), and 100X (oil) objectives. Hypothesis It is hypothesized that under certain conditions, the particles should self-organize into crystals with simple cubic symmetry, which is set by the size of the nano-size depletant. Increasing particle number density using a temperature gradient, i.e., thermophoresis, is expected to induce formation of crystallites. Three-dimensional structures that are impossible to create or reform on earth due to sedimentation issues (high density contrast between particles and fluid) should be observed in microgravity. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits Future space exploration may use self-assembly and self-replication to make materials and devices that can repair themselves. Self-assembly and evolutionarily optimized functional units are key to long-duration space voyages which will require use self-assembly and self-replication to make materials and devices that can repair themselves. This research will enable design and development of functional colloidal structures for new devices for chemical energy, communication, and photonics, including photonic materials to control and manipulate light. Such materials might include photonic crystals with programmed distributions of defects. Optical technology utilizing such materials may offer intriguing solutions to unavoidable heat generation and bandwidth limitations facing the computer industry. The beginning of this process is understanding the basic interactions between micro- and nanoscale particles, and how to control them using external sources such as temperature and light. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 5.02 TB PSI-86Version 4 Observation and Analysis of Smectic Islands in Space(OASIS) Investigation Submitted Date: 30-Sep-2018 Initial Release Date: 30-Sep-2018 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/hq75-xv78 Research Area: Complex Fluids - Soft Matter License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 09-01-2013 Investigation End Date 09-30-2018 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives OASIS studies the unique behavior of liquid crystals in microgravity, including their overall motion and the merging of crystal layers known as smectic islands. Liquid crystals are used for display screens in televisions and clocks, and they also occur in soaps and in cell membranes. The experiment allows detailed studies of the behavior of these structures, and how microgravity affects their unique ability to act like both a liquid and a solid crystal. The specific research objectives are: -To exploit the unique characteristics of freely suspended liquid crystals in a microgravity environment to advance the understanding of fluid state physics. -Study basic 2D hydrodynamics/fluid physics, probe droplet/island diffusion, hydrodynamic interactions, and droplet/island coalescence Approach The OASIS experiment’s goal is to better understand the unique behavior of liquid crystals in microgravity. OASIS observes the various aspects of liquid crystals behavior in microgravity such as overall fluid motion, diffusion (the movement of particles from an area of high concentration to low concentration) and the merging of liquid crystal film layers called islands, Fundamental studies of complex fluid physics behavior will be accomplished in two dimensional fluids using freely suspended liquid crystals. The impact of the research is to advance the understanding of two-dimensional system physics of complex fluids. Space helmets could use ferroelectric liquid crystal micro-displays. It could advance the understanding of well aligned very high speed electro-optic devices. Hypothesis In a microgravity environment, freely suspended smectic liquid crystal (FSLC) films will exhibit unique hydrodynamic and interfacial behaviors, such as reduced coarsening rates of island emulsions, enhanced 2D thermocapillarity effects, and distinct equilibrium spatial organization of islands, due to the absence of gravitational forces, convection, and sedimentation, enabling precise tests of theoretical models of 2D hydrodynamics and phase behavior. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits Future space helmets may use certain types of liquid crystals in small display screens directly applied to the face shield where astronauts can easily view them. Understanding how liquid crystals behave in microgravity helps researchers to design liquid crystal displays (LCDs) that can perform better in space. Liquid crystals can flow like a liquid, but contain molecules that are arranged in a specific pattern, just like a crystal. Greater understanding of the physics behind these structures could lead to improved liquid crystal display devices, including devices with improved color contrast and response times. It could also advance research in high-speed electro-optic devices used to control a light beam. Contact(s) Joseph Maclennanemail,Noel A. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 728.45 GB PSI-23Version 4 Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments-Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames(ACME s-Flame) Investigation Submitted Date: 05-Apr-2018 Initial Release Date: 05-Apr-2018 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/k57n-p030 Research Area: Combustion Science SubResearch Area: Flames of gaseous fuels License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Proposal Title Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 02-05-2015 Investigation End Date 11-24-2019 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives A series of experiments is proposed with the following specific objectives, in both soot-free and sooty flames, to compare with detailed computational simulation to assess transport properties and detailed chemical kinetics (including chemiluminescence): Objective A. Measure and characterize the transient structure (such as temperature and species distribution) of diffusion flames established at initially non-steady, spherical flame structures for mixtures of different H2/CH4/diluent ratios (soot-free) and different C2H4/diluent ratios (sooty), for different flow rates. Objective B. Determine the quasi-steady convective/chemical-kinetic extinction limits (low system Damköhler numbers) and radiative/chemical-kinetic extinction limits (high system Damköhler numbers) for mixtures of different H2/CH4/diluent ratios (soot-free) and different C2H4/diluent ratios (sooty). Objective C. Determine the existence (for different Zeldovich number, Ze), onset (as a function Da), and nature (i.e. mode, frequency, amplitude) of pulsating instabilities theoretically predicted to occur in transient spherical diffusion flames using fuel/diluent mixtures that are above a critical Lewis number. Approach A series of experiments is proposed in which mixtures of various gaseous fuels and diluents will be issued into an oxidizing environment through a spherical porous burner and ignited to obtain, nominally, a spherical, one-dimensional stabilized flame. Synchronized measurements are to be made including spectrally resolved images, flame and burner temperatures, radiative flux measurements, and system operating conditions (including reactant flow rates, ambient temperatures, pressures and acceleration levels, etc.). These data are to be used for comparisons of flame behavior and structure with detailed numerical simulations of the flames. Conventional gaseous fuels including hydrogen, methane, and ethylene will be used. Hydrogen is the simplest fuel and its reaction mechanism is also reasonably established. Methane is the simplest hydrocarbon and extensive studies have been conducted on its combustion chemistry. Ethylene is a typical sooty fuel and is also an important intermediate for the oxidation of higher hydrocarbons. Diluents mixed with fuel are to include nitrogen and helium to adjust mixture diffusivities, and carbon dioxide to influence flame radiation characteristics. Hypothesis The transient numerical simulation of spherical flames developed as part of this program includes detailed chemistry and transport models, especially radiation mechanisms. Each description of the flames obtained from the experiment, including measurements of aspects of the flame structure, growth or flame front velocities, and the specific test conditions where steady state flames, flame extinctions, flame front instabilities, soot suppression limits, etc., comprise a rigorous test of the detailed model. Together they provide a measure of the comprehensiveness of the chemical kinetic and transport models. The numerical simulation is also being used as a predictive tool to develop the science requirements for this experiment, especially the collection of test conditions and most aspects of the measurement systems. Due to time and g-jitter limitations, little of the planned test matrix can be adequately explored in the ground based test facilities, and the flight experiment definition will rely on the best effort in the modeling work. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits The impact of this work consists of both practical and fundamental aspects. Practically, with diffusion flame burning as the basis in many combustion engines and devices, understanding the underlying dynamics and chemistry of diffusion flames is important in improving performance in terms of power, efficiency, pollutant emissions, and reliability. Fundamentally, the unique buoyancy-free environment offered by microgravity affords simple aerodynamic flow fields to acquire diffusion flame data of high fidelity, with the prospect of understanding unit thermochemical processes as well as quantifying the associated physico-chemical parameters. impacts: The impact of this work consists of both practical and fundamental aspects. Practically, with diffusion flame burning as the basis in many combustion engines and devices, understanding the underlying dynamics and chemistry of diffusion flames is important in improving performance in terms of power, efficiency, pollutant emissions, and reliability. Fundamentally, the unique buoyancy-free environment offered by microgravity affords simple aerodynamic flow fields to acquire diffusion flame data of high fidelity, with the prospect of understanding unit thermochemical processes as well as quantifying the associated physico-chemical parameters.

detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 51.23 GB PSI-44Version 6 Coarsening in Solid-Liquid Mixtures(CSLM) Investigation Submitted Date: 31-Aug-2017 Initial Release Date: 31-Aug-2017 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/p5kb-p861 Research Area: Materials Science SubResearch Area: Solidification, Coarsening License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform Space Shuttle Investigation Start Date 28-Sep-2010 Investigation End Date 31-Aug-2017 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NASA Center Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) Objectives The primary objective of the microgravity experiment was to measure the temporal evolution of the average size-scale of a solid-liquid mixture during solidification. Specifically, the objective was to measure the average intercept length and the average section area of the solid particles at various times and for various volume fractions of solid. Using this data the amplitude of the temporal power law for the average section area. and intercept length was to be determined. Once the amplitude of the temporal power law is known, the objective is to compare the result to the theoretical predictions on the dependence of the amplitude of the power law on the volume fraction of the coarsening phase. The objective was also to determine the steady-state particle size distribution by measuring the distribution of section area of of the particles in a plane and the intercept length distribution. Approach The sample holder in the Sample Processing Unit (SPU) contained four Lead-Tin samples of 12 mm diameter and 6 mm thickness for various volume fractions of Tin. The SPU heated the samples up to 185 degree C in less than 9.5 min, held the temperature for a predetermined time at 185 ± 0.1 degree C ranging from 0.25 to 48hrs (coarsening phase). The heating system consists of two disc resistance heaters and one ring heater to insure uniform heating with four resistance temperature devices (RTD) installed mid-way between the discs 1 to measure temperature of the samples. Subsequent to the predetermined coarsening time the samples were quenched using pressurized air to nearly room temperature in approximately 1 minute. Once the samples were returned to earth they were sectioned and the measurements of particle size and distribution was performed. Hypothesis The theory of coarsening has been described by Lifshitz, Slyozov and Wagner (LSW) predicts that for the limit of zero volume fraction particles grow with time as the cube root of the average radius, and the particle size distribution becomes independent of time. The investigation hypothesizes that finding a system which satisfies all the constraints of LSW theory such as particles are infinitely separated and there is no diffusional interaction between them is prohibitive for ground-based laboratory condition due to effects of particle sedimentation and buoyancy-induced convection and therefore the theory can only be tested by performing experiments in a microgravity environment. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits The importance of coarsening from a commercial perspective arises from the major effect that coarsening has on the properties of materials, for example materials can become stronger while undergoing coarsening. The CSLM experiment will assess the validity of the theory of coarsening that has been used to design materials. The result will be a more rational design of materials using a first-principles approach, reduced development cost for the production of new materials and better materials properties. Such a first-principles design of materials will enable NASA and industry to create materials in a rapid cost-efficient manner with the superior properties that are needed for space exploration. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 5.56 GB PSI-43Version 4 Coarsening in Solid-Liquid Mixtures-4(CSLM-4) Investigation Submitted Date: 31-Aug-2017 Initial Release Date: 31-Aug-2017 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/c02m-5s72 Research Area: Materials Science SubResearch Area: Solidification, Coarsening Related Investigation: PSI-44, PSI-40, PSI-41, PSI-42 License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 09-01-2016 Investigation End Date 08-31-2017 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives The objective is to study coarsening in solid-liquid mixtures at low volume fractions of solid. The topology and morphology of these dendritic mixtures will be determined using three-dimensional reconstructions and phase field simulations that employ these reconstructions as initial conditions will provide insights into the mechanisms of coarsening. These low volume fractions will enable the science team to examine coarsening of single or a few dendrites, something that is impossible on the ground. These studies will provide insights into the dynamics of morphological evolution of these systems and will point the way to the formulation of models of this technologically important coarsening process. Approach The CSLM-4 approach and hardware was essentially identical to the predecessor CSLM-3 investigations The solid volume fraction of the 4 Pb-Sn sample for CSLM-4 was 0.3. Isothermal holding times between 10 minutes and 15 hours were employed. After the requisite holding times the samples were quenched using pressurized gas. Upon receipt of the samples they were analyzed using three-dimensional reconstructions of the microstructure. The 3D reconstructions was used to determine the interfacial curvatures, the genus and the spatial distribution of curvature in the system. The experimentally measured structures were used to compare phase field simulations and experiment. Hypothesis The fundamental questions that this investigation attempts to answer are as follows: Does the Interface Shape Distribution (ISD) vary with position from the tip of the dendrite? If so, as is likely the case, does the ISD scale with time, as is usually the case during coarsening? How important is the spatial distribution of curvature in setting the evolution of the structure? How do diffusional interactions between the secondary, and perhaps tertiary, arms on different dendrites affect the evolution of the system? How does the ISD evolve when there are multiple dendrites in the system? Does scaling exist? Research Impacts/Earth Benefits Coarsening occurs on Earth during the processing of any metal alloy and thus the coarsening process affects a large spectrum of products from dental fillings to turbine blades. Since the properties of an alloy are linked to the size of the particles within the solid, coarsening can be used to strengthen materials. This is the case with the majority of aluminum alloys used commercially today. Conversely, if the coarsening process proceeds too long the material can weaken. This occurs in jet turbine blades and is one of the reasons why turbine blades must be replaced after a certain number of hours of service. This investigation will provide insights into the dynamics of dendritic morphological evolution and will point the way to the formulation of models of this technologically important coarsening process. Thus developing accurate models of the coarsening process and validating them using benchmark experimental data is central to creating a wide range of new materials encompassing those used in automobiles to those used in space applications. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 274.36 GB PSI-90Version 3 Packed Bed Reactor Experiment(PBRE) Investigation Submitted Date: 31-May-2017 Initial Release Date: 31-May-2017 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/cbnn-ym02 Research Area: Fluid Physics License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 03-01-2014 Investigation End Date 05-31-2017 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives The PBRE studies the behavior of gases and liquids when they flow simultaneously through a column filled with fixed porous media. The porous media or “packing” can be made of different shapes and materials and are used widely in chemical engineering as a means to enhance the contact between two immiscible fluid phases (e.g., liquid-gas, water-oil, etc.). Packed columns can serve as reactors, scrubbers, strippers, etc. in systems where efficient interphase contact is desired, both on Earth and in space. Approach The PBRE investigation employs an approach that combines theoretical modeling with rigorous experimental testing to achieve its objectives. Here's a breakdown of the key aspects: 1. Theoretical Modeling: Existing Models: PBRE builds upon existing models for pressure drop and flow regime transitions in packed bed reactors, particularly those developed by Motil et al. (2003) and Guo et al. (2004). Model Validation: The experiment focuses on validating these models, extending them to lower flow rates relevant to water recovery systems, and bridging them with other models. New Models: The data collected through PBRE is used to develop new models and scaling laws that accurately predict flow characteristics in 0-g and partial-g environments. 2. Experimental Setup and Procedures: Test Sections: PBRE utilizes two identical test sections, each a 60 cm long, 5 cm diameter cylindrical column. One section is packed with glass beads (wetting), the other with Teflon beads (non-wetting) to isolate surface tension effects. Fluid Flow: The experiment uses nitrogen and water as the gas and liquid phases, with a wide range of flow rates, from very low to high, to cover operational regimes. Instrumentation: A comprehensive suite of sensors is used to measure flow rates, temperatures, and pressures. The experiment also includes two high-speed video cameras to visualize flow patterns. Test Matrix: The investigation is organized into several test series (''Ops''), each focused on specific flow conditions and packing materials. Data Acquisition: The experiment meticulously collects data, with careful time-correlation of measurements to ensure accurate analysis. 3. Addressing Anomalies: Flow Rate Control: The team encountered anomalies with the GN2 flow rate and pressure fluctuations, leading to troubleshooting and adjustments in the experiment's setup and procedures. High-Speed Video: The cameras experienced limitations with operating at the desired frame rates, requiring modifications to data acquisition strategies. 4. Data Analysis: Model Validation: Data is analyzed to compare experimental results with model predictions, identifying any discrepancies and refining the models. New Model Development: The collected data is used to develop new models and scaling laws, aiming for greater accuracy and applicability in microgravity environments. 5. Data Organization: Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI): The PBRE team meticulously organizes the experimental data in PSI, a database for physical sciences data, to ensure accessibility and analysis. The PBRE investigation relies on a combination of theoretical modeling, rigorous experimental testing, and comprehensive data analysis to achieve its objectives. This approach is designed to contribute to a deeper understanding of the behavior of packed bed reactors in microgravity, leading to improved design tools and operational strategies for future space applications. 6. Dissemination of Results: The findings of the PBRE-2 investigations were disseminated through: Peer-reviewed publications: Publishing research papers in scientific journals to share the results with the broader scientific community. Presentations at conferences: Presenting the research findings at relevant scientific conferences and workshops. Reports and documentation: Preparing detailed reports and documentation of the experimental procedures, data analysis, and conclusions. Hypothesis It is hypothesized that the gravity plays a significant role in determining the flow characteristics (pressure drop, flow regime transitions, liquid holdup, and mass transfer) of gas-liquid flows through porous media. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits Water-recovery systems, fuel cells and other equipment on the International Space Station use packed bed reactors, but currently none are designed to handle both liquid and gas at the same time. With improved understanding of how packed bed two-phase flow works in microgravity, scientists are be able to design more efficient, lightweight thermal management and life support systems that use less energy, benefiting the Space Station and future lunar and Mars missions. Design rules for gas-liquid flows through packed columns are well developed on Earth (i.e., for normal gravity) but lacking for reduced or zero gravity. The Packed Bed Reactor Experiment seeks to fill this knowledge gap by studying the hydrodynamics of gas-liquid flows in zero gravity through packed columns. By understanding how gravity affects gas-liquid flows through packed columns (or packed beds, as they are known in the industry) better, more predictive correlations for pressure drops and flow regime maps can be developed with the proper gravity-dependent terms included. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 860.39 GB PSI-69Version 5 Flame Extinguishment Experiment(FLEX) Investigation Submitted Date: 31-Jul-2016 Initial Release Date: 31-Jul-2016 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/mbq8-0451 Research Area: Combustion Science SubResearch Area: Spacecraft Fire Safety License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Proposal Title Droplet Flame Extinguishment in Microgravity Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 08-01-2007 Investigation End Date 07-31-2016 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives The FLEX (Flame Extinguishment Experiment) investigation aims to map the flammability limits of liquid fuels in microgravity environments, measure the effectiveness of various gaseous fire suppressants such as CO2, He, and SF6, and develop reliable predictive models for combustion limits under reduced gravity conditions. The mission seeks to validate and improve simplified models by incorporating detailed chemical reactions, heat transfer, and material movement, using both space-based data and extensive ground-based tests. Key flight experiment goals include obtaining high-resolution measurements of droplet burning rates, flame extinction behavior, heat radiation, soot levels, and temperature profiles, while systematically analyzing the effects of different ambient conditions and suppressant concentrations. These investigations are essential for advancing the fundamental understanding of combustion processes in microgravity and enhancing fire safety protocols for future space missions. Approach The FLEX experiments involve igniting and observing the burning behavior of relatively large droplets. A primary objective of the experiments is to determine the Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) as a function of ambient pressure and determine how the presence of a suppressant influences the LOI . The basic outline of the procedure to construct this diagram is as follows: 1. Select the test pressure (0.5 − 1.5 atm) for the LOI tests. 2. Select a smaller droplet size (≈ 3 mm) 3. Select an ambient oxygen mole fraction that, based on ground-based testing, will support droplets burning to completion (as opposed to extinguishing at a finite droplet size). 4. Perform a droplet combustion test. 5. Increase the droplet size or repeat the test (if finite extinction diameter at flame extinction observed). 6. Continue steps 4 and 5 until flame exists for only a short time after ignition (radiative extinction). 7. Continue steps 4 thru 6 at a decreased ambient oxygen mole fraction. 8. Continue step 7 to an ambient oxygen mole fraction where the droplet does not ignite. There were ambient conditions where the extinction droplet sizes at all ambient oxygen mole fractions were too small to either be observed or measured with the available diagnostics. In this case, the determination of the LOI is similar, but more iterative. Instead of observing flame extinction, however, the procedure involved an iterative sequence of tests (burn to completion followed by a no ignition test) with progressively smaller increments in ambient oxygen mole fraction to determine the LOI . For the slow flow tests (in the flight experiment), the configuration of the flight hardware did not allow for adequate diagnostics over the entire test for a droplet in a uniform, steady convective flow. In these tests, the procedure will be to duplicate tests above which yield finite-sized extinction droplet diameters. Near the end of the tests, prior to flame extinction, the droplet will be subjected to a small, sub-buoyant, convective flow (imparted by translating the droplet at a slow, uniform speed). The goal of the experiment is then to see how the presence of this flow influences the extinction process. Note, a large number of the tests involve free droplets (as opposed to fiber-supported droplets) and a number of these tests will have droplets with a slow drift velocity. Data gathered from these tests to examine the influences of a small, sub-buoyant flow on both the burning and extinction process. Hypothesis The primary hypothesis of the FLEX mission is that microgravity conditions fundamentally alter the combustion and extinction characteristics of liquid fuel droplets due to changes in species and energy transport dynamics, radiative heat loss, and chemical kinetics. Specifically, the hypothesis posits that the lack of buoyant convection in microgravity will lead to significant differences in the flammability limits and suppression efficacy of various fire suppressant agents compared to normal gravity conditions. This hypothesis underpins the design of the FLEX experiments, which aim to map flammability boundaries, quantify suppressant efficacy, and develop predictive models to improve fire safety in space environments. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits The research impacts and Earth benefits of the FLEX mission are significant and multifaceted. By enhancing our understanding of microgravity combustion, the mission directly contributes to improved fire safety protocols for future space missions, ensuring the safety of crew members in environments where traditional fire suppression methods may be ineffective. On Earth, the insights gained from these experiments have the potential to advance fire safety in confined and reduced-gravity environments, such as submarines or high-altitude aircraft. The mission's findings on the effectiveness of various fire suppressants, including CO2, He, and SF6, in microgravity can lead to the development of more efficient and less harmful fire suppression systems, reducing the risk of toxic byproducts during fire events. Additionally, the study of ''cool flames'' and low-temperature combustion processes observed in microgravity can inform the design of advanced combustion engines, leading to improved fuel efficiency and reduced emissions in automotive and industrial applications. Overall, the FLEX mission's contributions to combustion science have the potential to enhance both space exploration safety and terrestrial fire safety technologies. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 43.60 MB PSI-40Version 4 Coarsening in Solid Liquid Mixtures-2(CSLM-2) Investigation Submitted Date: 30-Sep-2014 Initial Release Date: 30-Sep-2014 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/mfaa-wk03 Research Area: Materials Science SubResearch Area: Solidification, Coarsening License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform ISS Investigation Start Date 01-May-2000 Investigation End Date 30-Sep-2014 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NASA Center Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) Objectives The objective of the CSLM-2 investigation was essentially the same as the original CSLM investigation with the addition of higher solid volume percent samples requiring longer times to reach steady state coarsening rates. Approach The CSLM-2 approach and hardware was identical to the predecessor CSLM investigation. The solid volume fraction of the 4 samples for CSLM-2 were 0.3. 0.5, 0.7, and 0.8. Hypothesis The theory of coarsening has been described by Lifshitz, Slyozov and Wagner (LSW) predicts that for the limit of zero volume fraction particles grow with time as the cube root of the average radius, and the particle size distribution becomes independent of time. The investigation hypothesizes that finding a system which satisfies all the constraints of LSW theory such as particles are infinitely separated and there is no diffusional interaction between them is prohibitive for ground-based laboratory condition due to effects of particle sedimentation and buoyancy-induced convection and therefore the theory can only be tested by performing experiments in a microgravity environment, For CSLM-2 it is hypothesized that for large volume fraction solid samples the transient coarsening process will be longer and steady state will be reached much later compared to low volume fraction solid particles. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits Coarsening occurs on Earth during the processing of any metal alloy and thus the coarsening process affects a large spectrum of products from dental fillings to turbine blades. Since the properties of an alloy are linked to the size of the particles within the solid, coarsening can be used to strengthen materials. This is the case with the majority of aluminum alloys used commercially today. Conversely, if the coarsening process proceeds too long the material can weaken. This occurs in jet turbine blades and is one of the reasons why turbine blades must be replaced after a certain number of hours of service. Thus developing accurate models of the coarsening process is central to creating a wide range of new materials encompassing those used in automobiles to those used in space applications. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 3.86 GB PSI-41Version 5 Coarsening in Solid-Liquid Mixtures-2 Reflight(CSLM-2R) Investigation Submitted Date: 30-Sep-2014 Initial Release Date: 30-Sep-2014 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/4h4p-e750 Research Area: Materials Science SubResearch Area: Solidification, Coarsening License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform ISS Investigation Start Date 01-Oct-2007 Investigation End Date 30-Sep-2014 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NASA Center Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) Objectives The objective of the CSLM-2R investigation was essentially the same as the original CSLM investigation with the focus on lower solid volume percent samples. Approach The CSLM-2R approach and hardware was identical to the predecessor CSLM-2 investigation. The solid volume fraction of the 4 samples for CSLM-2R were 0.05. 0.10, 0.15, and 0.20 and the coarsening times ranged from 1.6 to 48 hours. Hypothesis The theory of coarsening has been described by Lifshitz, Slyozov and Wagner (LSW) predicts that for the limit of zero volume fraction particles grow with time as the cube root of the average radius, and the particle size distribution becomes independent of time. The investigation hypothesizes that finding a system which satisfies all the constraints of LSW theory such as particles are infinitely separated and there is no diffusional interaction between them is prohibitive for ground-based laboratory condition due to effects of particle sedimentation and buoyancy-induced convection and therefore the theory can only be tested by performing experiments in a microgravity environment. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits Coarsening occurs on Earth during the processing of any metal alloy and thus the coarsening process affects a large spectrum of products from dental fillings to turbine blades. Since the properties of an alloy are linked to the size of the particles within the solid, coarsening can be used to strengthen materials. This is the case with the majority of aluminum alloys used commercially today. Conversely, if the coarsening process proceeds too long the material can weaken. This occurs in jet turbine blades and is one of the reasons why turbine blades must be replaced after a certain number of hours of service. Thus developing accurate models of the coarsening process is central to creating a wide range of new materials encompassing those used in automobiles to those used in space applications. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 27.26 GB PSI-42Version 4 Coarsening in Solid-Liquid Mixtures(CSLM-3) Investigation Submitted Date: 04-Mar-2014 Initial Release Date: 04-Mar-2014 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/fsys-gt59 Research Area: Materials Science SubResearch Area: Solidification Related Investigation: PSI-44, PSI-40, PSI-41, PSI-43 License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Proposal Title Coarsening of Dendritic Solid-Liquid Mixtures Flight Platform International Space Station Investigation Start Date 09-28-2010 Investigation End Date 03-04-2014 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NASA Center Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) Objectives The objective of this investigation was to study dendritic coarsening in solid-liquid mixtures at low volume fractions of solid. Specific interest was in examining dendritic structure close to the dendrite tip. Additional objectives included measuring the rate at which topological singularities occur when a secondary dendrite arm separates from the main dendrite stem or when two arms fuse together. Approach The CSLM-3 approach and hardware was essentially identical to the predecessor CSLM and CSLM-2 investigations. The solid volume fraction of the 4 Pb-Sn samples for CSLM-3 were 0.1, 0.2, 0.3 and 0.4. Isothermal holding times between 10 minutes and 48 hours were employed. After the requisite holding times the samples were quenched using pressurized gas. Upon receipt of the samples they were analyzed using three-dimensional reconstructions of the microstructure. The 3D reconstructions was used to determine the interfacial curvatures, the genus and the spatial distribution of curvature in the system. The experimentally measured structures were used to compare phase field simulations and experiment. Hypothesis The fundamental questions that this investigation attempts to answer are as follows: Does the Interface Shape Distribution (ISD) vary with position from the tip of the dendrite? If so, as is likely the case, does the ISD scale with time, as is usually the case during coarsening? How important is the spatial distribution of curvature in setting the evolution of the structure? How do diffusional interactions between the secondary, and perhaps tertiary, arms on different dendrites affect the evolution of the system? How does the ISD evolve when there are multiple dendrites in the system? Does scaling exist? Research Impacts/Earth Benefits Coarsening occurs on Earth during the processing of any metal alloy and thus the coarsening process affects a large spectrum of products from dental fillings to turbine blades. Since the properties of an alloy are linked to the size of the particles within the solid, coarsening can be used to strengthen materials. This is the case with the majority of aluminum alloys used commercially today. Conversely, if the coarsening process proceeds too long the material can weaken. This occurs in jet turbine blades and is one of the reasons why turbine blades must be replaced after a certain number of hours of service. This investigation will provide insights into the dynamics of dendritic morphological evolution and will point the way to the formulation of models of this technologically important coarsening process. Thus developing accurate models of the coarsening process and validating them using benchmark experimental data is central to creating a wide range of new materials encompassing those used in automobiles to those used in space applications. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 25.94 GB PSI-27Version 4 Binary Colloidal Alloy Test - 3(BCAT-3) Investigation Submitted Date: 31-Dec-2013 Initial Release Date: 31-Dec-2013 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/1tss-tk09 Research Area: Complex Fluids - Soft Matter SubResearch Area: Colloids Related Investigation: PSI-28, PSI-29, PSI-30 License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Proposal Title Dynamics and Structure in Colloidal Suspensions Far from Equilibrium Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 11-01-2003 Investigation End Date 10-31-2007 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives The BCAT-3 investigation aimed to exploit the long range ordered structures formed using the self-assembly of colloidal particles and demonstrate the use of colloid engineering to synthesize new materials with novel properties. The goal was to use a mixture of two different materials or binary alloys to greatly increase the flexibility of the resultant colloidal structures and qualitatively study the phase behavior and crystallization properties of these binary alloys. In addition, the investigation proposed to study the properties of mixtures of colloids and polymers where the addition of the polymer induces weak attractive interactions between the colloidal particles by the depletion mechanism, leading to a rich phase behavior for the colloidal particles. Approach BCAT-3 is implemented in a bench-top investigation which is set up on the Maintenance Work Area (MWA) on ISS. The samples are contained within a Fluids Module (FM) which held 10 samples in couvettes in individual wells. The ten samples in BCAT-3 were selected as part of three separate experiments examining different physical processes: critical point, binary alloys, and surface crystallization. The samples were manually homogenized using a stir-bar (a Teflon coated mixing magnet) inside each couvette. Samples are mixed, examined and imaged using a digital EarthKAM camera, to document the separation of colloid and liquid components and the formation of colloidal crystals over time. Hypothesis Colloidal particles would exhibit behaviors analogous to atoms, allowing the study of phase transitions, crystallization, and self-organization without the interference of sedimentation and convection present on Earth. This investigation hypothesizes that by taking advantage of microgravity and avoiding sedimentation binary alloys with very different materials and sizes and by addition of polymers particles to induce attractive forces can lead to exciting and promising form of colloidal engineering to synthesize a new class of materials. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits Self-assembly of micron and submicron colloidal particles into highly ordered three-dimensional structures offers an alternative to traditional lithographic techniques, which are often limited to surface-level patterning. These ordered arrays of particles can exhibit novel optical properties, such as redirecting light via diffraction or altering local photon densities, enabling the creation of advanced optical filters, switches, and sensors. Moreover, these structures can serve as templates for macroporous materials, which have diverse chemical applications, including catalysis, separation media, and biomaterials. Precision macroporous ceramics and polymers can also be used as lightweight insulators, chromatographic materials, and catalytic supports, offering transformative solutions across industries such as energy, manufacturing, and medicine. detail_text: menu_open Search Bar infoDescription table_viewExperimental Table table_viewModeling Table menu_bookRead Me palletHardware imageRepresentative Images/Videos sim_card_downloadData files and documents menu_bookPublications view_timelineVersion History Physical Sciences InformaticsHomeData & Tools Contact Us 14.28 GB PSI-28Version 4 Binodal Colloidal Aggregation Test - 4(BCAT-4) Investigation Submitted Date: 31-Dec-2013 Initial Release Date: 31-Dec-2013 notifications share DOI: 10.60555/kxn0-p943 Research Area: Complex Fluids - Soft Matter SubResearch Area: Colloids Related Investigation: PSI-27, PSI-29, PSI-30 License: CC0-1.0 Cite this Investigation info Description Project Project Type Microgravity Investigation Flight Platform International Space Station (ISS) Investigation Start Date 12-18-2007 Investigation End Date 12-31-2013 Sponsoring Agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NASA Center Glenn Research Center (GRC) Objectives The goal of the BCAT investigations is to further investigate critical, fundamental problems in colloid science and evolve the field of ‘colloid engineering’, which creates materials with novel properties using colloidal particles as precursors. The BCAT-4 investigation had two primary objectives corresponding to specific samples: Critical Point (BCAT-3-4-CP): Depending on their relative distances and energies with respect one another, atoms and molecules organize themselves to form gases, liquids, or solids. By varying the concentrations of the microscale spheres, this experiment studied the critical point of these systems where gases and liquids no longer exist as separate entities and a new state of matter forms when one reaches a critical point. Polydispersion (BCAT-4-Poly): BCAT-4-Poly will use model hard-spheres (suspended in a liquid that makes them transparent) to explore pure and seeded colloidal crystal nucleation and the effects of polydispersity, providing insight into how to understand and control the processes used by nature to bring order out of disorder. Approach BCAT is implemented in a bench-top investigation which is set up on the Maintanence Work Area (MWA) on ISS. The first set of samples was composed of mixtures of colloids and polymers near their liquid-gas critical point. The second set consisted of spherical colloidal particles with effective volume fractions resulting in an amorphous or glassy phase in normal gravity. The samples are contained within a Fluids Module (FM) which held 10 samples in couvettes in individual wells. The samples were manually homogenized using a stirbar (a teflon coated mixing magnet) inside each couvette. Samples are mixed, examined and imaged using a digital EarthKAM camera to document the separation of colloid and liquid components and the formation of colloidal crystals over time. Hypothesis Colloidal particles would exhibit behaviors analogous to atoms, allowing the study of phase transitions, crystallization, and self-organization without the interference of sedimentation and convection present on Earth. This investigation hypothesizes that by taking advantage of microgravity and avoiding sedimentation binary alloys with very different materials and sizes and by addition of polymers particles to induce attractive forces can lead to exciting and promising form of colloidal engineering to synthesize a new class of materials. Research Impacts/Earth Benefits The findings of BCAT-4 can directly contribute to the development of advanced materials for use in space missions, such as lightweight and durable composites for spacecraft or self-assembling structures for space habitats. Additionally, understanding colloidal behavior aids in the optimization of life support systems, such as those used for water recycling and air purification, which are vital for sustaining long-duration missions to destinations like Mars. On Earth, the results of BCAT-4 have practical applications across multiple industries, including consumer goods, medicine, and manufacturing. For instance, the study of colloidal stability and crystallization informs the design of more stable food products, cosmetics, and pharmaceutical formulations. The findings also enhance industrial processes like 3D printing, where precise control of particle interactions is crucial for producing high-quality materials. Furthermore, BCAT-4 contributes to advancements in medicine by improving drug delivery systems that rely on colloidal suspensions, ensuring more effective treatments. By expanding the understanding of fundamental physical processes, BCAT-4 drives innovation in material design and production, benefiting diverse sectors and improving everyday products and technologies.
